annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to use IPsec tunnel mode to encrypt network traffic between endpoints, or if you must use transport mode instead, to wrap it within an IP tunnel for additional protection. Most organisations get this right by accident when they deploy proper VPN gateways, then spend months wondering why they didn't just use tunnel mode from the start.

The control is refreshingly straightforward because there's basically one right answer here, though you'd be shocked how often organisations skip this and then wonder why their supposedly "secure" tunnels are about as useful as a chocolate teapot.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that IPsec connections automatically refresh their encryption keys at least every four hours to limit the window of time that a compromised key could be exploited. annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to configure your IPsec security associations (SAs) to re-key every four hours or less, because apparently the cryptographic keys protecting your tunnels shouldn't be trusted any longer than your average afternoon meeting. The idea is sound though—shorter SA lifetimes reduce the window an attacker has to abuse a compromised key—so just bite the bullet and automate the re-keying rather than pretending you'll remember to do it manually.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must follow the Australian Signals Directorate's communications security policies and procedures for managing and operating high assurance cryptography systems. In practice, this means your organisation needs to actually read ASD's current HACE comms security policy and then prove you're doing what it says, which sounds simple until you discover nobody kept a copy and half your team thinks HACE is a typo.

annotations.ai_view: When transporting cryptographic equipment that contains keys, you must choose transport methods and security measures that match how sensitive or classified the keying material inside it is. In practice: get your classification right, use appropriate physical security (couriers, locked containers, the whole deal), and document the journey like it matters, because it does.

annotations.ai_view: You must create and maintain two types of network diagrams: high-level diagrams showing all entry points into your networks, and detailed diagrams identifying critical servers, valuable systems, and security devices. annotations.ai_view: Organizations must create and keep current detailed documentation describing their network architecture, components, and connections. annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to document your network—what's connected, how it's configured, who can access what—and actually keep that documentation current instead of letting it fossilize in some forgotten SharePoint folder while your infrastructure drifts into undocumented chaos. Yes, this means updating it when things change, which everyone swears they'll do and approximately nobody does, but it turns out you can't secure what you can't see, and you can't see what nobody bothered to write down.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to use technical measures—such as port security, MAC address filtering, or network access lists—to automatically block devices that aren't authorised to connect to your networks. It matters because unauthorised devices can introduce malware, create backdoors for attackers, or be used to intercept sensitive data, so preventing them from ever connecting in the first place is far more effective than detecting them later.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Implement technical controls to stop random laptops, printers, and that one guy's personal NAS from connecting to your network—basically, treat your network perimeter like a bouncer who actually checks IDs instead of just looking vaguely intimidating. This means 802.1X, MAC filtering, port security, or whatever your budget allows, because apparently "please don't plug in unauthorized devices" isn't sufficient guidance for humans. Yes, this will require you to actually know what's supposed to be on your network, which is somehow the hard part.

annotations.ai_view: Organisations must turn off Internet Protocol version 6 (the newer internet protocol) on network devices that support both IPv6 and the older IPv4 unless they actively need it. It exists because IPv6 dual-stack deployments create a lovely shadow network that most organisations neither fully understand nor adequately monitor, making it an ideal hiding spot for attackers who know that your security team is probably still focused on IPv4.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that you don't rely on VLANs alone to isolate traffic between networks of different security levels (such as separating a public-facing system from an internal classified network). VLANs can be misconfigured or bypassed, so they're insufficient security boundaries; you need additional network controls like firewalls and air-gapping to properly enforce separation between security domains. This prevents attackers who compromise one network segment from easily pivoting to a more sensitive environment.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: If you've got networks handling different security classifications or trust levels, VLANs alone won't cut it—you need actual network segmentation with proper isolation mechanisms, not just broadcast domain separation. So unless you've got routers, firewalls, or other Layer 3 controls doing the heavy lifting between those security domains, congratulations—you've achieved the cybersecurity equivalent of a beaded curtain.

annotations.ai_view: Network devices that manage virtual network segments (VLANs) must be administered only from your most secure and controlled network environment—typically a dedicated administrative network isolated from general user traffic. annotations.ai_view_snarky: Restrict VLAN management to your most hardened, trustworthy network segment—basically, treat it like the keys to the kingdom because misconfigured VLANs are how attackers sidestep your entire segmentation strategy. It's the kind of thing that sounds reasonable until you try explaining to someone why they can't manage the network from their laptop at their desk.

annotations.ai_view: Disable any physical network ports (like Ethernet or USB ports) on network devices that aren't actively in use, such as spare ports on switches or unused interfaces on routers. annotations.ai_view_snarky: Disable every physical port on your network devices that isn't actively carrying traffic, because apparently we need to spell out that unused ports are just sitting there waiting to become someone's unauthorized entry point. It's the networking equivalent of locking doors you're not using, and yet somehow it remains perpetually neglected at organisations that simultaneously spend six figures on their security infrastructure.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that network devices managing virtual network segments with different security classifications must use separate physical or logical connections rather than sharing a single trunk line. Isolating different security domains prevents accidental or intentional leakage of traffic between systems that shouldn't communicate, and reduces the blast radius if one segment is compromised. annotations.ai_view_snarky: Network devices can't use the same VLAN trunk to carry traffic between security domains—basically, you need separate physical pipes so data classified at different levels doesn't accidentally mingle on the same wire. It's less about the tags being inherently insecure and more about accepting that humans are fundamentally unreliable.

annotations.ai_view: Organisations must keep public wireless networks (like guest Wi-Fi) completely separate from their internal networks and systems where sensitive data or operations reside. annotations.ai_view_snarky: Isolate your public WiFi network from your internal systems using network segmentation—because apparently we still need to tell organisations that guest networks shouldn't touch corporate infrastructure. It's network hygiene 101, yet you'd be shocked how many organisations treat this like a nice-to-have suggestion.

annotations.ai_view: Use firewalls or proxies that understand video conferencing and IP telephony protocols when these types of traffic pass through your network gateways, rather than relying on generic firewalls that treat them as ordinary data. annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to deploy firewalls or proxies that actually understand video conferencing and VoIP protocols instead of just hoping your generic packet inspector won't obliterate the call quality while pretending to inspect it. Most organisations skip this, discover their Teams calls sound like they're being routed through a potato, and then frantically retrofit awareness rules at 2 AM on a Sunday.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to use secure real-time transport protocol (SRTP) or equivalent encryption when conducting video conferences and IP phone calls, ensuring voice and video data cannot be intercepted or eavesdropped on in transit. Enable crypto on your conferencing platform before someone records your strategy meeting and posts it somewhere unfortunate.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that when your organisation sets up video calls and phone calls over the internet, they must use a secure protocol to establish the connection—essentially a locked handshake that prevents attackers from intercepting, hijacking, or eavesdropping on these communications. Yes, this means TLS encryption on the signalling layer, and no, adding "secure" to your config file doesn't automatically make it so.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to keep video conferencing and IP telephony traffic separate from your general data network using either physical separation (different network cables and equipment) or logical separation (different virtual networks or dedicated channels). In practice, you'll find most organisations ignore this until someone in executive leadership experiences a dropped call, then suddenly separation becomes urgent.

annotations.ai_view: Email servers must be configured to only send and receive emails for their own domains—they cannot act as a relay for arbitrary emails from unknown external sources. annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must direct all email traffic through centralised gateways rather than allowing direct connections to external email servers, ensuring a single point where security controls can inspect, filter, and log messages. annotations.ai_view: If your organisation uses backup or alternative email systems, keep them updated with the same security patches, configurations, and protections as your primary email gateway—otherwise attackers could exploit neglected systems as a backdoor into your network. annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to route all incoming and outgoing emails through centralised gateways using authenticated and encrypted connections, rather than allowing direct point-to-point email transmission. annotations.ai_view: Email servers must automatically attempt to encrypt connections when sending or receiving email over the internet, even if the receiving server doesn't explicitly request it. It's the bare minimum that should have been default in 1995, yet here we are.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to publish Sender Policy Framework (SPF) records that list which mail servers are allowed to send emails on behalf of your organisation's domains. annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to publish SPF records that tell the world which mail servers are actually allowed to send email from your domain—because apparently letting literally anyone forge your sender address was too convenient to pass up without explicit documentation. annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must create and keep up-to-date a policy and plan that clearly defines how to detect, respond to, and recover from security breaches and incidents. Update it occasionally so it doesn't become the 2019 document everyone ignores while your SIEM quietly fills up with noise.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that security-important events from Windows systems—such as login attempts, permission changes, and security policy modifications—are collected and stored in a central location rather than left only on individual machines. annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to send Windows security events to a central logging system instead of letting them rot on individual machines where nobody will ever look at them. The whole point is that when something goes wrong, you want evidence waiting in one searchable place rather than scrambled across a hundred workstations that have already been reformatted.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires your systems to record six key pieces of information whenever an event occurs: when it happened, who or what caused it, which files were involved, what actually occurred, a description of the event, and which device was affected. annotations.ai_view_snarky: Capture seven specific data points every time something happens on your system: when, who did it, what file they touched, what actually occurred, which box it happened on, and describe it in English rather than interpretable gobbledygook—basically, log events in a way that would survive five minutes of scrutiny from someone who isn't the person who set up the logging. annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must create and keep current a policy that sets out how multifunction devices (printers, copiers, scanners, faxes) can be used safely and securely. annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need a documented policy governing multifunction device usage—you know, those ancient fax-scanner-printer hybrids that somehow still exist in every office despite being security nightmares waiting to happen. Nobody reads it and half your staff will print sensitive documents to the wrong tray regardless, but having this policy means you can at least point to *something* when an auditor asks why your MFD was hemorrhaging unencrypted documents to random people's email.

annotations.ai_view: Don't use multifunction devices (like photocopiers with scanning features) to handle documents classified higher than the security level of the network they're connected to, as this could expose sensitive information through the device's storage or network connections. annotations.ai_view: Multifunction devices (such as printers and scanners) must use the same strength of authentication—passwords, passphrases, or other login protections—as the computers they're connected to on the network. annotations.ai_view_snarky: Multifunction devices—those temperamental boxes that print, scan, and mysteriously decide to become network bridges whenever they feel like it—need the same authentication strength as your actual workstations. Turns out MFDs can be compromised just like any other network device, which is apparently news to roughly 87% of organisations.

annotations.ai_view: When you connect the same peripheral device (like a printer or external drive) to multiple systems, you must use a switch that has been independently tested and certified to ensure it properly isolates data between systems. It's the control equivalent of telling people to drive safely while handing them the keys to a shared car with no brakes—technically compliant, practically optimistic.

annotations.ai_view: You must involve the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) before adding or changing any connections to cross-domain solutions (systems that handle data at different security classifications), and you must follow any guidance they provide. Basically: consult first, implement second, regret never.

annotations.ai_view: Personnel must receive training on the secure use of cross‑domain solutions (CDSs) before being granted access, ensuring they understand the controls and procedures.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Train your humans on the CDS before they touch it—because untrained users are the fastest way to turn a controlled interface into a data leak.

annotations.ai_view: System administrators managing gateways must have only the specific access permissions they need to do their jobs, with unnecessary privileges removed. annotations.ai_view_snarky: Gateway admins get exactly the access they need to do their job and nothing more—which sounds obvious until you discover someone has Domain Admin rights because "it's easier" and has been running production changes via RDP since 2019. This is your least-privilege enforcement checkpoint: document what each gateway admin actually does, strip away everything else, and audit it quarterly because privilege creep is basically entropy in a lab coat.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must ensure that anyone managing gateways receives formal training covering how to operate and configure them correctly. This matters because gateways control network traffic between your systems and the outside world—misconfigured or poorly managed gateways create openings for attackers to breach your network, and skilled administrators significantly reduce this risk through proper setup, monitoring, and maintenance.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your gateway admins need formal training on how to actually operate and manage the gateway systems they're responsible for—not the five-minute hallway conversation they currently received. Yes, this means documented training programmes and verifiable completion, because apparently we can't assume someone knows what they're doing just because they have root access to the thing sitting between your network and the internet. It matters because a gateway run by someone who doesn't understand it is basically a very expensive, very dangerous door that doesn't know when to lock.

annotations.ai_view: Gateway system administrators who manage connections to classified Australian networks (Australian Eyes Only or Releasable To) must be Australian nationals. annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your gateway admins touching Australian Eyes Only or Releasable To networks need to be Australian nationals—because apparently citizenship is the credential that stops foreign intelligence services better than, say, actually monitoring what those admins do. Yes, you'll need to verify this before they get access and probably maintain documentation proving it, because when the auditor arrives, your sheepish "we think Dave is Australian" isn't going to cut it.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that no single gateway administrator has complete authority over all critical administrative tasks—duties must be divided among multiple people so that actions like approving changes, implementing them, and auditing them involve different individuals. annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to split gateway admin duties so no single person can both authorize changes and implement them—because apparently we've learned that giving one admin total control over your network's front door is a recipe for disaster, whether through negligence, malice, or just a really bad day. In practice, this means your gateway admins need oversight, approval workflows, and ideally some version of four-eyes-principle for anything that touches firewall rules, access controls, or authentication mechanisms. Yes, this creates friction. Yes, everyone will complain. Yes, it's still the only thing preventing someone from quietly creating a backdoor during their exit interview.

annotations.ai_view: When your organisation uses gateways to access other networks, users must authenticate directly to those networks rather than relying solely on gateway authentication. annotations.ai_view_snarky: Yes, users need to actually authenticate when they hop through your gateway to access other networks—radical concept, I know. This means no "just trust the gateway" nonsense or assuming that because someone got past your perimeter they automatically get a free pass to everything behind door number two. Implement separate authentication at the gateway layer itself, because apparently relying on a single security checkpoint is the information security equivalent of having one lock on your front door and assuming it protects your safe deposit box in the back bedroom.

annotations.ai_view: When your organisation connects to other networks through gateways (such as firewalls or proxy servers), those gateways themselves must prove their identity to the networks they're accessing, using credentials or authentication mechanisms. This prevents attackers from impersonating your gateway or intercepting traffic, and ensures your organisation's network traffic is routed through legitimate, verified connection points rather than compromised intermediaries. It's a critical layer of protection when reaching beyond your direct network boundaries.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Look, when your IT equipment crosses a gateway to access another network, it needs to prove it actually is what it claims to be—not just waltz through like it owns the place. This means implementing mutual authentication, certificate-based verification, or whatever cryptographic handshake your gateway supports, because apparently the honour system died in 2015. You'd be shocked how many organisations skip this and then act genuinely confused when lateral movement happens.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that when you connect networks classified at SECRET or TOP SECRET level to networks in different security domains, you must use a Cross Domain Solution (CDS) as the gateway between them. This is critical because it prevents unauthorised data flows and ensures classified information cannot inadvertently move to incompatible security domains where it shouldn't be accessible. Without such controlled gateways, a compromise in one domain could give an attacker access to highly classified networks.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: If you're moving classified data between networks that don't trust each other—which, let's be honest, is basically all of them—you need a Cross Domain Solution (CDS) sitting in the middle playing border guard. These aren't just firewalls; they're purpose-built gateways that actually inspect and mediate data crossing between SECRET/TOP SECRET domains and everything else, because a VLAN and a prayer won't cut it. Deploy one of these before someone inevitably copies a classified document onto a USB drive and walks it over to the unclassified network "for convenience."

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to deploy gateways (such as firewalls or proxy servers) at the boundaries between networks that have different security classifications or purposes. Gateways act as controlled checkpoints that inspect and regulate traffic flowing between these separate networks, preventing unauthorized access and limiting the spread of threats. This is essential because without such boundaries, a compromise in one network could easily cascade to others, and sensitive systems need protection from less-trusted networks.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Install network gateways—yes, the actual physical or virtual checkpoint devices—between networks that trust each other about as much as rival departments trust each other's budgets. This means if your OFFICIAL:Sensitive network and your PROTECTED network exist in the same building, don't just cable them together like they're best friends; put a gateway between them so one compromised network can't immediately invite itself into the other's house. You'd be amazed how often this simple concept gets interpreted as "we'll add a VLAN and call it done."

annotations.ai_view: When networks at different security levels connect through a gateway, any shared equipment must be controlled by administrators from the higher security domain or by a neutral third party—never by the lower-security side alone. This prevents less-trusted network administrators from tampering with shared components to breach into more sensitive systems. The arrangement ensures that critical infrastructure protecting higher-security networks stays under appropriate oversight.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: When your network gateway straddles two security domains—because apparently we all love living dangerously—whoever administers the shared bits needs to be from the higher security domain or some neutral third party you've both agreed on, not just whoever's closest to the coffee machine. This prevents the lower-security side from quietly tweaking gateway rules to let their sketchy stuff through, though good luck enforcing this when the higher domain's admins are perpetually understaffed and the "mutually agreed third party" is your mate Derek from the contractor panel. In practice, document this arrangement clearly, because your next audit will ask, and your current chaos will not be a defensible answer.

annotations.ai_view: Gateways must be configured to block all data flows by default and only permit traffic that has been explicitly approved—nothing should pass through unless it's been specifically authorized. This prevents unauthorized data from leaving or entering your network, stopping accidental exposure of sensitive information and blocking potential data theft or malware communications. It's a foundational security practice that treats every potential data path as suspicious until proven legitimate.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your gateway should reject everything by default and only let through the specific data flows you've explicitly blessed in writing—which sounds straightforward until you realise nobody actually documents what "authorised" means and you're debugging mysterious blocked traffic at 2 AM because someone hardcoded an IP address that changed last quarter. It's the "deny all, allow by exception" principle that works perfectly in theory and requires religious discipline in practice, which is why you'll probably find seventeen shadow flows doing whatever they want while you're reading this.

annotations.ai_view: All security‑relevant gateway events must be centrally logged, including permitted inbound/outbound packets, attempted outbound packets, and real‑time intrusion alerts, to support detection and audit.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Log everything that passes, tries to leave, or screams “intrusion” at your gateway—because nothing says “we care” like a SIEM full of noise you never review.

annotations.ai_view: Systems must use separate, isolated network paths for data moving into and out of controlled data stores—preventing data from different security zones from mixing on the same network route. This segregation limits the damage if one path is compromised, stops attackers from using inbound traffic to reach outbound connections, and makes it harder for unauthorized data to leave the system undetected. It's a foundational technique for protecting classified and sensitive information from exfiltration and lateral movement.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your Cross-Domain Solution needs to physically or logically separate the network paths that move data up to higher classification levels from the paths moving data down—because apparently we can't trust that one cable won't accidentally become sentient and route SECRET to UNCLASSIFIED if given the chance. It's the networking equivalent of a one-way mirror, except both sides are actually transparent and someone will absolutely plug them together anyway. Implement this before your auditor arrives looking for evidence that you've at least *tried* to prevent classification leakage.

annotations.ai_view: When external users or organisations need to access your services, you must create a demilitarised zone—a separate network area that sits between the internet and your internal systems, allowing controlled access without exposing your core infrastructure. It's a foundational practice for any organisation that provides internet-facing services to customers or partners.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: If you're silly enough to let external parties touch your systems, at least have the decency to stick a DMZ in between so the damage stays contained when—not if—someone gets compromised. Somehow this basic hygiene still surprises most organisations during their first breach post-mortem.

annotations.ai_view: Use firewalls that have been independently tested and certified to protect connections between networks that handle different types of classified or sensitive information. annotations.ai_view_snarky: Deploy firewalls that have actually undergone independent evaluation testing between any networks operating at different security levels—because apparently the unvetted appliance someone grabbed from a liquidation auction doesn't count. annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to use tested and certified data diodes—specialised hardware devices that enforce one-way data flow—when connecting your internal networks to public networks or the internet. Good luck finding organisations that actually do this instead of settling for software "gateways" that technically go both ways but have good intentions.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that data diodes (one-way security devices) protecting connections between classified networks and public internet infrastructure must have undergone rigorous independent security testing and certification. annotations.ai_view: This control requires your organisation to block files that content filtering systems identify as malicious or cannot safely examine—rather than allowing them through. annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must automatically isolate files that content filtering systems flag as potentially dangerous, preventing them from reaching users until a security reviewer examines and explicitly approves them. annotations.ai_view_snarky: When your content filters flag something dodgy—which they will, constantly, some percentage of which will actually matter—you've got to stick those files in quarantine like digital remand prisoners until a human being reviews them and decides whether they're threats or just false positives. annotations.ai_view: When staff manually transfer data into systems, that data must be checked with security tools to detect viruses, malware, and other harmful content before it's allowed in. annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to automatically scan all files moving in and out of your organisation through network gateways or cross-domain solutions for malicious content, policy violations, or other threats. The whole point is preventing exfiltration and infection at the perimeter, which beats discovering the problem six months later in your logs.

annotations.ai_view: You must check and validate all data transfer logs from your classified (SECRET and TOP SECRET) systems at least once every month to confirm that data movements are legitimate and authorized. annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to actually review your data transfer logs for SECRET and TOP SECRET systems every month—and I mean *fully* verify them, not just glance at the summary and call it done. annotations.ai_view: Individuals who transfer data to or from systems are held accountable for those transfers, providing traceability and responsibility for data movement.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to create and maintain documented processes and procedures that govern how data moves between systems, locations, or organisations. annotations.ai_view: Before any data leaves a classified system, someone in a position of trust must review what's being exported and formally approve it. annotations.ai_view: Only people and systems verified and authorized by the chief information security officer may act as trustworthy data sources for SECRET and TOP SECRET systems.

annotations.ai_view: When staff manually export data from highly classified systems, they must verify digital signatures to confirm the data hasn't been altered and search for sensitive keywords to prevent accidental inclusion of classified information. annotations.ai_view_snarky: Before you manually yeet classified data out of a system, you need to actually verify the digital signatures are legit and scan all the text for keywords you shouldn't be exporting—because apparently people can't be trusted to remember what "SECRET" means. annotations.ai_view: This control requires that security-relevant events occurring on cross-domain solutions—systems that transfer data between networks of different security classifications—must be recorded and sent to a central logging location rather than stored only on the gateway device itself. annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to send all the security events your Cross Domain Solution generates to a central logging system—yes, all of them, not just the ones you remember to check. Spoiler: they won't be, so set this up now before your auditors ask you questions you can't answer.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that when data leaves a classified system at SECRET or TOP SECRET level, it must be digitally signed by a trusted source to prove its authenticity and that it was authorised for export. annotations.ai_view_snarky: When you export classified data from your spooky networks, slap a digital signature on it from someone who actually knows what they're doing — because apparently "trust me bro" doesn't meet the bar for SECRET and TOP SECRET material. annotations.ai_view: When files move in or out of your systems through gateways or cross-domain solutions, you must verify they haven't been altered or corrupted by checking their digital signatures or cryptographic checksums. annotations.ai_view_snarky: When files cross your gateway or CDS boundaries sporting a digital signature or checksum, you actually need to verify the damn thing instead of just letting it through because it looks official. Somehow this remains the control that everyone reads, nods at, and then quietly ignores until someone's ransomware sample bypassed it because they were "too busy" to set up proper hash verification.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that Bluetooth capability must be completely disabled on mobile devices that process classified information at SECRET or TOP SECRET level. annotations.ai_view_snarky: Disable Bluetooth on any device handling SECRET or TOP SECRET data—because apparently wireless is where classification goes to die. Yes, this actually matters: Bluetooth is a proximity attack vector with all the security properties of leaving classified documents in a café, just more convenient for the attacker.

annotations.ai_view: Mobile devices accessing classified information (SECRET or TOP SECRET) must run on platforms that the Australian Security Directorate has officially approved for this purpose, and you must follow the security instructions that come with each approved platform. annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to ensure that any mobile device touching SECRET or TOP SECRET data is running a platform that ASD has formally blessed—no iPhone running last year's iOS on your classified briefing, no matter how convenient. annotations.ai_view: This control prevents classified information from being accessed on personal devices that fall outside your organisation's management and security oversight. annotations.ai_view_snarky: Don't let people access classified systems from their personal MacBook Pro that also has their banking apps and that sketchy torrent client they swear they only use for Linux ISOs. It's straightforward: classified data lives on organisation-issued kit only, full stop.

annotations.ai_view: Organisations must establish and maintain documented processes and procedures to quickly erase data from mobile devices in emergency situations—such as loss, theft, or security breaches. annotations.ai_view: All cyber security documentation must be reviewed at least once a year and carry a “current as at [date]” statement to show currency.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Once a year you dust off the policy stack, stamp a date on it, and pretend it’s still relevant—until the next audit proves otherwise.

annotations.ai_view: A change and configuration management plan must establish authorized baseline configurations, distinguish routine from urgent changes, and detail how changes are requested, tracked, documented, consulted on, approved, and notified, plus any extra processes before, during, and after changes. This controls modifications and prevents unauthorized drift.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: A bureaucratic flowchart that slows deployments; everyone signs off, then the urgent change bypasses it anyway.

annotations.ai_view: When malicious code is found, isolate the infected systems, scan and isolate any media used before the infection, remove the code with antivirus tools, and if removal fails, restore from a clean backup or rebuild the system.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: The standard panic‑scan‑pray‑rebuild cycle — because ‘clean backup’ is a myth until you test it.

annotations.ai_view: Physical cable colour coding is used to quickly identify different classification levels of data flowing through your infrastructure. This control requires that cables carrying unclassified, official sensitive, or protected data use colours other than salmon pink or red—which are reserved for higher classification levels—to prevent accidental misdirection of sensitive information or interference with classified systems. Proper colour segregation reduces the risk of human error when installing, maintaining, or troubleshooting cabling, and helps staff visually distinguish between different data sensitivity levels at a glance.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to make sure your cables aren't salmon pink or red—apparently someone decided that colour-coding your network infrastructure like a Christmas decoration was a security risk. This mostly just means don't grab the classified-only cable colours for unclassified systems, which is a weirdly specific way to prevent a cable swap, but here we are. In practice, this means sticking to blues, greens, yellows, or whatever else your org picks, which you'll discover nobody actually tracks until an audit.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to use push-to-talk communication devices (handsets or headsets) in classified areas marked as SECRET or TOP SECRET to prevent accidental audio transmission. Push-to-talk technology ensures that microphones only transmit when the user actively presses a button, eliminating the risk of unintended classified conversations being captured or broadcast when the device is idle. This protects sensitive government communications from being overheard by unauthorised people or intercepted through open audio channels.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: If you're handling SECRET or TOP SECRET material, your comms gear needs to be push-to-talk only—because apparently someone decided that the existential horror of an accidentally-live microphone picking up classified conversations warranted banning normal handsets. The intent is sound (off-hook audio can leak sensitive information), but I've never met an organisation that didn't have at least one person using a regular headset anyway, usually while insisting their particular conversation "wasn't really classified."

annotations.ai_view: Choose application vendors that prioritize secure development practices from the start, particularly those using memory-safe programming languages or equivalent protections to prevent common vulnerabilities like buffer overflows. This reduces the risk of exploitable flaws being built into software you rely on, since preventing security problems during development is far more effective than trying to patch them later. Favoring vendors committed to these principles helps ensure your applications are more resilient to attack.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to buy applications from vendors who actually care about not shipping garbage—specifically ones using memory-safe languages or at least pretending they've heard of buffer overflow prevention. Yes, this means you're probably going to have some very awkward vendor conversations about their "secure development practices," and yes, they'll send you a glossy PDF that says nothing, but document it anyway because accountability matters more than their marketing department's competence.

annotations.ai_view: When you manually move data between separate security domains using rewritable media (like USB drives or external hard drives), you must completely erase that media after each transfer to prevent sensitive data from being accidentally exposed to unauthorised users. This matters because rewritable media can be reused multiple times, and deleted files can sometimes be recovered if not properly sanitised, creating a risk that confidential information from one domain leaks into another.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Every time you manually shuffle data between systems on different security domains using a USB drive or external hard drive, you've got to wipe that media clean afterward—not just delete files like some kind of amateur, but actually sanitise it so the data can't be recovered. Apparently the theoretical threat of someone fishing classified data off a rewritable stick justifies the operational overhead, which explains why you'll find people using the same thumb drive across domains without incident until the one time it matters.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to use one of three methods to restrict which applications can run on systems: cryptographic hashing (allowing only specific software versions), publisher certificates (trusting software from authorized publishers), or path rules (controlling execution from specific directories). By implementing application control through these mechanisms, you prevent unauthorized or malicious software from executing, which significantly reduces your risk of compromise from malware, supply chain attacks, or unvetted tools.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to pick at least one of three methods—cryptographic hashes, publisher certificates, or file paths—to decide which applications are allowed to run, which is security theater's way of saying "make a list and stick to it." In practice, most organisations will configure path rules (the easiest), watch them get bypassed within six months via DLL injection or some creative symlink nonsense, then blame the users for clicking suspicious executables.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to maintain and enforce an approved allowlist of domain names or website categories that controls which internet sites users can access through network gateways. By filtering web traffic at the gateway level, organisations prevent employees from accessing malicious, inappropriate, or non-work-related websites that could introduce malware, cause data loss, or waste productivity. This approach protects the network perimeter and ensures internet usage aligns with organisational policy and security requirements.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to set up an allowlist or category-based blocklist for all HTTP/HTTPS traffic hitting your network gateway—basically treating the internet like a bouncer who only lets in people on the guest list. This is supposed to stop users from wandering into the dodgy corners of the web, though in practice everyone will immediately request access to whatever site you blocked, and your gateway logs will become an unread graveyard of policy violations within three months. It's not glamorous, but it works if you actually maintain the list instead of letting it calcify into irrelevance.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation should use web content filters to block active content (like scripts and plugins) from running unless it comes from domains you've explicitly approved. This prevents malware, drive-by downloads, and other web-based attacks from reaching your users' devices through compromised or malicious websites. By maintaining a strict allowlist rather than a blocklist, you significantly reduce the attack surface and ensure users can only access web content you've deemed safe.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You're going to filter active content like Flash, Java, and JavaScript so that only code from your blessed whitelist of domains can execute on user machines—because apparently we still haven't learned that users will click literally anything, and attackers are very creative about where they host their malware-laden ads. Good luck maintaining that whitelist when someone's inevitable request to unblock "totally-legitimate-analytics.ru" lands in your inbox at 4:47 PM on a Friday.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to deploy web content filtering at your network gateway to block access to websites and content that could pose security risks—such as malware-hosting sites, phishing pages, or other harmful resources. It matters because it prevents employees from accidentally (or intentionally) visiting dangerous websites that could compromise systems, steal data, or spread malware throughout your organization. By filtering at the gateway level, you catch threats before they reach individual devices and reduce the attack surface your organization exposes to web-based threats.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to deploy a web content filter at your gateway that blocks websites the filter vendor has decided are "potentially harmful"—which apparently includes everything from malware distribution sites to whatever category your risk officer is worried about this quarter. Yes, this is the control that gets bypassed more creatively than any other, but it does stop the obviously bad stuff and gives you something to point at during audits when someone inevitably downloads ransomware from a PDF hosting site anyway.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires development teams to apply the Open Web Application Security Project's Application Security Verification Standard when building web applications, which provides a comprehensive framework for identifying and mitigating common web application vulnerabilities. It matters because web applications are frequent attack targets, and using this established standard helps ensure developers consistently implement security controls for authentication, access control, input validation, and other critical areas throughout the development lifecycle. By following a recognized verification standard, organisations reduce the risk of deploying applications with preventable security flaws that attackers commonly exploit.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Use OWASP's Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) when developing web applications—basically, treat it as your security checklist so your developers stop inventing their own validation logic at 3 AM. This matters because web apps are where attackers make their easiest kills, and ASVS gives you a standardized baseline that's actually been thought through by people who've seen things. Yes, your org probably already has some homegrown security requirements, but those definitely won't be as thorough, which is why this control exists.

annotations.ai_view: Require multi‑factor authentication for all unprivileged human users of systems. Even regular accounts can be leveraged for lateral movement if compromised.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Now every regular user needs MFA too. Because apparently the help desk enjoys resetting second‑factor tokens as much as they enjoy resetting passwords.

annotations.ai_view: Ensure all systems logging security events use the same accurate time source so timestamps are reliable and consistent across your organisation. Misaligned clocks make it difficult to correlate events, investigate incidents, and establish a credible timeline of what happened when. This matters because attackers often exploit time gaps to hide their tracks, and regulators expect you to prove the integrity of your security records.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your logs need to all agree on what time it is, using a single authoritative source—because nothing builds confidence in a security investigation like timestamps that differ by three hours across your infrastructure and make it impossible to establish a causal sequence of events. Yes, we know you've got seventeen systems running on local time because someone set one up in 2015 and nobody touched it again; synchronise them to NTP or similar and call it done.

annotations.ai_view: When you need to establish secure shared secrets between two parties using public key cryptography, use Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) instead of the older Diffie-Hellman (DH) algorithm. ECDH provides equivalent security with much shorter key lengths, making it more efficient while offering better resistance to known mathematical attacks on DH. This preference helps ensure your cryptographic implementations remain secure and performant across all classification levels.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Use Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) instead of traditional Diffie-Hellman (DH) for key agreement—ECDH provides equivalent security with smaller key sizes, better performance, and fewer implementation gotchas. Yes, this means you need to deprecate DH if you're still using it, which I'm sure your legacy systems running since 2003 are thrilled about. It's the right call though: ECDH is simply the better algorithm for the job in basically every scenario that matters today.

annotations.ai_view: When authenticating IPsec network connections, you must use one of the specified HMAC-SHA2 variants for integrity checking, or preferably use no separate authentication method if you're already using AES-GCM encryption (which provides built-in integrity protection). This ensures that data transmitted over your network hasn't been tampered with in transit, protecting against attacks that could modify communications between systems. Using cryptographically strong authentication algorithms prevents attackers from forging or altering network traffic without detection.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You must use one of three HMAC-SHA2 variants for IPsec authentication, though the control's real preference—revealed in that parenthetical "preferably NONE"—is that you skip authentication altogether and let AES-GCM handle it, which is simultaneously the most secure and most organizationally unlikely outcome you'll ever see implemented. Yes, the control is essentially saying "do the cryptographically elegant thing" while knowing full well that most shops will pick whichever HMAC variant their vendor defaulted to and call it a day.

annotations.ai_view: Use strong key exchange methods (Diffie-Hellman or Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman) when establishing IPsec connections, with preference for 384-bit elliptic curve, 3072-bit, or 4096-bit key sizes. This ensures that attackers cannot feasibly intercept and decrypt the initial key exchange, protecting the confidentiality of your encrypted network traffic. Weaker key sizes are vulnerable to modern cryptanalytic attacks and should be avoided.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: When establishing IPsec tunnels, you'll use Diffie-Hellman or Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman for key exchange—preferably the 384-bit random ECP group, 3072-bit MODP Group, or 4096-bit MODP Group, because apparently anything smaller is basically skywriting your encryption keys. Yes, organisations still ship with weaker defaults and wonder why compliance audits are painful; no, "we've always done it that way" is not a cryptographic justification. Pick one of the three approved groups and move on.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that IPsec connections use Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS), which ensures that session encryption keys are generated independently and cannot be compromised by the theft of long-term keys. If an attacker later obtains your organization's master encryption keys, they cannot use them to decrypt previously captured IPsec traffic—protecting the confidentiality of historical communications. This is essential for maintaining security of sensitive data transmitted over IPsec tunnels, especially given the increasing threat of retroactive decryption attacks.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your IPsec tunnels need to use Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS), which means generating new encryption keys for each session so that compromising a long-term key doesn't retroactively decrypt your entire conversation history—a feature that should be table stakes but apparently isn't, given how often you'll find organisations running with it disabled. This applies across all sensitivity levels, which tells you the ASD thinks it matters everywhere, and they're right, even though configuring it correctly seems to elude roughly 90% of network teams. Check your IKE phase 2 settings and enable PFS groups; it costs you microseconds of CPU and saves you from explaining to executives why last year's encrypted traffic is now readable.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to protect network management traffic—the communications used to configure and monitor your network devices—from being intercepted or tampered with by unauthorised people. Implement practical measures like encryption, strong authentication, and access controls to ensure only legitimate administrators can view or modify this sensitive traffic. This matters because attackers who gain access to network management communications can take control of your entire network infrastructure, making this a critical security boundary to defend.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Look, someone needs to actually stop your network admins from shouting their credentials across the coffee room and leaving management traffic as readable as a newspaper on the bus. Implement encryption (TLS, SSH, SNMPv3—pick literally anything over plaintext), restrict management access to authorised personnel and networks, and for the love of the ISM, disable Telnet and HTTP for device management. Yes, I know your vendor's 2003-era equipment "doesn't support" modern security—time to update it anyway.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to install RF (radio frequency) shielding in buildings that use classified wireless networks, so the wireless signal doesn't leak beyond your facility's boundaries where unauthorised people could intercept it. Shielding prevents adversaries outside your premises from detecting or eavesdropping on sensitive communications, significantly reducing the risk of signal interception or attacks against your wireless infrastructure. This is particularly critical for SECRET and TOP SECRET networks where unauthorised access could compromise national security.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Slap RF shielding on your facilities so that your SECRET or TOP SECRET wireless networks don't broadcast into the car park, the coffee shop across the street, or directly into a threat actor's van. It's basically Faraday cage 101—block the signal from leaving your building's perimeter, because apparently "just don't transmit classified data wirelessly" isn't an option anyone wants to hear. Yes, people will still complain about the cost and the dead zones in the bathroom; no, that doesn't make it optional.

annotations.ai_view: Every user of an IP phone handling classified conversations must have their own individual login credentials rather than sharing a common account. This ensures you can identify who made or received sensitive calls, detect unauthorized access, and maintain accountability if conversations are compromised. Without individual logins, you cannot audit phone usage or hold users responsible for their actions on classified systems.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Each IP phone must have individual user logins enabled—a deceptively straightforward requirement that somehow nobody implements correctly because "the shared phone works fine" until it mysteriously doesn't and you're explaining to an auditor why three people have the same credentials for a device handling classified conversations. The point is accountability: when something goes wrong, you need to know which user was holding the handset, not just that someone *probably* was.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must create and maintain a documented plan for responding to denial of service attacks that target your video conferencing and phone systems, covering detection, mitigation, and recovery procedures. This matters because these communication services are critical for business continuity, and a coordinated response plan minimises downtime and maintains operational resilience when attackers attempt to disrupt them. Regular review and updates ensure the plan stays relevant as your systems and threat landscape evolve.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to actually write down what you'll do when someone floods your video conferencing or IP telephony systems with traffic, then document that you've done it, then keep doing it. Yes, this means having a plan before the attack happens rather than improvising furiously in a Teams chat while your CEO can't dial in—revolutionary concept, I know. Make sure you revisit this document occasionally so it doesn't become the digital equivalent of a fire evacuation plan from 2003 that nobody's actually read.

annotations.ai_view: When your organization blocks emails because they lack proper security markings or have incorrect classifications, you must notify both the people who were supposed to receive those emails and whoever sent them. This ensures senders understand why their messages failed to deliver and recipients know to expect important communications through alternative channels, while helping your organization maintain consistent security classification practices across email communications.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: When your email gateway inevitably rejects a message because someone forgot to slap a protective marking on it—which happens roughly every 47 seconds in any organisation—you've got to actually tell both sides what happened, rather than letting them sit around wondering if their email evaporated into the void. Notification matters because people need to know *why* their critical message got bounced so they can either fix the marking and resend it, or contact the recipient through some other medium before their boss asks why the budget proposal never arrived. In practice, this means configuring your email system to generate bounce messages that are simultaneously helpful enough to be useful and vague enough to not inadvertently leak classification information to the person who didn't mark their email correctly in the first place.

annotations.ai_view: When email delivery fails, your system should only send bounce-back notifications to senders whose addresses have been verified as legitimate—typically through authentication methods like SPF records or other trusted verification means. This prevents attackers from using your mail system to send notifications to arbitrary recipients (a technique called backscatter), which could be used for spam distribution or social engineering. By restricting bounce notifications to verified senders, you reduce your organisation's involvement in email-based attacks and protect your reputation.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: When your mail server bounces an email, it has to actually verify the sender isn't some spoofed address before helpfully telling them "delivery failed"—otherwise you're just confirming valid email addresses to attackers while they spam you. Use SPF records or equivalent authentication to validate that bounce notifications go to legitimate senders, not to the forged "From:" addresses that comprise roughly 87% of what gets rejected anyway. Yes, this means configuring your email system correctly, which apparently requires stating explicitly.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must verify that incoming emails have valid DomainKeys Identified Mail signatures, which cryptographically confirm an email genuinely came from the claimed sender's domain. This prevents attackers from spoofing legitimate organisations to conduct phishing or fraud attacks, and helps you identify compromised external accounts being used to send malicious emails. Implementing this check is a foundational email security measure that works alongside SPF and DMARC to authenticate message sources.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your email system needs to actually verify DKIM signatures on inbound mail instead of just... receiving it and hoping for the best. This means checking that the cryptographic signatures legitimately match the sending domain, which catches spoofed emails pretending to be from your CEO or some other trusted source—though good luck getting users to notice when the signature fails anyway. It's table stakes for not getting catastrophically owned by basic email impersonation, which somehow remains shocking in how often it works.

annotations.ai_view: Ensure that email distribution lists used by external senders preserve the cryptographic signature that proves the sender's identity and that the message hasn't been tampered with. If distribution list software modifies emails in ways that invalidate this signature, recipients lose the ability to verify the message actually came from the claimed sender, making it easier for attackers to impersonate legitimate external contacts. Properly configured distribution lists pass emails through without breaking these security checks.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: When you set up email distribution lists for external senders, don't let them mangle the DKIM signature in the process—because apparently we still need to tell people not to break the one thing that actually proves an email is legitimate. This matters because a busted DKIM signature turns your "verified sender" status into "could be anyone pretending to be you," which defeats the entire purpose of having it. You'd be amazed how many organisations discover this the hard way after their CEO's email address has been merrily forwarding phishing campaigns for three months.

annotations.ai_view: Deploy a system at your network boundaries that automatically monitors and blocks suspicious traffic entering or leaving your organisation. This catches attacks, malware, and unauthorised data exfiltration before they reach your internal systems or leave your network, protecting you from external threats and insider risks. It's your first line of defence where your network meets the outside world.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Deploy a network-based intrusion detection or prevention system at your network boundaries—you know, that magical gateway where your carefully secured network meets the internet's beautiful chaos. This means actually monitoring traffic flowing in and out to the unmanaged networks you've trusted with your data, which I'm sure everyone's doing rigorously and not just rubber-stamping as "configured" while it logs to /dev/null. It's basically admitting you don't fully trust your internet connection, which is the one thing we can all agree on.

annotations.ai_view: Place a network intrusion detection or prevention system immediately inside your outermost firewall to monitor all incoming and outgoing traffic, configured to log events and alert you when traffic violates your firewall rules. This positioning allows you to catch suspicious activity that your firewall permits or blocks, helping you detect attacks, policy violations, and anomalous behavior before they reach your systems. It provides visibility into what's actually crossing your network boundary and helps you identify whether your firewall rules are working as intended.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Place your network intrusion detection or prevention system right behind your outermost firewall so it can log and alert on traffic that your firewall ruleset is already supposed to be blocking—essentially paying for redundant visibility into the traffic you've explicitly told your firewall to deny, which is somehow still necessary because firewalls are stateless rule engines, not omniscient security appliances. Yes, you'll generate a lot of noise from legitimate traffic hitting firewall rules, but that's what tuning and a reasonable SOC are for, assuming you have either. This is the networking equivalent of installing cameras to watch your locked door; theoretically pointless, practically invaluable.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must install host-based intrusion prevention or endpoint detection and response tools on servers that are critical to operations or contain valuable data, so you can detect and stop malicious activity at the point where attackers are most likely to cause serious harm. This matters because servers are high-value targets—compromising one can give attackers access to sensitive information or let them disrupt services that other systems depend on. By catching threats early at the server level, you reduce the window of opportunity for attackers to move laterally through your network or steal data.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to stick some kind of Host-based Intrusion Prevention System or Endpoint Detection and Response tool on your critical and high-value servers—you know, the ones that actually matter and would cause an incident if compromised. Yes, this means identifying which servers those are first, which half your organisations somehow haven't done yet. It's not glamorous and it won't stop a determined attacker, but it'll at least make opportunistic threats work for it and give you better visibility into what's happening on the boxes that matter most.

annotations.ai_view: Place multifunction devices (printers/scanners/copiers with fax capability) in shared or monitored areas where staff activity can be observed, rather than in isolated locations. This prevents unauthorised use of sensitive functions like sending faxes or scanning confidential documents without witnesses, and deters misuse or theft of information. The visibility also helps catch accidental data exposure, such as leaving printed documents in the output tray.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Place your multifunction devices somewhere people can actually see them being used—a radical concept apparently, given how many organisations tuck these document-eating monsters into unmonitored corners where they quietly leak sensitive information to whoever wanders by. The idea is that observable use deters unauthorised printing, scanning, and the time-honoured tradition of leaving confidential documents face-down on the output tray, though results may vary depending on how much your staff actually care about being watched fumbling with the collating options.

annotations.ai_view: You must regularly test your network gateways (firewalls, proxies, and similar boundary devices) to confirm they're configured correctly and haven't drifted from their intended security settings—doing this at least twice yearly and whenever you make configuration changes. This matters because gateways are critical checkpoints that protect your network; misconfigurations or undetected changes can leave security gaps that attackers exploit to breach your systems.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: After you've meticulously configured your gateway to reject everything that looks vaguely suspicious, you need to actually verify it still does that—both when someone inevitably "just makes a quick change" and every six months whether anything changed or not. Consider this your permission slip to finally run those security tests your team keeps saying they'll get to, plus the bureaucratic alibi when the next audit rolls around asking why your critical security perimeter controls aren't validated.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that servers, network devices, and cryptographic equipment containing classified information be physically located in secure rooms with access controls and protections that match the sensitivity level of the data they hold. It matters because physical access to these systems is a direct attack vector—an unauthorised person with hands-on access can steal data, install malware, or sabotage operations far more easily than attacking remotely. By isolating critical equipment in properly secured spaces, you prevent casual or opportunistic breaches and force potential attackers to overcome significant physical barriers.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to lock up your classified gear in a proper security zone—so not the server room next to the kitchen, and definitely not that cabinet in the hallway someone keeps propping open. The classification of your equipment determines what kind of physical protections that room actually needs, which means you'll want to check what "suitable for their classification" means before your auditor inevitably finds your PROTECTED servers gathering dust in a space designed for nothing more than keeping pigeons out. Yes, this is as straightforward as it sounds, and yes, organisations still somehow fail this one.

annotations.ai_view: Disable LAN Manager and NT LAN Manager authentication across your systems, as these legacy protocols use weak cryptographic hashing that can be rapidly cracked by attackers—even offline—to compromise user credentials. These outdated methods are unnecessary on modern networks and leaving them enabled significantly increases the risk of unauthorized access to systems and data. This control applies to network-connected devices, operating systems, and servers that might still support these protocols by default.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Disable LAN Manager (LM) and NT LAN Manager (NTLM) authentication on your systems—yes, those protocols from the Windows 95 era that somehow keep shambling through your network like digital zombies. These methods use laughably weak cryptography that would make a security researcher weep into their coffee, and any competent attacker can crack them faster than you can say "why is this still enabled?" Realistically, if you're still relying on LM/NTLM in 2024, you've got bigger problems than this control, but disabling them is table stakes for not being a walking security incident.

annotations.ai_view: All sensitive data written to physical storage devices—such as hard drives, USB drives, tapes, and memory cards—must be encrypted so that if media is lost, stolen, or discarded, the data remains unreadable to unauthorised people. This protects your organisation against data breaches that could occur during device transportation, storage, or disposal, and ensures compliance with data protection obligations. Encryption is the practical safeguard that prevents data exposure when you cannot physically control a device.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Encrypt everything on physical media before it leaves your organisation's control, because apparently the concept of "don't lose a USB stick with unencrypted data" requires regulatory backing. This applies whether you're storing classified intelligence or the office birthday calendar, though naturally you'll find someone's laptop full of unencrypted backups in a desk drawer next year.

annotations.ai_view: Before erasing magnetic hard drives, you must reset the host-protected area (a hidden storage section used by drive firmware) and the device configuration overlay table (which stores drive settings), as these areas can retain sensitive data even after standard sanitisation and could be exploited to recover information. This prevents attackers from extracting classified or sensitive information that standard wiping procedures might miss, ensuring complete data destruction when hard drives are decommissioned or repurposed.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Before you wipe that hard drive, you need to reset the host-protected area and the device configuration overlay table—basically the sneaky firmware-level storage spaces that most people forget exists and that conventional wiping tools completely ignore. Yes, it's tedious and yes, most organisations skip this step until they're explaining a data breach to regulators, but if you don't clear these hidden sectors, your sanitisation effort is about as effective as locking the front door while leaving the back windows open.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires using the ATA secure erase command alongside block overwriting software to completely remove data from hard drives, including the defect management areas that standard deletion methods often miss. This two-layer approach prevents adversaries from recovering sensitive information from discarded or repurposed drives, even when they attempt data recovery techniques. It's essential for organisations handling classified or sensitive data to ensure nothing can be reconstructed from magnetic media before it leaves their control.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to nuke hard drives using both the ATA secure erase command *and* block overwriting software together—because apparently one method of obliterating data isn't paranoid enough, and someone decided the growth defects table was worth the belt-and-suspenders approach. In practice, this means your IT team will spend three hours wiping a drive that could've been done in one, while most organisations will still just throw the old hardware in a closet and hope no one notices. Technically sound; operationally ignored.

annotations.ai_view: Every system must have one clearly identified person responsible for its overall security and operation. This ensures accountability for decisions about access, updates, and incident response, and prevents security gaps that occur when no one is clearly in charge. A designated owner provides a single point of contact for managing risks and coordinating with other teams when security issues arise.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Someone needs to own your system, and that someone needs to be *named*, not vaguely waved at during meetings as "probably the infrastructure team." This control exists because when security incidents occur, you'll quickly discover that "everyone owns it" means "nobody owned it," and accountability dissolves faster than a classified document in a toilet. Designate an actual person with an actual name, even if they spend half their time explaining why they can't unilaterally approve purchases—that clarity beats the alternative of a post-incident finger-pointing festival.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that any service provider accessing or managing your systems must have a formal written contract explicitly authorising that access. It matters because unauthorised or undocumented access by external parties creates security gaps, makes accountability unclear, and increases the risk of data breaches or system compromise—a contract ensures there's a clear agreement about what access is permitted, under what conditions, and who is responsible for security.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need a written contract before letting any service provider poke around your systems—which sounds obvious until you realize how many organisations discover they've got vendors with admin access and no paperwork to show for it. The control basically says: get it in writing first, not after your contractor has already deleted production databases and claimed "nobody told me I couldn't." Without a contractual arrangement explicitly covering system access and administration, you've got nothing but a handshake and plausible deniability when things inevitably go wrong.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires your organisation to manage access to physical spaces housing critical infrastructure—server rooms, network equipment, and security containers—by carefully controlling who holds keys or has other entry mechanisms like keycards or biometric access. Proper key management prevents unauthorised physical access that could lead to data theft, equipment tampering, or system outages, and ensures accountability by tracking who enters these sensitive areas and when.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to actually control who has keys or keycards to the rooms where your servers, network gear, and crypto equipment live—meaning not just handing them out like candy at Christmas and definitely not leaving spares under the doormat "for emergencies." This is the part where most organisations discover they have seventeen copies of the master key floating around, three of which belong to people who left five years ago. Keep an inventory, restrict distribution, and don't let Karen from accounting hold a spare "just in case."

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to remove temporary image burn-in or ghosting from screens by displaying a solid white image for several hours, rather than discarding the equipment. This matters because it extends the lifespan of displays while preventing potential data leakage—residual images could theoretically reveal sensitive information that was previously displayed on the screen.

Yes, this includes that "innocent" dropdown menu and the search box your mate insisted couldn't possibly be exploited—implement it anyway, because your mate is wrong and history agrees with me.

annotations.ai_view: Web applications must encode (convert) all data before displaying it to users' browsers to prevent attackers from injecting malicious code through user inputs or compromised data sources. This stops common attacks like cross-site scripting (XSS) where an attacker tricks a browser into running harmful JavaScript by embedding it in web content. Proper encoding ensures that special characters are treated as data rather than executable commands, protecting both users and the application itself.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Encode literally everything your web app spits out—HTML, JavaScript, URLs, the works—so attackers can't inject malicious code and make it execute in users' browsers. Yes, this includes that one parameter you're "sure" is safe because you validated it on the client side. No, it doesn't matter that it's worked fine for five years; one XSS vulnerability is all it takes, and your application logs will be the only witness to the incident postmortem.

annotations.ai_view: Organisations must create and keep a current inventory of all databases that store or process data, documenting key details like location, owner, and contents. This register should be reviewed regularly to ensure it remains accurate and complete. Maintaining this inventory is essential because it enables you to identify which databases hold sensitive information, track what data exists across your systems, and manage security risks effectively—without knowing what databases you have and what they contain, you cannot adequately protect them.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to maintain a comprehensive inventory of every database your organisation owns, knows it owns, or suspects it might own somewhere—then actually keep that thing up to date instead of letting it fossilise into irrelevance within six months like everyone does. Verify the register regularly so you can at least pretend you know what's running on your network, which will inevitably reveal seventeen databases nobody remembered existed and three that were supposedly decommissioned in 2019.

annotations.ai_view: After installing server applications, you must delete all temporary files and logs that were created during the installation process. These leftover files can contain sensitive information like passwords, configuration details, or system paths that attackers could exploit, and they consume unnecessary disk space. Removing them reduces your attack surface and keeps your servers clean and secure.
