annotations.ai_view_snarky: Delete the installer cruft and logs once your shiny new server application is actually running, because apparently leaving behind diagnostic files, temporary scripts, and detailed installation transcripts on production systems is where we draw the line on security theater. Yes, this means actually tracking what got created during setup and cleaning it up—something that sounds obvious until you find a decade of forgotten .tmp directories containing plaintext credentials and verbose error messages describing every vulnerability the installer encountered.

annotations.ai_view: Server applications must be configured to their most secure baseline using hardening guides from both the Australian Signals Directorate and the software vendor, applying whichever guidance is stricter when the two conflict. This prevents security gaps by eliminating unnecessary features, closing default vulnerabilities, and enforcing strong settings before systems go live. Properly hardened servers significantly reduce the attack surface and limit what an attacker can exploit if they gain access.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Apply hardening guidance to your server applications—specifically ASD's stuff and whatever the vendor recommends—and when they inevitably contradict each other (they always do), go with the stricter option because apparently "secure by default" is still a radical concept in 2024. Yes, this means you'll need to actually read both documents, cross-reference them, and make decisions; no, there's no magic tool that does this for you, which is why most organisations just pick one and hope nobody asks questions during an audit.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to disable or remove any user accounts, software components, services, and features on servers that aren't actively needed for operations—essentially removing unnecessary attack surfaces. It matters because unused accounts and services can become security gaps that attackers exploit, and they consume resources while creating maintenance burdens; keeping only what's required reduces the number of potential vulnerabilities you need to monitor and patch.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Strip your servers down to the bare essentials—delete every default user, disable every service you're not actively using, and rip out any functionality that's just sitting there looking decorative. Yes, that thing that came pre-installed and nobody's touched in three years needs to go; it's a door you forgot you had. This is less about paranoia and more about basic math: fewer things running means fewer things an attacker can exploit, which is apparently a controversial position given how many organisations I've seen running SQL Server with Guest enabled.

annotations.ai_view: Server applications must each run under their own user account with only the specific permissions required to operate, rather than sharing accounts or running with excessive privileges. This limits the damage an attacker can do if they compromise an application—they gain only the narrow access that application needs, preventing them from escalating to system-wide control or accessing other applications' data. It also makes it easier to audit what each application is doing and detect suspicious activity.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Run your server apps under dedicated user accounts with only the permissions they actually need to function—not under admin, not under a shared generic account, and definitely not under whatever was convenient at 3am on a Friday. Yes, every organisation knows this is the right move. Yes, every organisation still finds seventeen legacy services happily executing as root because someone forgot it existed in 2009.

annotations.ai_view: Server applications should run under user accounts with minimal file system permissions—only accessing files and directories they genuinely need to function. This limits the damage if an attacker compromises the application, preventing them from reading sensitive data, modifying system files, or spreading malware across the server. It's a foundational containment measure that stops a single compromised service from becoming a full system breach.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Run your server applications under accounts with filesystem permissions locked down to only what they actually need—which, despite what developers claim, is almost never "full access to everything." If your web server is running as root or with blanket read/write permissions across the entire drive, congratulations, you've just handed attackers a skeleton key to your entire system once they compromise that one vulnerable service.

annotations.ai_view: Access rights for database users—including read, insert, update, and delete—must be limited to what their role requires. Role‑based restrictions enforce least privilege and reduce the risk of unauthorized data manipulation.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Give each account just enough rope to do its job, because the last thing you need is the intern dropping the production tables.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires implementing file system-level permissions and access restrictions on the actual database files stored on disk, ensuring that only authorized users and processes can read, modify, or delete them. By restricting file access at the operating system level, you prevent unauthorized personnel from bypassing database security controls to directly manipulate sensitive data. This is particularly important in multi-user environments where database administrators, operators, and applications have different privilege levels and need to be prevented from accessing files outside their designated scope.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Yes, you need to actually lock down the files your database lives on — filesystem permissions, not just relying on whatever access controls the database itself claims to enforce, because apparently we've learned the hard way that a misconfigured OS permission is far easier to exploit than waiting for the DBA to remember their password policy. This is the "belt and suspenders" approach applied to what should have been obvious since the 1990s, yet somehow every second organisation manages to leave their database files world-readable on a shared drive.

annotations.ai_view: When you deploy server applications, you must change, disable or remove any default user accounts and credentials that come pre-configured with the software—these defaults are widely known and easily exploited by attackers. This prevents unauthorised access to critical systems and data, as attackers commonly target default credentials as an initial entry point. Taking this step during setup ensures your systems aren't left vulnerable to exploitation from day one.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Change, disable, or remove any default accounts and credentials that come pre-baked into server applications before you stick them on a network—yes, including that 'admin/admin' combo the vendor swears nobody will ever think to try. This matters because default credentials are the digital equivalent of leaving your front door unlocked with a welcome mat, and attackers will absolutely walk straight through while you're still admiring your shiny new database.

annotations.ai_view: Each server application should have its own dedicated administrator account rather than sharing a single privileged account across multiple applications, so that you can identify exactly which administrator performed which actions and isolate the impact if one account is compromised. This separation makes it harder for attackers to move laterally between systems and helps you audit who did what during security investigations.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Each server application gets its own dedicated admin account rather than sharing a master "break glass in case of emergency" credential across your entire infrastructure—a concept that somehow still shocks organisations that have been running everything under a single "root" user since 2003. This prevents one compromised application from handing an attacker the keys to every other system, which is theoretically excellent until you realize you've now got 47 different passwords to rotate and three of them are written on a Post-it in someone's desk drawer. The control exists because audit trails become meaningless when you can't tell which application actually did something, and privilege creep becomes inevitable when developers just keep adding "temporary" access to whoever asks nicely.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to limit database access so users can only see and work with the data they actually need for their job, using tools like restricted views, role-based permissions, and data masking techniques. This prevents unauthorized viewing of sensitive information and reduces the risk of data breaches or misuse by restricting exposure to only essential data. It's a fundamental way to protect confidential database contents from both malicious insiders and compromised accounts.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Restrict database access so users only see what they actually need to do their job—which sounds obvious until you realize half your organisation has SELECT * privileges and someone's using a production admin account to run reports. Implement this through minimum privileges, views that hide sensitive columns, role-based access controls, and tokenisation where appropriate; it's the database equivalent of not leaving the keys in the ignition, except everyone keeps doing it anyway.

annotations.ai_view: Database servers and web servers must operate on separate systems rather than running together on the same infrastructure. This separation limits the damage an attacker can cause if they compromise a web application—they cannot directly access the database without crossing an additional security boundary. Isolating these functions reduces attack surface and contains breaches to a single tier of your system rather than allowing attackers to pivot directly to sensitive data.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Keep your database servers and web servers on different machines—yes, really, apparently this needs to be explicitly mandated. The theory is sound: if some script kiddie pops your web server through a SQL injection attack, at least they won't be sitting directly on the database itself, though they'll probably get there anyway through your network that wasn't segmented properly. This separation buys you a speed bump, not a wall, but it's the speed bump you're apparently contractually obligated to have now.

annotations.ai_view: Database servers must reside on a separate network segment from user workstations, isolating them from direct client traffic. Network segmentation reduces the attack surface and limits lateral movement if a workstation is compromised.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Put the database in its own VLAN and pretend the workstations can’t find it. It’s the network equivalent of “don’t talk to strangers.”

annotations.ai_view: Restrict database servers so they can only communicate with the specific systems and networks that genuinely need to access them, using network-level controls like firewalls or security groups. This limits the damage an attacker could do if they compromise the database or gain unauthorized network access, since they won't be able to use it as a pivot point to reach unrelated systems or move laterally across your network.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Look, the concept is straightforward: you're going to firewall your database server so only the actual systems that need to talk to it can reach it, rather than letting your entire network treat it like a public kiosk. Yes, this means you'll need to document which servers and applications legitimately require access—which somehow always turns into a six-month archaeology project where nobody remembers why that ancient reporting tool needs direct connectivity. Do it anyway, because an unfiltered database server is basically a neon sign advertising your crown jewels to anyone who gets past your perimeter.

annotations.ai_view: If your database only needs to be accessed locally (from the same server), turn off the database application's network features or configure it to accept connections only from localhost, preventing remote attackers from reaching it over the network. This limits your attack surface by ensuring the database isn't exposed to threats from outside the system or other machines on your network, even if the database software has security vulnerabilities.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: If your database genuinely doesn't need to talk to anything on the network—which, let's be honest, is rarer than you'd think—then yank the network socket out and make it listen only to localhost instead of broadcasting itself to whoever bothers to scan your subnet. This prevents the inevitable situation where some well-meaning developer enables remote access "just in case," and six months later you're explaining to management why attackers found your database before your own staff did.

annotations.ai_view: Database servers used for development, testing, staging and production must be kept completely separate from each other so that problems, unauthorised changes or security incidents in non-production environments cannot affect live systems or data. This separation prevents developers from accidentally or intentionally accessing production data during testing, stops malware or compromised test systems from spreading to production, and ensures that production environments remain stable and secure even if development work introduces vulnerabilities or instability.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Separate your database servers by environment so that a developer's midnight schema experiment or a tester's creative data corruption doesn't accidentally torpedo production data—a concept apparently simple enough to fit on a napkin yet somehow requiring this control to exist because someone's always "just quickly" running queries against prod to debug an issue. Yes, staging counts as its own thing too, not a "basically production" server that people treat like a personal sandbox until everything breaks.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to prevent production database data from being copied into non-production environments (like development or testing) unless those environments have security protections equivalent to production. It matters because production data often contains sensitive information, and if a development or test environment is compromised by an attacker or careless developer, that data exposure could harm people and the organisation.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Don't copy production data into your dev and test environments unless you've somehow convinced yourself that a laptop with a sticky note password is "secured to the same level" as your prod setup—which, let's be honest, nobody actually does. The intent here is sound: production databases contain real customer data, credentials, and other fun things you don't want floating around your engineers' machines, so either sanitise it properly or accept you're running non-prod at production-grade security (spoiler: you're not). Yes, this gets violated constantly because developers need "realistic data" and sanitisation is apparently harder than nuclear physics.

annotations.ai_view: Software must validate all database queries to block harmful commands (such as SQL injection attacks) and ensure they follow correct syntax before execution. This prevents attackers from manipulating queries to access, modify or delete unauthorised data, or to execute unintended operations on your database. Implementing input validation and parameterised queries are practical ways to meet this control.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your developers need to validate every database query before it goes anywhere near your actual database—checking that it's syntactically sound and contains only the data it's supposed to contain. Yes, this means implementing input validation and parameterised queries instead of just concatenating user input into SQL strings like it's 1997, which somehow still happens constantly. It's the control equivalent of "don't leave your keys in the ignition," except hackers have been using those keys for about twenty-five years and apparently it's still worth stating formally.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires developers to use parameterised queries or stored procedures when their software accesses databases, rather than building database commands by concatenating user input directly into query strings. This prevents SQL injection attacks, where attackers insert malicious code through input fields to manipulate or steal data from the database. Using these safer methods keeps user input completely separate from the database instructions, making injection attacks impossible.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Use parameterised queries or stored procedures instead of concatenating user input directly into SQL strings—a practice so fundamental it shouldn't need saying, yet somehow remains the leading cause of database breaches across the Commonwealth. This prevents SQL injection attacks where an attacker can manipulate queries by inserting malicious SQL fragments, because the query structure and data are kept strictly separate. Yes, this means you actually have to write slightly more careful code, but apparently that's controversial.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to encrypt all data transmitted between your web servers and database servers to prevent interception of sensitive information like credentials, personal data, or business records. Unencrypted traffic between these systems can be read by attackers on the network, even within your own infrastructure. Use protocols like TLS/SSL to establish encrypted connections and verify that encryption is active before data flows between these critical systems.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Encrypt the traffic between your web servers and databases, because apparently sending queries and results in plaintext over your network is still somehow a surprise finding in audits. This covers the actual data in transit—use TLS/SSL or equivalent, and yes, that means properly validating certificates and not just ticking the encryption box with a self-signed cert from 2015. It's not glamorous work, but it's the baseline that somehow still needs explaining.

annotations.ai_view: Web applications should be configured to return minimal error messages when database queries fail, avoiding details about database structure, table names, or field layouts that attackers could exploit. Detailed database errors exposed to users or logs can help attackers map your system's architecture and craft targeted injection attacks or other exploits. This control requires hiding technical database details behind generic error messages while logging detailed errors securely for legitimate debugging purposes.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Ensure your web applications keep their mouths shut about database structure—no schema details, table names, or field info in error messages, logs, or responses. Yes, attackers will still find ways to map your database through timing attacks and inference, but at least don't gift-wrap the blueprint by leaking it in a 500 error page. It's security theatre, but it's the kind that occasionally actually works.

annotations.ai_view: Check all files moving through network gateways or cross-domain solutions to ensure they contain only expected content and haven't been tampered with or infected. This prevents malware, data exfiltration, and policy violations from crossing security boundaries where manual inspection may be impractical. Content validation acts as a critical checkpoint, catching threats that signature-based scanning alone might miss.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Every file that enters or exits your network through a gateway or cross-domain solution needs to be examined for malicious content, policy violations, or other nastiness—because apparently people still try to sneak executable payloads through file transfers, and we have to pretend this is surprising. This means actually running content validation tools (antivirus, sandboxing, metadata inspection, whatever you can afford) rather than just logging the transfer and hoping for the best. Yes, this slows things down and generates false positives that users will complain about; yes, someone will eventually ask why legitimate PDFs are being blocked; implement it anyway because a compromised file is infinitely worse than a Friday afternoon of help desk tickets.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that any files moving into or out of your organisation through gateways or content delivery systems must be converted to a safe format (such as converting documents to PDF or removing potentially dangerous code). This process removes hidden threats like malware or malicious macros that attackers could use to compromise your systems. It's essential because file conversion acts as a security filter, preventing dangerous content from entering your network while still allowing legitimate work to proceed.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: When files cross a gateway or CDS boundary, they must be converted to a 'safe' format—think PDF instead of Word, or plain text instead of Excel—because apparently we still haven't figured out how to trust file formats. Yes, this means your users will complain endlessly about losing formatting, macros, and their will to live, but it does genuinely strip out embedded nasties that could phone home or execute arbitrary code, so there's that.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires your organisation to clean or strip potentially dangerous content from files that move in or out of your network through gateways or cross-domain solutions. It matters because files can carry malware, exploits, or malicious code that bypass normal security checks, so removing threats before they enter your systems prevents compromise and data theft.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: When files cross your gateway or CDS boundary, you need to strip out anything that could be weaponised—macros, scripts, embedded objects, the works—because apparently humans will click literally anything. Yes, this means your Word documents arrive as neutered shadows of their former selves, and yes, you'll still get that one user complaining their Excel file "doesn't work right" when it's actually just missing the macro that was definitely a virus. Do it anyway, because the alternative is watching attackers waltz through your gates via a "totally legitimate" PDF.

annotations.ai_view: Your organization must scan all files moving through network gateways or cross-domain solutions with at least two different antivirus engines before allowing them through. This layered approach catches malware that a single scanner might miss, since different engines use different detection methods and databases. It's a practical way to prevent infected files from entering or leaving your network, reducing the risk of malware spreading through file transfers.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Run every file crossing your gateway or CDS through at least two different antivirus engines before letting it through—because apparently one vendor's signature database is just too trusting. Yes, this means your already-screaming gateway now needs even more screening, and yes, organisations consistently skip this because "performance," but multi-engine scanning does genuinely catch the stuff that lone vendors miss, so here we are.

annotations.ai_view: Archive files (like ZIP or TAR files) passing through your organisation's gateways or controlled data services must be extracted and scanned for malware and policy violations before they're allowed through—compressed files can hide threats that standard scanning misses. This prevents attackers from smuggling malicious content, sensitive data, or policy-breaking files into your network by disguising them inside archives. Without unpacking, your security controls become ineffective since they can't see what's actually inside the compressed container.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: When archive files (you know, those zip files everyone loves to send through your gateway because they think compression magically makes malware disappear) arrive via gateways or Content Disarm and Sanitization systems, you need to actually extract and scan them before letting them through—not just check the wrapper like some kind of security theatre. Yes, this means your gateway needs enough resources to handle the inevitable barrage of nested RAR files someone's definitely going to test this with. Spoiler alert: most gateways you'll encounter have this turned off because it slows things down, which is exactly why you're reading this after an incident.

annotations.ai_view: When your organisation receives archive files (like ZIP or RAR files), you must extract and process them in a way that doesn't overwhelm or disable your content filtering systems—such as by unpacking too many files at once or files that are extremely large. This protects against both accidental disruptions to security monitoring and deliberate attacks that use archive bombs or other techniques to bypass your defences by exhausting system resources.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: When you extract archive files at your gateway, don't just yeet them all at once like you're speed-running a pentesting challenge—do it methodically so your content filters don't choke and your systems don't fall over. Turns out, processing fifty thousand files simultaneously makes security tools about as responsive as a Windows XP box, which is fine if you enjoy living dangerously. Control your extraction rate and resources, because apparently this needs spelling out.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must decrypt encrypted files at gateway or content delivery system checkpoints so security tools can scan them for malware, data breaches, or policy violations before they enter or leave your network. This is necessary because encrypted files bypass standard content filtering, creating a security blind spot where threats could pass undetected. The decryption happens temporarily for inspection purposes and is essential to maintain visibility over data flows without weakening your encryption protections.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your gateway has to decrypt encrypted files so it can actually look inside them and make sure nobody's smuggling malware or classified shopping lists through your perimeter—because apparently "encrypted" and "security" are somehow at odds when a content filter needs to do its job. Yes, this means you're creating a decryption chokepoint that's simultaneously a prime target and a performance nightmare, but that's the trade-off between letting bad things through undetected and knowing exactly what's moving across your boundary. Do it anyway, and yes, you'll need a very solid key management story to explain why you're decrypting everything in transit.

annotations.ai_view: You must review and verify data transfer logs (records showing what data moved into or out of your systems) at least once per month to check that only authorised transfers occurred and to detect any suspicious activity. This helps you spot unauthorized data movement, insider threats, or compromised accounts that might be exfiltrating sensitive information before they cause serious harm. Regular verification is a practical detective control that catches problems early and demonstrates you're actively monitoring data security.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to spot-check your data transfer logs at least monthly—specifically a sample of them, since "partially verified" is apparently the hill we're dying on instead of just auditing the whole thing. Nobody's thrilled about this control because it basically guarantees you'll miss the exfiltration that happened on the Tuesday you didn't check, but it does force you to at least *occasionally* look at what's actually leaving your systems instead of hoping it doesn't.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to physically protect network equipment located in accessible areas—such as switches, routers, and servers in common spaces—using measures like lockable cabinets, cages, or restricted rooms to prevent damage, theft, or tampering. It matters because network devices in public areas are vulnerable to deliberate sabotage, accidental damage, or theft by unauthorised people, which could disrupt critical services or create security weaknesses that attackers could exploit. Without these protections, an adversary could easily unplug equipment, install malicious devices, or access sensitive network connections.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to physically secure network equipment that sits in public areas—you know, the switch someone could just yank out of the wall or the router mounted in the lobby that nobody's watching. Think bollards, locked cabinets, cable ties that actually discourage tampering, or at minimum keeping your critical gear out of the hallway where every contractor and their mate can give it a friendly kick. Yes, this seems obvious, and yet.

annotations.ai_view: Before letting employees use personal phones or computers to access your organisation's systems or data, get legal advice to understand the risks and obligations involved. This matters because personal devices fall outside your security controls, may contain unauthorised software, and create legal complications around data ownership, privacy laws, and incident response. Legal review upfront helps you set appropriate boundaries and protections before problems occur.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Before you let Karen from Accounts check her email on her personal iPhone, get your legal team involved—because apparently the lawyers need to decide which of your organisation's terrible security decisions they're willing to be complicit in. This applies across all classifications, which means yes, even for that unclassified spreadsheet someone insists is fine to sync to their home laptop. You'll find that most organisations skip this step entirely and just hope nothing goes wrong, then act shocked when a contractor's dodgy Android device becomes a pivot point in a breach.

annotations.ai_view: Personnel must receive clear advice about the specific risks they face when using mobile devices in other countries, such as hostile surveillance, compromised networks, and local legal requirements that may differ from Australia. This matters because overseas travel creates higher exposure to theft, interception, and government access to sensitive data—awareness helps staff make better decisions about what information to access and how to protect their devices. Practical guidance before departure is more effective than hoping people will recognize risks on their own.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Tell your staff that taking their phones overseas is risky—specifically, brief them on the increased exposure to local surveillance, network interception, physical theft, and social engineering in foreign jurisdictions before they pack their bags. Yes, this is technically a "control," though it mostly requires you to deliver a talk that people will forget by the time they've cleared security at the airport. Document that you delivered this briefing anyway, because audit trails are apparently what keep the lights on.

annotations.ai_view: Personnel are advised to follow a series of mobile‑device hygiene practices — such as never leaving devices unattended, avoiding untrusted networks, using VPNs, and disabling unused radios — to reduce loss, theft, and interception risks.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: A laundry list of “don’t do this” that everyone will ignore until a device goes missing — then the audit team will point to this control and sigh.

annotations.ai_view: On return staff must wipe and reset all devices and media, revoke any credentials that were out of their control, and flag any device whose integrity is uncertain. This prevents lingering malware or stolen credentials from persisting.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Wipe everything, burn the credentials, and write a confession if you’re not sure the phone is clean. The only thing more thorough is the audit that follows.

annotations.ai_view: During initial setup of network devices, you must change, disable, or remove any default user accounts and credentials that come pre-configured from the manufacturer. Default credentials are widely known and publicly documented, making them an easy entry point for attackers to gain unauthorised access to your network infrastructure. This control ensures that only authorised personnel can access and manage your network devices.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Change, disable, or remove every default account and credential that ships with your network devices during setup—yes, that includes the "admin/admin" combinations that manufacturers helpfully bake in and apparently expect you to forget about. This matters because default credentials are the first thing attackers try, and leaving them active is basically handing someone a keyring to your infrastructure while you're setting up the device. You'd think this wouldn't need to be a control, but here we are.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must not use SNMP versions 1 or 2 on any networks, as these older protocols lack encryption and authentication mechanisms, allowing attackers to intercept sensitive network management information and potentially compromise network devices. Instead, use SNMP version 3, which provides encrypted communication and strong authentication. This prevents unauthorised access to network configuration details and reduces the risk of network devices being manipulated or monitored by malicious actors.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Don't use SNMP v1 or v2 anywhere on your network—yes, we know you've probably got some ancient Xerox printer and a Cisco device from 2003 still happily broadcasting credentials in cleartext, but they've got to go. These protocols send authentication and data unencrypted across the wire like it's 1995, which makes them a security control's fever dream and an attacker's shopping list. Migrate to SNMP v3 (which actually has encryption and authentication) or better yet, find monitoring solutions that don't rely on a protocol that treats your network like a public bulletin board.

annotations.ai_view: Network devices come with default community strings (shared passwords) that are widely known and documented, making them easy targets for attackers to access and modify your network settings. This control requires you to change these defaults and turn off write permissions so that only authorized administrators can make configuration changes, preventing unauthorized people from tampering with your network infrastructure. Taking these steps closes a simple but critical vulnerability that attackers routinely exploit to gain control of network devices.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to change the embarrassingly obvious default SNMP passwords (usually "public" and "private" — yes, really) that ship on network gear, and you absolutely must turn off write access unless you enjoy watching someone casually reconfigure your entire network from anywhere on the planet. This is genuinely one of the easiest wins in security and yet somehow remains the most reliably violated control across every organisation that's ever existed.

annotations.ai_view: Ensure every wireless device connecting to your network has Wi-Fi Alliance certification, which verifies it meets established security and compatibility standards. This reduces the risk of devices with weak security implementation or undisclosed vulnerabilities being used on your network. Certification provides independent assurance that devices properly support security protocols like WPA2 and WPA3, protecting against unauthorized access and data interception.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to buy wireless devices that have Wi-Fi Alliance certification, because apparently we can't trust that the router someone grabbed from the bargain bin actually works properly or won't silently exfiltrate your credentials to Belarus. It's the bare minimum gate-keeping that somehow still requires enforcement at most organisations, suggesting that "wireless device" procurement often defaults to "whatever was cheapest on Amazon yesterday."

annotations.ai_view: Disable remote management access to wireless access points over the wireless network itself—only allow administrative connections through wired network connections. This prevents attackers who have gained wireless access to your network from directly reconfiguring or compromising the access points, which could otherwise let them expand their control across your entire wireless infrastructure. It forces administrators to physically connect to the network via Ethernet, adding a practical barrier that makes unauthorized changes much harder.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Disable wireless access to your wireless access point's admin interface—yes, you need to manage the thing that manages your wireless, but only over a wired connection, because apparently people keep handing out admin credentials to anyone with a laptop in the parking lot. This forces attackers to at least physically touch your network instead of just lounging on your guest SSID with a coffee, which is technically a win.

annotations.ai_view: Change the default network names (SSIDs) that come pre-configured on wireless access points before deploying them. Default SSIDs are publicly known and advertise both the manufacturer and model of equipment, making it easier for attackers to identify vulnerable devices and launch targeted attacks. This simple step removes an obvious fingerprint that attackers use for reconnaissance.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Change your wireless access points' default SSIDs to something other than what the manufacturer printed on the box—yes, this apparently needs to be a formal control because organisations routinely ship networks broadcasting "Linksys" or "TP-Link Guest Network" to the entire suburb. A predictable SSID combined with default credentials is essentially a welcome mat for attackers, so at minimum make them guess what you've called the thing. It won't stop a determined adversary, but it will stop the automated scripts and your bored neighbours from trying the obvious stuff first.

annotations.ai_view: Hide identifying information in your wireless network names so outsiders cannot easily determine which organisation owns the network, where your premises are located, or what the network is used for. An obvious network name like "CompanyName-Building3-Finance" makes it easier for attackers to target your organisation or specific locations and systems. Use generic or meaningless names instead to reduce reconnaissance opportunities and avoid broadcasting sensitive operational details.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Don't name your WiFi "AustralianTaxOffice-Building3-SecureNetwork" or anything equally helpful to someone scoping your premises from the car park—use something generic that gives away nothing about who you are, where you're located, or what the network does. Yes, this means you can't name it after your department, yes, people will complain it's confusing, and no, that's not a valid reason to ignore it. It's a trivial information disclosure control that nonetheless requires the discipline to resist the urge to be helpful with your naming conventions.

annotations.ai_view: Wireless networks should broadcast their network names (SSIDs) openly rather than hiding them, as this improves security visibility and makes networks easier to manage without creating meaningful obstacles for attackers. Hidden networks can encourage weaker security practices and complicate legitimate user connections, while visible SSIDs allow your organisation to clearly identify which wireless networks are authorised and operating under your control. This straightforward approach supports better network governance and reduces confusion about which access points users should connect to.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Keep your wireless network's SSID broadcast enabled so clients can actually find and connect to your access points—yes, this is apparently necessary to state explicitly because security theatre convinces people that hiding the network name provides meaningful protection when it really just creates user friction and forces them toward more dangerous workarounds. Disabling SSID broadcast doesn't stop determined attackers (who'll find your network anyway), but it does reliably break legitimate connections and tempt users to manually configure their devices or worse, connect to rogue networks. Think of it as the networking equivalent of requiring a secret handshake instead of just putting up a sign.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to avoid manually assigning fixed IP addresses to wireless devices, instead using dynamic assignment methods like DHCP. Static IP addresses on wireless networks increase security risks by making devices easier to locate, track, and target; they also complicate device management and can lead to address conflicts when devices move between networks. Dynamic addressing provides better mobility support, simplifies administration, and reduces the attack surface by making device locations less predictable.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Don't assign static IP addresses to wireless devices—use DHCP instead. Yes, this is the control that exists because someone, somewhere, thought hardcoding 192.168.1.50 into their laptop was a clever networking hack, and somehow it keeps happening across government organisations. The practical upside is that dynamic addressing reduces address conflicts and makes device tracking harder for attackers, though let's be honest, if someone's already on your wireless network, the IP they got is probably the least of your problems.

annotations.ai_view: Do not rely on MAC address filtering as your primary method to control which devices can connect to wireless networks. MAC addresses can be easily spoofed or cloned by attackers, making this control ineffective at preventing unauthorized access; instead, use stronger authentication mechanisms like WPA2/WPA3 with robust passwords or certificate-based authentication to verify device legitimacy.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Don't rely on MAC address filtering as your wireless security blanket—it's trivially spoofed and everyone knows it, yet somehow it still shows up in half the network diagrams you'll ever see. Use proper authentication (WPA2/3, 802.1X) instead, because filtering based on hardware addresses is like locking your front door with a Post-it note that says "only nice people allowed." Yes, this control explicitly tells you *not* to do this thing that seems like it should help but absolutely doesn't.

annotations.ai_view: Network access must use 802.1X with EAP‑TLS for mutual authentication, and all other EAP methods must be disabled on both supplicants and authentication servers.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Only EAP‑TLS is allowed—because supporting PEAP or TTLS would be too convenient for attackers.

annotations.ai_view: Only evaluated (certified) supplicants, authenticators, and authentication servers may be deployed for 802.1X implementations.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You can’t just download any RADIUS server; it has to be on the approved list, which is surprisingly short.

annotations.ai_view: Both devices and human users must present X.509 certificates when authenticating via 802.1X.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Every laptop and IoT toaster now needs a client cert—because passwords are so last decade.

annotations.ai_view: Certificates for 802.1X must be issued by an evaluated certificate authority or generated within a hardware security module.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Self‑signed certs are a hard no; you need a proper PKI or an HSM, which everyone loves to budget for.

annotations.ai_view: Certificates must be safeguarded with access controls and encryption, and certificates issued to people must require authentication (e.g., PIN or biometric) before they can be used.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your user certs sit in a smart card or TPM, because leaving a PFX file on the desktop is a classic.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that cached authentication credentials for wireless network access (Pairwise Master Keys) expire and be refreshed at least every 24 hours, rather than being stored indefinitely. This limits the window of opportunity for attackers to use a compromised cached credential to gain network access, reducing the risk from credential theft or device compromise. Regular re-authentication also ensures that access permissions are periodically re-validated, removing users who should no longer have network access.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Yeah, so your network's going to cache those 802.1X authentication credentials anyway because reasons, but you need to make sure it forgets them after 24 hours maximum—otherwise you're basically handing out all-day passes to anyone who managed to grab a PMK earlier. It's the security equivalent of "fine, you can keep the spare key, but we're changing the locks daily," which sounds reasonable until you realize nobody's actually changing the locks. Just set it and move on; this one's mercifully straightforward and almost never the smoking gun in a breach, but someone will definitely ask about it during your audit.

annotations.ai_view: Use WPA3-Enterprise in 192-bit mode to encrypt all wireless network traffic, ensuring that data transmitted over your organisation's Wi-Fi cannot be intercepted or tampered with by unauthorised parties. This is the strongest widely available wireless security standard and protects against both current and near-future threats to confidential information. This requirement applies across all classification levels, making it essential for securing any sensitive data accessed wirelessly.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to use WPA3-Enterprise with 192-bit encryption for every wireless network—yes, even that guest Wi-Fi nobody's supposed to be using anyway. It's the gold standard for keeping eavesdroppers out of your traffic, assuming your users actually connect to the right network and your APs are configured correctly, which statistically they aren't. If you're still running WPA2, congratulations on living in 2015; time to upgrade before someone finds out.

annotations.ai_view: Organizations must ensure their wireless networks operate on frequencies that are sufficiently separated from neighboring wireless networks to prevent interference, signal degradation, or unintended cross-communication. This separation prevents attackers from exploiting overlapping frequencies to intercept traffic, inject packets, or cause denial-of-service conditions. Proper frequency planning protects network availability and confidentiality, particularly in shared environments like multi-tenant buildings or congested urban areas.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Ensure your wireless networks don't operate on the same frequency as your neighbour's router, your building's access points, or literally anything else broadcasting on 2.4GHz—which, let's face it, is about as crowded as a shopping centre car park on Boxing Day. This prevents interference that degrades performance and creates convenient gaps in coverage that users will somehow always find and complain about. Spoiler alert: most organisations discover this requirement exists only after their wireless network mysteriously stops working and everyone spends three days blaming the ISP.

annotations.ai_view: Wireless access points must be configured to enable the 802.11w amendment, which protects management frames from being intercepted, forged, or replayed by attackers. Without this protection, adversaries can perform denial-of-service attacks or force devices to disconnect from legitimate networks. This control ensures that the administrative communications between devices and access points remain secure and trustworthy.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your wireless access points need to support and enable 802.11w (Management Frame Protection), which stops attackers from spoofing deauthentication frames and kicking users offline or intercepting their connection attempts—a surprisingly effective attack that somehow still works because, well, most places don't enable this. Yes, it's a checkbox in the config that actually matters, despite living in the same paragraph as seventeen other things nobody implements. Just turn it on; it's been a standard for over a decade.

annotations.ai_view: Deploy multiple low-power wireless access points instead of fewer high-power ones to limit the signal range of your network beyond your physical boundaries. This reduces the risk of unauthorized users outside your building from detecting and accessing your wireless network, while still providing coverage where you actually need it. Containing your wireless footprint makes it harder for attackers to find and target your network infrastructure.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Deploy lots of weak access points instead of a few screaming ones—because apparently, when your WiFi signal reaches the parking lot three blocks away, it becomes everyone's problem. This reduces your wireless footprint's attack surface and makes it harder for random people to connect, though in practice most organisations will just slap down whatever APs came in the bulk order and call it a day. The math checks out: smaller coverage areas mean fewer external parties can feasibly reach your network, which is nice when people actually follow this.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must deploy host-based intrusion prevention or endpoint detection and response software on all workstations to detect and stop malicious activity at the device level. This matters because workstations are frequent targets for attacks, and local protection catches threats that network defences miss—stopping malware, suspicious behaviour, and unauthorised system changes before they can spread or cause damage.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Install either a Host-based Intrusion Prevention System (HIPS) or Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solution on your workstations—basically, software that watches your users' machines for suspicious activity and either blocks it outright or alerts you so you can deal with it later (spoiler: you won't deal with it later). This sits on top of your firewall and antivirus, because apparently those two layers weren't enough to stop someone from clicking a malicious link or running that sketchy executable they definitely shouldn't have. It's actually a sensible control that works reasonably well when properly configured, tuned, and not immediately disabled by frustrated users who find it slowing down their systems.

annotations.ai_view: Organizations must create and keep current a written policy that sets clear rules for how removable media (USB drives, external hard drives, memory cards, etc.) can be used within the organization. This policy matters because removable media represents a significant security risk—data can be easily stolen, malware can be introduced, or sensitive information can be lost if devices are misplaced. A well-maintained policy helps reduce these risks by establishing who can use removable media, what data can be stored on it, and what security measures must be applied.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to write down the rules for how your organisation actually uses USB sticks, external drives, and memory cards—then make sure those rules exist somewhere official and that people theoretically follow them. It's the control equivalent of posting a sign that says "please don't steal the office supplies," except this one genuinely matters because someone *will* email the entire client database to their personal Gmail account if you don't document what not to do. Update it regularly so it reflects reality rather than the fantasy you created three years ago and forgot about.

annotations.ai_view: When your organisation destroys physical media (like hard drives, USB devices, or paper documents), you must use equipment that has been officially approved by either the Security Construction and Equipment Committee or ASIO. This ensures media is destroyed thoroughly enough that sensitive data cannot be recovered, protecting your organisation from data breaches if old equipment or documents fall into the wrong hands. Using non-approved or improvised destruction methods risks leaving recoverable traces of classified or sensitive information.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to destroy media using equipment that's been blessed by either the Security Construction and Equipment Committee or ASIO—because apparently your industrial shredder from the office supply catalogue doesn't count, even though it probably works just fine. This is one of those controls that sits at the intersection of "technically sensible" (you do want to actually destroy sensitive data) and "practically ignored" (most organisations just outsource this to whoever's cheapest and calls it compliant). The approval requirement exists so that when you inevitably have an audit, you can point to something official-looking rather than explaining why you used Dave from facilities with a sledgehammer.

annotations.ai_view: Network devices that handle virtual networks must use separate physical network ports for each distinct security level or domain, rather than mixing them on the same port. This prevents accidental or malicious traffic from crossing security boundaries when virtual network configurations are misconfigured or compromised. Isolating security domains at the physical layer provides a fundamental boundary that virtual network settings alone cannot guarantee.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your VLAN management device can't be that lazy—if you're segregating traffic between security domains, each one gets its own physical port instead of sharing a trunk line like some kind of network efficiency speedrun. Yes, it's more cabling and configuration; no, this isn't optional if you actually want that VLAN separation to mean something rather than being a feel-good checkbox. This is what happens when someone finally asks "wait, if an attacker compromises the VLAN tag processing, what stops them jumping domains?" and the answer is "well, at least they're stuck on one physical wire."

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must install security updates on mobile devices immediately when vendors release them, rather than delaying or deferring patches. This prevents attackers from exploiting known vulnerabilities that could compromise sensitive data or enable unauthorised access to your systems. Rapid patching is critical because mobile devices often access corporate networks and hold valuable information, making them attractive targets for cyber attacks.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Yes, you actually need to patch your mobile devices the moment security updates drop—not whenever you get around to it, not after the next mandatory restart, but *as soon as they become available*. This means configuring auto-update where possible and treating manual patches like they're on fire, because threat actors have approximately thirty seconds to weaponise vulnerabilities before someone's CEO clicks a dodgy email link on their iPhone. Good luck explaining to your board why a six-month-old patch gap turned into a data breach.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that when encrypting data transmitted over TLS connections, you must use the AES-GCM cipher suite, which combines strong encryption with built-in authentication to detect tampering. AES-GCM is considered cryptographically robust and resistant to known attacks, making it essential for protecting sensitive data in transit across networks. By mandating this specific algorithm, the control ensures consistent, standards-based protection for communications involving classified or sensitive government information.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Mandate AES-GCM for TLS encryption because apparently we need to specify the exact algorithm now, not just "use TLS" like normal people do. This gives you authenticated encryption that simultaneously scrambles your data and prevents tampering, which is objectively better than the alternatives, though you'll find half your legacy systems still choking on cipher negotiation. At least when your audit fails, you'll know it's not because the cryptography was weak.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that when renegotiating TLS connections (re-establishing encryption parameters mid-session), only the server can initiate the process—clients cannot request renegotiation. This prevents attackers from exploiting client-initiated renegotiation to inject malicious data, inject compression-based attacks, or cause denial of service by forcing expensive cryptographic operations. By restricting renegotiation to server control, you maintain tighter security boundaries and reduce the attack surface on your encrypted connections.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Only let the server ask for TLS renegotiation, never the client—because apparently someone decided that giving clients veto power over cryptographic handshakes was a security incident waiting to happen. It's a narrow technical requirement that blocks a surprisingly common attack vector, though in practice most people either disable renegotiation entirely or never think about it at all. If you're actually configuring this, you're already ahead of 95% of organisations that have TLS running somewhere and have never considered who gets to initiate these conversations.

annotations.ai_view: The control requires that TLS connections use ephemeral Diffie‑Hellman (DHE) or elliptic‑curve Diffie‑Hellman (ECDHE) for key establishment, providing forward secrecy. This prevents compromise of long‑term private keys from exposing past session traffic.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Enable DHE/ECDHE so that even if the server’s private key leaks, old traffic stays encrypted—assuming you actually configured it and didn’t just tick a box.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that organisations disable or avoid Anonymous Diffie-Hellman (anon-DH) cipher suites when configuring TLS connections, as these ciphers provide no server authentication and leave communications vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. Anonymous DH allows an attacker to intercept and manipulate encrypted traffic without being detected, defeating the primary security purpose of using TLS. By prohibiting this weak option, organisations ensure that TLS connections always authenticate the server and provide genuine protection for sensitive data in transit.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Don't use anonymous Diffie-Hellman (ADH) cipher suites when setting up TLS—it's the cryptographic equivalent of showing up to a secure meeting wearing a name tag that says "ATTACKER WELCOME." ADH provides zero authentication of the server, meaning an adversary can perform a textbook man-in-the-middle attack while your application happily exchanges keys with them. Yes, every TLS library lets you disable this by default, and yes, you still somehow find it enabled in production.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that digital certificates used to establish secure TLS connections use the SHA-2 hashing algorithm (such as SHA-256) rather than weaker alternatives like SHA-1. SHA-2-based certificates provide stronger cryptographic protection against tampering and forgery, ensuring that the identity verification during encrypted communications remains trustworthy. This is essential for preventing man-in-the-middle attacks and maintaining the integrity of sensitive data transmitted over networks.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Use SHA-2-based certificates for your TLS connections, because apparently SHA-1 certificates still exist in the wild despite being cryptographically dead for longer than some junior developers have been employed. This means your server certificates and the chain leading up to them need to use SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512 — not the deprecated SHA-1 that your legacy systems are screaming about. Yes, you'll probably find something still using SHA-1 during your next audit; no, that's not a reason to skip this control.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that Transport Layer Security connections use SHA-2 for generating message authentication codes and deriving encryption keys, rather than weaker alternatives like SHA-1. SHA-2 provides stronger cryptographic integrity and resistance to attacks, protecting the confidentiality and authenticity of data transmitted over your network connections. Implementing this ensures your organisation uses current cryptographic standards to defend against both known vulnerabilities and emerging threats to encrypted communications.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Use SHA-2 for HMAC and PRF functions in your TLS configurations—because apparently we still need to tell people not to use SHA-1 in 2024, which is somehow both obvious and chronically neglected in the wild. Yes, this means checking your cipher suites and TLS profiles actually match what you think they do, not what the vendor claimed during the sales pitch. It's depressingly common to find organisations running production systems with weaker hashing algorithms because no one bothered to validate the crypto stack post-deployment.

annotations.ai_view: Privileged human users must operate from separate privileged and unprivileged operating environments. Using distinct workstations reduces the risk that privileged credentials are exposed to everyday threats.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Give admins a “clean” laptop for admin tasks and a “dirty” one for email—because they’ll definitely keep them separate.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to physically or logically separate the systems and networks used to manage your IT infrastructure from both your general business network and internet access. This separation prevents attackers who compromise regular user systems or gain internet access from reaching your administrative tools and accounts, which are high-value targets that could give them broad control over your entire IT environment. Practical approaches include using dedicated management networks with restricted access, air-gapped administrative workstations, or secure jump servers that enforce additional authentication before allowing administrative connections.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Keep your administrative infrastructure—the keys to your kingdom—physically or logically separated from everywhere else so that when (not if) someone compromises your general network, they don't immediately gain root access to everything. This means your domain controllers, system administration tools, and privileged access workstations should live in their own walled garden with tightly controlled ingress/egress, because apparently the same people who can't be bothered to patch their desktops will absolutely need to administer critical systems from the coffee shop network. It's basic hygiene, costs almost nothing to implement properly, and somehow remains the exception rather than the rule.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that only designated administrative infrastructure—not user workstations, servers, or other general network devices—can initiate management traffic to your systems. It prevents unauthorized personnel or compromised devices from attempting to reconfigure, monitor, or control network equipment by restricting management access to a secure, controlled source. This limits attack surface and helps ensure only trusted administrators can manage critical infrastructure.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Restrict all network management traffic—your SSH sessions, SNMP queries, configuration pushes, and whatever else you use to poke at your infrastructure—to originate exclusively from designated administrative infrastructure, because apparently letting developers manage switches from their laptops was a security incident waiting to happen. This means your jump hosts, bastion servers, or whatever you're calling them this quarter need to be the only place management commands can come from, which sounds simple until you remember that someone's definitely going to need "just this once" access from their home office at 2 AM. Properly implemented, this stops an attacker who compromises a regular workstation from pivoting directly into your network gear—theoretically.

annotations.ai_view: Administrative staff must use dedicated jump servers as an intermediate step to access and manage systems, rather than connecting directly to production infrastructure. This approach creates an audit trail of administrative actions, isolates privileged access from regular networks, and reduces the risk of compromised credentials being used to directly attack critical systems. Jump servers act as a security checkpoint that can enforce stronger authentication, monitor suspicious activity, and contain the impact of compromised administrative accounts.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Route all your administrative access through dedicated jump servers instead of connecting directly to systems—because apparently we still need to learn that giving everyone direct admin access was a mistake, even though we've known this since 1995. This creates an audit trail, lets you enforce MFA, and concentrates your monitoring burden in one place rather than trying to police a thousand individual admin workstations, which is objectively impossible. Yes, it adds a hop to your workflow; no, this doesn't justify building shadow infrastructure that bypasses it.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that any executable files entering your network through external gateways or content delivery systems are automatically run in an isolated sandbox environment where their behaviour can be monitored for malicious activity. This approach catches sophisticated malware that might bypass static scanning tools by detecting what files actually do when executed, rather than just examining their code or signatures. It's a critical defence layer that stops infected files from reaching your systems even if they've been designed to evade traditional security checks.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Every executable that crosses your gateway or comes through a content delivery system gets automatically sandboxed to see if it tries anything shifty—because apparently we still live in a world where people download things without thinking. Yes, this means you need actual sandbox infrastructure running 24/7, which everyone budgets for enthusiastically until quarter three. The upside: you'll catch the obvious stuff that slipped past your email filters, assuming your sandbox doesn't just time out and let it through anyway.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that when you use application control rules based on file paths, you restrict who can modify approved files and write to approved folders—only users with legitimate business need should have these permissions. This matters because it prevents unauthorized changes to critical files and prevents malware or compromised user accounts from writing malicious code to system folders. By limiting write access to trusted users only, you reduce the risk of attackers modifying applications or system files to establish persistence or escalate their access.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Restrict who can modify whitelisted files and write to whitelisted folders—basically, lock down your blessed applications so random users can't fumble with them and introduce malware through a backdoor you graciously left open yourself. Yes, this means actually enforcing permissions on the stuff you've already said is safe, not just hoping people will read the memo about approved software. It's the control that makes application whitelisting work instead of becoming security theatre with extra steps.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that organisations ensure any external service providers—including any contractors they hire—properly protect Australian government data and information they access or handle. You need to verify through contracts and oversight that these providers implement security measures appropriate to the sensitivity of the data, creating a chain of accountability that prevents sensitive information from being compromised when work is outsourced. This matters because outsourced services are a common security weak point; if a service provider's security is inadequate, your organisation remains responsible for protecting government information.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to contractually require your service providers—and their service providers, and their service providers' service providers—to actually protect your data rather than, say, storing it in a publicly accessible S3 bucket or emailing it to their personal Gmail. This sounds obvious until you realise most organisations discover this requirement exists only after the breach, at which point the contract becomes excellent evidence for your lawyers. Make sure the protection level matches your data's classification, because requiring bank-vault security for your unclassified meeting notes is wasteful, but requiring it for PROTECTED data is just basic survival.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that when staff use personal devices to access sensitive or protected government information, that data must be kept completely separate from personal files and applications on the device. This separation prevents sensitive data from being exposed if the device is lost, stolen, or compromised, and ensures government information can be removed without affecting the user's personal content. It's essential because personal devices lack the security controls of managed government equipment and are more likely to be breached or used in unsafe environments.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to make sure that when someone checks their work email on their personal phone—which they're absolutely going to do anyway—the OFFICIAL:Sensitive or PROTECTED data stays completely separated from their cat photos and banking apps. Technically this means using containerisation, separate user profiles, or device management tools that enforce a clean partition; practically, it means accepting that humans will find creative workarounds unless you make compliance easier than the alternative. The spirit of the thing is sound—don't let sensitive government data get accidentally backed up to someone's personal cloud account or exfiltrated via their kid's TikTok habit—but you'll spend more time explaining this control to people who've already connected their personal device to the network than you will actually implementing it.

annotations.ai_view: Multi‑factor authentication must combine something the user has with something they know, or a possession factor unlocked by a knowledge or biometric factor. This defines acceptable factor pairs.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: The manual spells out the only acceptable MFA combos — because ‘any two factors’ was too vague for the auditors. Expect vendors to sell you ‘compliant’ tokens that barely meet the spec.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that any credentials stored on your systems must be protected using one of three methods: a dedicated password manager, a hardware security module, or cryptographic techniques (salting, hashing, and stretching) before storing them in a database. This matters because unprotected credentials are a high-value target for attackers—if compromised, they can be used to gain unauthorized access to other systems and data. By enforcing strong protection methods, you significantly reduce the risk that stolen credentials can actually be used for malicious purposes.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Store your credentials somewhere actually secure instead of in a sticky note under your keyboard or a spreadsheet titled "passwords_FINAL_v3_REAL.xlsx"—use a password manager, HSM, or at minimum salt-hash-stretch them in your database like it's 2024 and not 2004. Yes, this means your database admin can't just read passwords in plaintext, and yes, this apparently needs to be spelled out. Everyone nods during the briefing, then deploys systems with credentials stored one obfuscation away from plain text anyway.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to automatically lock user accounts after five unsuccessful login attempts, preventing attackers from repeatedly guessing passwords. This significantly slows down brute-force attacks and credential-based intrusions, which are common attack vectors targeting your systems. The exception for break glass accounts ensures administrators can still access systems during emergencies even if normal accounts are locked.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your system needs to automatically lock user accounts after five failed login attempts, because apparently we've learned nothing from the last two decades of breaches and someone still needs to be told this isn't optional. The one exception is break glass accounts—those emergency backdoors everyone forgets about until 3am on a Sunday—which get to skip this control because operational panic trumps security hygiene. Yes, someone will complain that five attempts is too strict; no, they won't implement it anyway, which is why you'll be documenting this non-compliance in your next audit.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires your organisation to automatically disable unprivileged user accounts that haven't been used for 45 consecutive days. This matters because inactive accounts become security risks—they're attractive targets for attackers, may retain access to sensitive data, and are harder to monitor for suspicious activity. Regular account suspension reduces your organisation's attack surface and ensures that access rights stay aligned with actual business needs.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Disable unprivileged user accounts after 45 days of no login activity—a straightforward concept that somehow trips up every organisation claiming they take security seriously. This prevents zombie accounts from lingering indefinitely as convenient backdoors for attackers, though you'll spend considerable time explaining to users why their account got suspended because they took a long weekend. Yes, you need a process to re-enable them; no, "they might need it someday" is not an acceptable reason to leave dormant accounts active.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must set up a central system that collects and stores security event logs from all relevant IT systems in one place. This makes it easier to detect suspicious activity, investigate incidents, and demonstrate compliance, rather than having logs scattered across separate systems where problems could be missed. Centralised logging ensures you have a complete audit trail to understand what happened during security breaches or system failures.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to funnel all your system events into one central logging repository instead of letting every server, application, and device scatter logs across the network like digital breadcrumbs. Yes, this means actually implementing infrastructure to collect and store these logs rather than discovering during an incident that your critical system has been logging to /dev/null for eighteen months. It's not glamorous, but centralised logging is the difference between forensics and forensic fiction.

annotations.ai_view: Standard Operating Environments (SOEs) are pre-configured, hardened baseline builds used across your organisation's workstations and servers to ensure consistent security settings and reduce vulnerabilities from the start. This control requires you to deploy these standardised images rather than allowing ad-hoc configurations, which prevents security gaps and makes it easier to patch, update and maintain systems at scale. Using SOEs significantly reduces your attack surface by removing unnecessary software, disabling risky services, and applying security baselines uniformly across your infrastructure.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to actually use Standard Operating Environments (SOEs) for your workstations and servers instead of letting every user and team build their own snowflake configurations. Yes, this means everyone gets the same baseline image, which is apparently controversial because someone's always got a special reason they need things different. It turns out consistency is foundational to security, so here we are stating the obvious in control form.

annotations.ai_view: Use only the current release or the immediately previous release of your operating system—avoid older versions that may have unpatched security vulnerabilities. This ensures your systems receive timely security updates and bug fixes, reducing exposure to known exploits. Regular updates are essential for maintaining a strong security baseline across your infrastructure.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Run either the current OS release or the one immediately before it—basically, stay within two versions or you're eating unsupported security patches for breakfast. Yes, this means you'll finally need to stop nursing that OS from 2015 in production, and no, "it works fine" is not a compliance argument, though you'll hear it anyway.

annotations.ai_view: Only 64‑bit operating system releases are permitted, ensuring modern memory protections and compatibility with current security features. This reduces exploit surface compared to 32‑bit legacy builds.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Run 64‑bit or go home—because 32‑bit is a museum exhibit and the attackers have already moved on.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to apply hardening configurations to operating systems by following guidance from the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) and your system vendor, choosing the stricter option whenever their recommendations conflict. This matters because hardened systems have unnecessary services disabled, security settings strengthened, and vulnerabilities reduced, making them significantly harder for attackers to compromise or exploit.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Strip your operating systems down to bare essentials using hardening guidance from ASD and your vendor—and when those two inevitably contradict each other (they will), pick the stricter one because apparently "secure" means "inconvenient." Yes, this means you'll spend three weeks arguing with your vendor's support team about why you've disabled half their recommended "features," but that's the price of actually following this control instead of just deploying defaults and hoping for the best.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to apply hardening settings to web browsers by following guidance from the Australian Signals Directorate and the browser vendor (such as Microsoft, Google, or Mozilla), choosing the stricter settings when the guidance conflicts. This matters because web browsers are frequent attack targets that can expose sensitive data or allow malware installation, so configuring them defensively—such as disabling plugins, blocking pop-ups, enforcing HTTPS, and restricting data collection—significantly reduces your organisation's exposure to web-based threats.
