annotations.ai_view_snarky: Configure your web browsers to match the most paranoid interpretation of hardening guidance available—whether that's ASD's recommendations or your vendor's safety manual, pick whichever one makes users suffer more when conflicts arise. Yes, this means you'll probably disable half the features that make browsers useful, but at least you can sleep knowing that if someone does breach your network, the attacker will have a *slightly* harder time pivoting through an unpatched extension. Apply this across all classification levels because apparently users need the same locked-down experience whether they're accessing a public website or handling classified intelligence.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to install and configure firewall software on individual workstations and servers that blocks network traffic unless it matches your organisation's approved list of legitimate applications and services. It matters because software firewalls act as a critical barrier against both external attacks trying to reach your systems and internal threats or compromised applications attempting to send data outward, significantly reducing the attack surface and limiting what malware can communicate with if installed.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Install a software firewall on every workstation and server, then actually configure it to block everything except the applications your organisation has explicitly approved — which means you'll need to maintain that blessed list and update it whenever someone decides Slack now requires a new port. Yes, this is simultaneously obvious security hygiene and the control that gets systematically ignored because end-users complain that their "critical business application" (browser games) won't load, so someone just disables it at 2 AM.

annotations.ai_view: Deploy antivirus on all workstations and servers with high‑level signature and heuristic detection, reputation checks, ransomware protection, daily signature updates, and scheduled scans of all fixed and removable media.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Install AV and actually turn on all the features—signatures, heuristics, reputation, ransomware protection—and update daily; otherwise it’s just a decorative icon.

annotations.ai_view: Disable the ability to read from USB drives, external hard drives, and other removable media unless your organisation specifically needs this capability for work purposes. This prevents attackers from introducing malware or stealing data through physical devices that could bypass your network security controls.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Disable USB ports and other removable media access unless your organisation actually needs them—which, spoiler alert, it doesn't, despite what every user claims. You can do this either by locking it down with software that enforces access controls or by physically disabling the ports themselves. It's a simple control that somehow takes organisations months to implement because apparently everyone's got a "critical business need" to read from random USB sticks in the parking lot.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that all software coding, updates, and modifications only happen in dedicated development environments that are separate from systems handling real data. This prevents accidental or malicious changes to production systems, reduces the risk of introducing vulnerabilities into live services, and ensures changes can be properly tested before deployment.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Keep your developers coding in dev environments, not production—yes, this is apparently something that needs explicitly stating in 2024. The control exists because someone, somewhere, definitely hotfixed production at 3am when they "just needed to quickly test something," which inevitably broke everything downstream. Segregate your environments properly and enforce it technically (firewall rules, access controls, code review gates) because relying on developers to self-regulate their urge to patch live systems has a 100% failure rate.

annotations.ai_view: You must not copy real production data (containing actual customer information, credentials, or business data) into development or testing environments unless those environments have security controls equal to or stronger than production. This prevents sensitive information from being exposed through less-monitored systems where developers have broader access, and stops attackers who compromise a development environment from easily accessing production-grade data.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: If you're going to copy production data into your dev environment so developers can actually test against realistic data—which, despite what your security policy says, everyone does—then that dev box better be locked down just as tight as production, because you're now holding the crown jewels in a room full of people running npm install on random packages. In practice, this means either keeping dev environments hermetically sealed with the same access controls and encryption as prod (good luck), or anonymising/masking that data so aggressively that it becomes useless for testing (the path most organisations actually take, then pretend they didn't).

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to restrict who can access and modify your software source code repositories and version control systems to only authorized developers and administrators. It matters because unauthorized access to source code could allow attackers to introduce malicious code, steal intellectual property, or identify vulnerabilities before they can be patched. Implement this by using strong authentication, role-based access controls, and audit logging on all code repositories.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Prevent people who shouldn't have it from accessing wherever you keep your actual source code—your version control system, repositories, or whatever medieval filing cabinet houses your "authoritative" copy. This means proper access controls, authentication, and ideally some audit trail so you can later discover which contractor's compromised laptop walked out the door with your entire codebase. It's straightforward in theory and catastrophically neglected in practice because apparently "just give everyone repo access" remains the path of least resistance at most organisations.

annotations.ai_view: Web servers must send three specific security instructions in their responses to web browsers: Content-Security-Policy (to prevent unauthorised scripts from running), HTTP Strict Transport Security (to force encrypted connections), and X-Frame-Options (to prevent your website being loaded inside another site's frame). These headers protect users from common attacks like cross-site scripting, man-in-the-middle interception, and clickjacking by instructing browsers how to safely handle your application before they even render the page.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your web server needs to actually send three specific HTTP headers—CSP, HSTS, and X-Frame-Options—because apparently browsers can't be trusted to make good decisions on their own and we certainly can't trust developers not to embed sketchy stuff. It's the digital equivalent of putting up a sign that says "don't click suspicious links" and being shocked when people click the suspicious links, except this time the sign is technically enforceable and most teams will half-implement it anyway by copying something from Stack Overflow.

annotations.ai_view: Your network gateways must check incoming traffic and reject packets that claim to come from internal IP addresses but arrive from external sources—a technique called IP spoofing that attackers use to bypass security controls and launch attacks. This prevents attackers from impersonating trusted internal systems to gain unauthorized access or evade detection. Implementing this filtering at your network boundary stops spoofed traffic before it enters your network, protecting the integrity of your internal communications and reducing the effectiveness of common attack methods.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your gateway needs to actually look at incoming traffic and reject packets claiming to come from IP addresses that couldn't possibly originate from outside your network—basically catching the digital equivalent of someone showing up to your office claiming to be you. It turns out spoofed source addresses are still a popular way to launch DDoS attacks and other nastiness, so filtering them is one of those "obvious in hindsight" things that everyone seems to skip until they get hit. Yes, this means your network team needs to configure ingress filtering properly, which apparently requires more oversight than you'd think.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to turn off IPv6 tunnelling on network devices unless there's a documented business need for it. IPv6 tunnelling can create hidden communication pathways that bypass security controls and monitoring, so disabling it by default reduces attack surface and prevents unauthorised data exfiltration. Organisations should only enable tunnelling when explicitly required and then monitor and control those connections carefully.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Turn off IPv6 tunneling unless your organisation has explicitly documented that it actually needs it—which it probably doesn't, but somehow half your network will still have it enabled anyway. IPv6 tunneling creates an alternate path into your network that most security teams forget exists, making it a reliable backdoor for anyone patient enough to look for it. Yes, this means auditing every router, firewall, and server, and no, the previous IT contractor didn't document any of this.

annotations.ai_view: Your network security devices must detect and prevent IPv6 tunnelling traffic at points where your organisation connects to external networks. This stops attackers from bypassing security controls by hiding malicious traffic inside IPv6 tunnels, which can go undetected if your organisation isn't actively monitoring for it. This is especially important if your network mainly uses IPv4, as IPv6 tunnels could provide a hidden pathway into your systems.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your firewall needs to actively block IPv6 tunnelling mechanisms at the perimeter—you know, those cute little workarounds where someone inevitably tries to sneak IPv6 traffic through IPv4 tunnels when they think nobody's looking. The intent is sound (IPv6 adoption requires careful planning, not improvisation), but in practice you'll spend considerable time explaining to well-meaning network engineers why their "temporary" 6to4 tunnel is actually a bypass waiting to happen. Block it at the boundary and save yourself the archaeological dig through your logs six months from now.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that when IPv6 addresses are automatically assigned to devices, you must use stateful configuration management that tracks each assignment and stores detailed logs in a central location. This matters because it lets you maintain visibility over which devices get which addresses, audit who accessed network resources at specific times, and detect unauthorised or suspicious network activity.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You've got to use DHCPv6 with actual state tracking—not that fire-and-forget nonsense—so your IPv6 addresses get handed out like they're supposed to. Every time someone's device checks in for a lease, that transaction needs to end up in a centralised logging system, because apparently "we'll figure it out later" isn't compliance-grade record-keeping. Spoiler: most organisations will skip this, get audited, panic, then scramble to retrofit logging they should've built in from the start.

annotations.ai_view: Engage cloud service providers to define DoS mitigation strategies, including their capacity to absorb attacks, cost implications, monitoring thresholds, service shutdown criteria, pre‑approved response actions, and upstream traffic blocking arrangements. This ensures a coordinated, rapid response to volumetric attacks.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Have the awkward conversation with your cloud vendor about who pays when the internet tries to DDoS you — and get it in writing before the attack hits. Because improvising during a flood is a great way to drown.

annotations.ai_view: Lock your domain names at your registrar to prevent unauthorised transfers or deletions that could take your online services offline or redirect traffic to malicious sites. Regularly verify that your domain registration details (registrant contact, technical contact, nameservers) remain accurate and haven't been altered by attackers. This stops adversaries from hijacking your domain and impersonating your organisation or disrupting your services.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Lock your domain names at the registrar level so some departing employee or compromised account can't quietly transfer your organisation's web presence to a competitor's server farm. Also, actually verify your registration details are current—revolutionary concept, I know, but you'd be amazed how many orgs discover mid-incident that their admin contact is a long-dead contractor's Hotmail account. It's the digital equivalent of checking whether your keys are actually in your pocket before you start blaming the locksmith.

annotations.ai_view: Keep your most important online services on separate network infrastructure from services that are common targets for denial-of-service attacks, so an attack on one doesn't automatically knock out the other. This reduces the risk that disruptions to less critical systems will cascade and disable essential services your organisation depends on. It's a straightforward way to improve resilience by ensuring attackers can't use easily-targeted services as a stepping stone to cripple your core operations.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to physically or logically separate your actually-important online services from the ones that attract every script kiddie with a botnet, because apparently your critical infrastructure can't just hang out with the riffraff without getting knocked offline. Put your customer-facing web portal on a different network segment than your crown jewels—not because attackers are polite about collateral damage, but because they will absolutely flood whatever's easiest to hit and take your payment system down with it. Yes, this means proper network segmentation; no, most organisations won't do it until after their first DDoS.

annotations.ai_view: Organisations must ensure their online services are hosted by cloud service providers rather than maintained on-premises or through other arrangements. This centralises responsibility for infrastructure security, allows access to provider expertise and security capabilities that may exceed what organisations can maintain independently, and ensures services benefit from the provider's established security controls and compliance frameworks. Using qualified cloud providers helps reduce the attack surface and operational security burden while maintaining availability and resilience of critical online services.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: This control requires you to actually use cloud service providers if you're hosting your online services in the cloud—which, and I say this with the weariness of someone who's audited fifty "cloud-first" organisations running everything on-premises, apparently needs to be stated explicitly. The real work starts after you've ticked this box: ensuring those providers are properly vetted, contractually bound, and monitored, which is the part everyone conveniently forgets about while they're busy migrating to whatever vendor was cheapest that quarter.

annotations.ai_view: When your website needs to be continuously available and accessible, use content delivery networks that cache your site's content across distributed servers. This improves performance and resilience by reducing downtime when your primary server fails or experiences traffic spikes. Caching through these networks ensures users can still access your website from nearby servers even if your main infrastructure becomes unavailable.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: If your website absolutely has to stay online and you're not running it from a potato-powered server in a basement, you need to use a CDN that actually caches your content—because apparently putting all your eggs in one geographic basket is still somehow controversial. This means distributing your site across multiple endpoints so that when your primary infrastructure inevitably catches fire, users can still access your content from somewhere that hasn't combusted yet. Yes, you'll need to think about what data you're comfortable letting a third party cache, but that's what vendors are for.

annotations.ai_view: When using a content delivery network to distribute your content, keep your actual web servers' addresses hidden from the public internet and only allow the CDN service and your authorised staff to access them directly. This prevents attackers from bypassing the CDN's protections to attack your servers directly, which would expose security controls and potentially compromise sensitive data or system availability.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: If you're using a CDN to hide your origin servers—which, let's be honest, is the whole point—don't then go and advertise their IP addresses everywhere like you've just won a prize. Restrict access to those origin servers to only the CDN and your management networks, because every attacker will happily bypass your shiny edge caching layer if you hand them the keys to the kingdom. Yes, this means doing the unsexy work of proper network segmentation and access controls instead of just hoping nobody figures out where your actual servers live.

annotations.ai_view: When your organisation uses elliptic curve cryptography, you must select curves that meet NIST SP 800-186 standards rather than using arbitrary or non-standard curves. This ensures you're using mathematically robust curves that have been thoroughly vetted by cryptography experts, reducing the risk of implementation weaknesses or intentionally compromised algorithms that could expose sensitive data.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: If you're going to use elliptic curve cryptography—which, let's be honest, most organisations stumble into without much deliberation—at least have the good sense to pick a curve that someone with actual credentials has vetted, specifically NIST SP 800-186. This means no homegrown curves, no "totally secure" parameters your contractor's cousin designed, and no mysteriously backdoored academic papers; stick to the boring, well-analysed options that won't embarrass you during an audit. The punchline is that this control exists because organisations have genuinely shipped custom curves before, so yes, apparently this needed to be spelled out.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires using ephemeral (temporary) Diffie-Hellman or Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange when establishing TLS connections, rather than static variants. Ephemeral variants generate new keys for each session, so even if a server's long-term key is later compromised, past encrypted communications remain protected—a property called forward secrecy. This is essential for protecting sensitive data because it limits the damage from key compromises to only current and future sessions, not historical traffic.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Use ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE) or elliptic curve variants (ECDHE) for TLS key establishment instead of the static versions—basically, generate new key material for each connection rather than reusing the same pair like some kind of cryptographic procrastinator. This matters because if an attacker ever compromises your long-term keys, they can retroactively decrypt all your historical traffic; ephemeral variants limit the damage to just the current session, which is the bare minimum of forward secrecy. In practice, you'll configure TLS cipher suites to prioritise ephemeral exchanges, though somehow this remains surprising to discover hasn't been done.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that SSH private keys—which grant access to systems and services—must be encrypted with either a strong password or a dedicated encryption key, preventing unauthorised use if the key file is stolen or compromised. Without this protection, anyone with access to your system's storage could use your private keys to impersonate you and gain unauthorised access to other systems. This is essential for maintaining the security of your infrastructure and preventing lateral movement by attackers.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to encrypt your SSH private keys with a passphrase or separate encryption key—basically, don't just leave them sitting around in plaintext like they're a grocery list. Yes, this means actually typing a password every time you use them, which is why every developer on earth will try to convince you they need an unencrypted key "just for automation," and yes, you still have to say no. The control exists because an unencrypted SSH key is functionally identical to handing someone your credentials in a gift-wrapped box.

annotations.ai_view: This control prevents microphones and webcams from being connected to computers that don't handle classified information (TOP SECRET level), even when those computers are located in areas where TOP SECRET work happens. The requirement protects against accidental or intentional audio and video capture of sensitive conversations and activities in classified work areas, reducing the risk that uncleared devices could record and transmit classified information.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: If you're handling TOP SECRET information, don't plug a microphone or webcam into a workstation that isn't cleared for TOP SECRET—basically, keep your fancy noise-makers and eyeballs off the lower-classified gear, even if you're physically sitting in a TOP SECRET area where everyone's already cleared. Yes, someone apparently needed this written down after discovering a classified conversation leaking through a consumer webcam that definitely wasn't air-gapped, so here we are. It's the infosec equivalent of "don't leave the keys in the ignition," except the ignition is a USB port and the car is your national security.

annotations.ai_view: Your contracts with external service providers must clearly document what types of data they'll handle and who owns that data. This prevents misunderstandings about data responsibilities, helps you maintain visibility over sensitive information, and establishes clear accountability if a breach or misuse occurs. Without this documentation, you risk losing control of your data and having difficulty enforcing security obligations.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Make sure your contracts actually spell out what data the service provider is touching and who owns it—sounds obvious, yet somehow every organisation discovers mid-incident that nobody wrote down whether the cloud vendor could see their tax records. Get it in writing before you hand over the keys, because "we assumed they knew" won't survive an audit or a breach notification letter.

annotations.ai_view: You must evaluate the security risks that suppliers of critical IT components and services pose to your systems before engaging them. This assessment helps you understand how a supplier's vulnerabilities, practices, or potential compromise could weaken your overall security posture. By identifying these risks upfront, you can make informed decisions about which suppliers to work with and what additional safeguards you need.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Before you plug in that shiny new operating system, application, widget, or "managed service," someone actually needs to sit down and figure out whether the supplier will burn your security house down—and document it, because apparently good intentions don't count. This means evaluating whether your vendor is competent, trustworthy, or at minimum won't hand your data to competitors/adversaries, then factoring that risk into your overall security posture. Yes, this applies to everything from Windows updates to that IoT device your procurement team found on special, and yes, you probably should have done this before signing the contract instead of after.

annotations.ai_view: Enable Perfect Forward Secrecy for all TLS connections so that if your long-term encryption keys are compromised in the future, past encrypted communications remain secure and cannot be decrypted retroactively. This protects sensitive data by ensuring each session uses unique, temporary keys that are destroyed after use, preventing attackers from harvesting encrypted traffic today and decrypting it later when they steal your keys. This is particularly important for highly sensitive communications where long-term confidentiality matters.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Configure your TLS connections to use cipher suites that support Perfect Forward Secrecy, which means even if someone obtains your private key tomorrow, they still can't decrypt today's traffic—a concept so theoretically sound that organisations universally ignore it until an audit shows up. Yes, this means using ephemeral key exchanges (ECDHE, DHE) instead of static RSA, which costs basically nothing in performance but apparently requires the kind of conviction usually reserved for religious conversions. If you're still using non-PFS ciphers in 2024, congratulations, you've just made a future breach archaeologist's job easier.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that authentication requests sent between devices and your remote access authentication server must be encrypted using either IPsec or TLS protocols, adding a protective layer beyond standard RADIUS encryption. This prevents attackers from intercepting login credentials or tampering with authentication messages on the network. It's particularly important for protecting remote access since these communications often traverse untrusted networks where interception is a realistic threat.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Wrap your RADIUS authentication traffic in either IPsec or TLS because apparently sending credentials in the clear—or with only RADIUS's frankly theatrical MD5 obfuscation—is still somehow a hill organisations choose to die on. This control basically says "yes, actually encrypt the thing that authenticates your people," which you'd think would be table stakes, yet here we are writing it down.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that devices allowing peripherals (like printers or storage drives) to be shared between classified systems at different security levels, or between systems in separate security domains, should undergo rigorous security testing and certification before use. This matters because shared peripherals create potential pathways for classified information to leak between systems that should remain isolated, so using thoroughly evaluated equipment significantly reduces the risk of accidental or intentional data compromise.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: If you absolutely insist on plugging the same printer into both your SECRET and TOP SECRET networks—and somehow your security committee signed off on this wonderfully creative approach to cost-saving—then at least buy a switch that's been formally evaluated to actually prevent data leaking between the classification levels. Yes, we all know someone will eventually plug an unevaluated one in anyway and everyone will act shocked when it inevitably becomes a problem.

annotations.ai_view: When you use software to isolate multiple workloads on a single physical server, choose a vendor whose isolation technology is built with security as a core priority from the start—demonstrating commitment to secure design, secure defaults, and either memory-safe coding languages or practices that prevent memory-related vulnerabilities. This matters because weak isolation mechanisms can allow one workload to breach another or escape to the host system, so the underlying software must be engineered defensively to minimize attack surface and prevent common exploitation techniques.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: When you're virtualizing multiple workloads on a single server, pick an isolation vendor that actually knows what they're doing—specifically one demonstrating genuine commitment to secure design, secure defaults, and not writing memory-unsafely like it's 1995. Preferably they've used memory-safe languages; if not, they'd better have ironclad memory-safe practices in place, because hypervisor escapes are a genuinely unpleasant Tuesday. Yes, this means you probably can't use that free hypervisor from the guy who updates it in his garage.

annotations.ai_view: When you use software-based tools (like virtual machines or containers) to run multiple classified environments on a single physical server, that server and all the environments it hosts must all have the same security classification and belong to the same security domain. This prevents accidentally mixing different classification levels on shared hardware, which could allow unauthorised access to more sensitive data if the software isolation fails or is compromised.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: If you're running virtual machines or containers on a single physical server to save money, congratulations—that whole server and every environment on it must be classified at the highest level of anything running on it, because software isolation is apparently held together with digital duct tape and optimism. This means if you want to run SECRET and TOP SECRET workloads on the same physical hardware, the entire infrastructure becomes TOP SECRET, which defeats most of the cost-saving argument everyone had for consolidation in the first place. Yes, organisations still try to do this anyway.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must use the most current versions of common software tools—including Microsoft Office or equivalents, web browsers, email programs, PDF readers, and antivirus or security software. This prevents attackers from exploiting known security vulnerabilities that have been fixed in newer releases, which is one of the most reliable ways to reduce your exposure to cyber attacks. Keeping these applications current is especially important because they're frequently targeted by threats and often process untrusted files from external sources.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Keep your office suites, browsers, email clients, PDFs readers, and security products at the latest version—yes, all of them, all the time, which is exactly as fun as it sounds when you've got legacy systems held together with prayers and deprecated libraries. The control statement doesn't actually define what "latest" means (bleeding-edge trunk builds? Last Tuesday's patch? Who knows), but the intent is clear: you're supposed to be running current versions because vulnerability patching is apparently still controversial. In practice, you'll spend the next six months negotiating with teams who insist they can't upgrade because "something broke last time" and their risk appetite is inversely proportional to their appetite for change management.

annotations.ai_view: Disable or remove any unnecessary features, add-ons, and services from common applications like Microsoft Office, browsers, email programs, PDF readers, and antivirus tools that your organisation doesn't actually use. This reduces the attack surface by eliminating potential vulnerabilities in unused code and prevents users from accidentally enabling risky features, while keeping only the functionality your organisation needs to operate.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Disable or remove literally every feature your users don't actually need from office suites, browsers, email clients, PDFs readers, and security tools—which sounds simple until you realize that every organisation has that one person who swears they need macros, plugins, extensions, and whatever else you're trying to rip out. The point is that every enabled component is another potential attack surface, so if your application doesn't strictly require it, it gets deleted; this includes all those "helpful" features that ship enabled by default and nobody ever touches.

annotations.ai_view: Use publisher and product names when setting up application control rules based on digital certificates, rather than relying on other certificate attributes alone. This ensures your allowlist controls are based on trusted, clearly identifiable software sources and makes it harder for attackers to bypass controls using certificates from the same issuer but different publishers. Properly configured certificate rules reduce the risk of unauthorized or malicious applications running on your systems.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: When you're using certificate-based application whitelisting, actually leverage the publisher name and product name fields from those certificates instead of just checking signatures like some kind of caveman—because relying solely on the cert thumbprint means you'll happily allow every version of legitimate software right alongside whatever malware the attackers signed with a borrowed cert yesterday. Yes, organisations genuinely implement this backwards constantly, which is why this control exists to remind everyone that granular publisher metadata is there for a reason and costs nothing to use.

annotations.ai_view: The Chief Information Security Officer must take active ownership of the organisation's entire cyber security program and verify that the organisation follows all relevant cyber security policies, standards, laws and regulations. This matters because having a single accountable leader ensures cyber security decisions are coordinated across the organisation, prevents gaps in security coverage, and demonstrates to regulators and stakeholders that the organisation takes security seriously and operates within legal requirements.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your Chief Information Security Officer needs to actually oversee the cyber security program instead of just attending steering committee meetings and approving purchase orders—meaning they're accountable for ensuring your organisation doesn't wander off into a compliance dumpster fire. Yes, this is stating the obvious, but apparently it needs stating since most CISOs spend their time fighting budget cuts and explaining why "we'll just patch it later" doesn't constitute a strategy. The control basically says: pick someone senior enough to make things happen, then hold them responsible when your organisation inevitably breaks every policy it wrote.

annotations.ai_view: Servers should be configured to communicate only with other servers they genuinely need to work with, limiting connections at both the network level (which servers can talk to each other) and file system level (what shared storage or files they can access). This reduces the attack surface by preventing a compromised server from easily spreading to or stealing data from unrelated systems, and makes it harder for attackers to move laterally across your network if they gain initial access.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your servers need to stop gossiping with each other like they're in a high school cafeteria—restrict both network traffic and file system access between them to only what's genuinely necessary. This means no casual "let me just mount that share" situations and no "I'll ping everything to see what's alive" discovery protocols, which somehow always sound reasonable at 3pm on a Friday. In practice, you'll document what inter-server communication is actually required, implement segmentation rules to enforce it, and then watch someone bypass it next quarter when they "just need quick access" to something.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that when you use switches to share physical peripherals (like printers or USB devices) between classified and unclassified systems, those switches must have undergone rigorous independent security testing to ensure they can't leak data between the different classification levels. This matters because shared peripherals are a potential bridge for attackers to move classified information from high-security systems to less protected ones, so the switching hardware itself must be trustworthy enough to maintain that separation.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: If you're somehow sharing peripherals like printers between your SECRET network and anything less classified, the switch doing that handoff needs to be formally evaluated to high assurance standards—because apparently someone decided that a $50 unvetted KVM switch was the perfect ingress vector for data spillage. Yes, this really happens, and yes, organisations really try to skip this step until an auditor's laser-focused stare makes them suddenly find the budget for proper equipment.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that when personnel use organisation-owned devices to access work systems or data, classified information must be kept separate from personal data—typically through technical measures like separate user accounts, encryption, or containerization. This separation prevents accidental exposure of sensitive information if the device is lost or compromised, and ensures that personal activity doesn't interfere with the security and integrity of classified work data.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your organisation needs to technically prevent classified data from mixing with whatever personal photos, messaging apps, and sketchy downloads your staff inevitably load onto their mobile devices—basically, build a wall between "work stuff that matters" and "personal stuff that will eventually get you breached anyway." You can achieve this through containerisation, separate user profiles, or MDM policies that actually get enforced (the last part being the part everyone skips). Without this, a single compromised personal app becomes a backdoor into your classified networks, which regulators find approximately as amusing as a data breach at 2 AM.

annotations.ai_view: Ensure that internet-facing server applications (such as web servers, mail servers, and APIs) are kept current with the latest available releases rather than running outdated versions. This reduces exposure to known security vulnerabilities that attackers actively exploit, since older versions typically lack security patches that have been released in newer versions. Regularly updating these applications is one of the most effective ways to prevent compromise of systems accessible from the internet.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Keep your internet-facing server applications on the latest release—yes, the one that dropped yesterday and probably has three critical CVEs you haven't heard about yet, but statistically older versions have more discovered ones. This is your basic hygiene control: if you're running something publicly accessible, you're either patching regularly or you're just volunteering your infrastructure to the internet's most motivated penetration testers. It's not sophisticated, it's not fun, but it works because most attackers are genuinely lazy and will absolutely skip your server to find the one running software from 2019.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires configuring web browsers to block advertisements from loading and displaying while users browse the internet. Blocking ads reduces exposure to malicious content, as ad networks can be compromised to deliver malware, phishing pages, or exploit kits that target browser vulnerabilities. Disabling ads also improves performance and reduces data usage while removing a common attack vector for compromising systems.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Block all web advertisements from reaching your users' browsers—because apparently we need a formal control to prevent people from clicking on "You've won a free iPad" scams and malicious ad networks that treat your endpoints like a all-you-can-compromise buffet. This means configuring browsers with ad-blocking mechanisms, content filters, or network-level controls, which is simultaneously obvious security hygiene and something you'll discover half your workforce has already disabled by lunchtime on day one. Yes, it's in the Essential Eight because ads are a legitimate attack vector; no, this doesn't mean your organisation will actually enforce it consistently.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires disabling or removing Java execution capabilities in web browsers to prevent malicious code from running when users visit untrusted websites. Java applets are a known attack vector that can be exploited to compromise systems, so blocking this functionality reduces the risk of drive-by downloads and remote code execution. This is a foundational hardening measure that removes an unnecessary and dangerous capability from browsers.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Disable Java execution in web browsers because, despite being theoretically obsolete since 2010, Java applets remain a reliable vector for remote code execution and nobody's actually patched their browser settings. This applies across all classification levels because threat actors don't discriminate between your unclassified cat videos and your TOP SECRET documents—they'll exploit whatever runs. Yes, you'll need to do this manually in most browsers since vendors stopped making it easy; yes, someone in your organisation will bypass it anyway to run that one legacy application; yes, you should still enforce it.

annotations.ai_view: Write access to Trusted Locations is restricted to privileged personnel who validate macros for safety, preventing unvetted code from executing. Trusted Locations bypass macro security, so limiting write rights stops malicious or accidental macro deployment.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: So the only people who can drop a macro in the “trusted” folder are the ones who actually read the code—assuming they have time. Everyone else gets a read‑only view and a sad face.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires your organisation to prevent Microsoft Office files downloaded from the internet from executing macros automatically. Macros are a common attack vector—adversaries distribute malicious files via email or websites that run harmful code when opened—so blocking them stops a major infection pathway. Enabling this protection is fundamental to preventing compromise and is required across all security classifications and system types.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Block macros in Office files downloaded from the internet because that's apparently where all the ransomware decides to live these days. Your users will complain that their "definitely legitimate" spreadsheet from that sketchy vendor won't run macros, but you'll sleep better knowing you've closed the door on one of the most reliable attack vectors in existence—even if half your organization will find creative workarounds within a week.

annotations.ai_view: Macro security configuration (e.g., disable all macros with notification) is locked down so users cannot lower the protection level. Users often downgrade settings to run unsigned macros, exposing the system to attack.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Because “I need this macro to work” is the universal excuse, we make the setting immutable. Expect a surge of “IT, why can’t I enable macros?” tickets.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to implement application control mechanisms on servers that are directly accessible from the internet, restricting which programs can run and preventing unauthorized or malicious software from executing. This matters because internet-facing servers are primary attack targets—application controls act as a critical safeguard by allowing only approved applications to run, significantly reducing the risk of exploitation and lateral movement if a server is compromised. This is a foundational hardening measure that protects your systems and network from common attack vectors.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to deploy application controls (whitelisting, AppLocker, SELinux, or equivalent) on any server that touches the internet, because apparently we've learned that letting arbitrary code execute on your perimeter is bad—a lesson that somehow requires annual reminders. This covers everything from web servers to mail gateways, and yes, it matters even though every third-party vendor will immediately tell you their software requires an exemption. The persistent surprise across organisations is that this actually stops a meaningful portion of attacks, even the boring ones.

annotations.ai_view: Unprivileged users are blocked from executing scripts via Windows Script Host, PowerShell, Command Prompt, WMI, and HTA, limiting the script‑based attack surface.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Stop regular users from firing up PowerShell, CMD, or any script host—because nothing says “secure” like letting the intern run arbitrary scripts.

annotations.ai_view: Enable built-in operating system protections that prevent attackers from exploiting software vulnerabilities to gain unauthorised access or execute malicious code—such as address space layout randomisation, data execution prevention, and control flow guard. This stops many common attack techniques from working even when a software flaw exists, reducing the window of opportunity for compromise. It's a fundamental hardening step that significantly raises the barrier to exploitation with minimal performance impact.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Enable whatever exploit protection features your operating system vendor bothered to build in — address space layout randomisation, control flow guard, data execution prevention, that sort of thing. Yes, it's remarkable how many organisations leave these switched off by default, essentially gift-wrapping their systems for attackers. Turning them on won't stop a determined adversary, but it will at least stop the script kiddies and make your auditors moderately less disappointed.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must create and regularly update a documented list of all software installed on workstations, servers, network devices and other connected equipment, then verify these records are accurate. This matters because an accurate inventory helps you detect unauthorised or outdated software, manage security patches effectively, and identify compliance gaps—without knowing what software is running, you can't protect against vulnerabilities or manage licences properly.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to maintain an actual inventory of what software is installed across your IT estate—workstations, servers, the lot—and actually keep it current instead of letting it fossilize in some spreadsheet from 2019. Verify it regularly (yes, this means checking that your list matches reality, a concept that apparently requires formal documentation to enforce), because you can't patch what you don't know you have, and you definitely can't audit what you can't account for.

annotations.ai_view: When a vendor stops supporting an operating system, you must replace it with a supported version rather than continue running it. Unsupported systems receive no security patches, leaving them vulnerable to known exploits that attackers can easily target. This control ensures your infrastructure stays current and protected against threats that vendors are no longer actively defending against.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to actually replace operating systems when the vendor stops supporting them—not leave them running on production systems while hoping nobody notices, which somehow remains the default at most organisations. This means patching stops eventually, vulnerabilities don't get fixed, and your system becomes a deliberate liability rather than an accidental one. It applies across all classification levels because even OFFICIAL data deserves better than Windows XP, apparently.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires your email system to automatically block incoming messages from external sources that falsely claim to come from your organization's email domain or subdomains. This prevents attackers from spoofing internal email addresses to deceive employees into trusting malicious messages, which is a common tactic in phishing and social engineering attacks. By enforcing this check at your email gateway, you stop fraudulent emails before they reach user inboxes.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Block emails that claim to be from your own domain but arrive through external gateways — because apparently, spoofing your organisation's email address is still someone's idea of a fun Friday afternoon, and we need to make it slightly inconvenient for them. This catches the obvious impersonation attempts before they hit your users' inboxes, though it won't stop the determined adversary who's already inside your network or using a lookalike domain with one character swapped. It's basic hygiene, like locking your front door while leaving the kitchen window open.

annotations.ai_view: Multi‑factor authentication is required for human users accessing online services that handle sensitive organisational data. MFA adds a critical layer beyond passwords.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Force a second factor on every login—because ‘password123’ was never a security strategy, just a bad joke.

annotations.ai_view: Apply multi‑factor authentication for human users accessing data repositories. Protecting data stores directly limits the impact of credential theft.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Data repositories get MFA — finally a control that touches the actual data. Watch the DBAs argue that ‘service accounts’ don’t count.

annotations.ai_view: Disable SSH version 1 on all systems and require SSH version 2 instead, as version 1 contains fundamental cryptographic weaknesses that allow attackers to intercept and decrypt remote access sessions. This is a baseline security requirement because version 1's flawed key exchange and encryption mechanisms make it trivial for an attacker with network access to compromise administrator credentials and gain control of critical systems. Enforcing version 2 ensures your remote access uses modern, validated cryptography resistant to known attacks.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Disable SSH version 1 because it's been cryptographically broken since the late '90s and yet somehow still shows up in production environments like a security zombie that refuses to stay dead. This means explicitly configuring your SSH daemon to reject v1 connection attempts entirely—not just "preferring" v2, actually blocking it. Yes, this is still worth a control in 2024, which tells you everything you need to know about the state of legacy infrastructure out there.

annotations.ai_view: When someone requests special access rights to a system or its data, you must verify and approve that request before granting it. This prevents unauthorized people from gaining elevated privileges and helps ensure that only those who genuinely need admin or privileged functions receive them. Validation at the point of request creates an important gate that reduces the risk of insider threats and accidental over-provisioning of access.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Before handing someone the keys to your systems, actually check that they're supposed to have them — novel concept, I know. This means validating the request when it first comes in (not three months later during an audit), confirming the person needs that access for their role, and documenting who approved it. Somehow this remains the part where organisations reliably fumble.

annotations.ai_view: Privileged accounts must be granted only the minimum permissions needed for the user’s responsibilities. Restricting privileged access limits the impact of credential theft or misuse.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Admin rights are like fireworks—fun for a moment, disastrous when handed out to everyone.

annotations.ai_view: Organizations must collect and store logs of all privileged access activities (such as administrator logins, system changes, and elevated permission use) in a central location where they can be monitored and reviewed. This creates an audit trail that helps detect unauthorized access, insider threats, and misuse of administrative accounts, while also supporting investigations when security incidents occur. Centralized logging makes it harder for attackers to cover their tracks across multiple systems and helps your organization demonstrate compliance with security obligations.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to funnel every privileged access event—every su, sudo, admin login, domain controller touch, the lot—into a central logging system so you've actually got a prayer of finding the smoking gun when someone inevitably does something they shouldn't. Yes, this means every organisation will generate terabytes of logs they'll never actually look at until the incident response team is already sweating through their third coffee. The whole point is that when the audit happens or something goes sideways, you can at least prove you were *theoretically* monitoring who had the keys to the kingdom.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must create and keep current a written policy for how it will preserve digital information over time, including decisions about what to keep, how long to keep it, and in what formats. This matters because digital files can become unreadable as technology changes, and without a clear preservation approach you risk losing important records that may be needed for compliance, investigations, or recovery after a security incident. A good policy ensures your organisation can reliably access critical data years into the future, even as systems and file formats evolve.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to actually write down how you're going to keep your digital stuff readable and findable five years from now, then follow that plan instead of just hoping formats don't become obsolete and your backup tapes don't mysteriously degrade. Yes, this means documenting file formats, migration strategies, and storage requirements—riveting stuff that nobody wants to own until the audit finds a folder of critical 1997 Excel files nobody can open anymore. It applies across all classification levels, which should tell you something about how universal this particular problem is.

annotations.ai_view: You must establish and maintain regular backups of your organisation's data, applications, and system settings based on how critical each asset is to your business and your ability to keep operating during a disruption. This matters because backups are your primary defence against data loss from ransomware, hardware failure, or accidental deletion—without them, you may lose essential information permanently or face extended downtime. The control ensures backups are done consistently and kept long enough to meet both your recovery needs and any legal or regulatory requirements.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to actually back up your data, applications, and settings—and keep those backups around long enough to be useful when (not if) something goes sideways, with retention periods tied to how much it would hurt if you lost them. Yes, this means documenting your backup strategy, testing that restores actually work, and storing copies somewhere that won't burn down with your primary systems; no, most organisations won't do this adequately until they've already lost something critical. The sooner you define what's actually business-critical versus the stuff you keep "just in case," the sooner you can stop backing up 47 copies of everyone's browser history and start backing up things that actually matter.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must regularly test whether data, applications and settings can be successfully recovered from backups to a specific point in time, particularly during disaster recovery exercises. This testing verifies that your backups are actually usable and complete—not just that they exist—ensuring you can genuinely restore operations after a security incident, system failure or data loss. Without tested backups, you risk discovering during a real crisis that your recovery plan doesn't work or that critical data is missing or corrupted.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to actually test that your backups work by restoring them to a single point in time during disaster recovery exercises—not just cross your fingers and hope they'll magically work when your systems are on fire. Turns out, the backup that's been sitting in your vault for two years tends to be corrupted, missing critical files, or incompatible with your current infrastructure, which you'll discover at precisely the worst moment if you haven't tested it beforehand. So yes, run the drill, document that it either succeeded or spectacularly failed, and fix whatever broke; your future self screaming at 3 AM during an actual incident will thank you.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that microfiche and microfilm—formats that store document images at reduced size—must be destroyed using equipment that reduces them to fine powder, ensuring no readable text fragments remain (particles can contain no more than five consecutive characters). This matters because microfilm is a compact, durable storage medium that remains readable long after other storage methods deteriorate, so standard shredding or incineration may leave recoverable images that compromise sensitive information.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need a shredder powerful enough to pulverize microfiche and microfilm into dust where no particle contains more than five consecutive readable characters — because apparently someone, somewhere, reconstructed classified film from larger shreds and now we all pay the price. Yes, this is real, yes it's overkill for a medium most organisations stopped using in 2003, and yes, you'll still find boxes of undestroyed microfiche in the basement marked "TO BE DESTROYED" from 2015.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that people managing gateways—critical systems that control network traffic and access—must be properly vetted through employment screening and security clearance processes appropriate to the sensitivity of what they're protecting. It matters because gateway administrators have significant power to intercept, redirect, or block communications, so you need confidence they're trustworthy and suitable for that level of access before giving them the role.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your gateway admins need to be vetted through employment screening and hold security clearances proportional to whatever classified data their gateways touch—which sounds straightforward until you realize half your organizations treat "gateway admin" as a job title bestowed upon whoever remembers their password longest. The control essentially says don't give someone the keys to your perimeter just because they're convenient; make sure their background check didn't turn up anything too inconvenient first.

annotations.ai_view: Gateways must insert protocol breaks—physical or logical points where traffic transitions between different network protocols or security layers—at each layer of your network architecture. This prevents attackers from exploiting protocol vulnerabilities to traverse your entire network undetected, as they must interact with different security mechanisms and logging points at each layer. Protocol breaks effectively compartmentalize your network so that a compromise at one layer cannot automatically cascade to others.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your classified data store needs protocol breaks—basically air gaps or inspection points—at each network layer so that traffic can't just waltz through unchanged from one layer to another like it owns the place. Yes, this means actually inspecting and re-encapsulating data as it crosses boundaries instead of just letting packets flow through unmolested, which is apparently what everyone's natural instinct is to do. In practice, this stops an attacker who compromises one layer from using that foothold to pivot through your network infrastructure like they're on a highway with no exits.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires gateways to maintain separate security enforcement mechanisms for traffic flowing in different directions—one set of rules and filters for data moving up (to higher classification networks) and another independent set for data moving down (to lower classification networks). This separation prevents a single security failure or misconfiguration from compromising both directions, and ensures that each data flow receives appropriate scrutiny based on its specific risk direction. It's particularly important in classified environments where upward and downward transfers have different security implications and threat profiles.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your classified data system needs separate security enforcement mechanisms for traffic going up the classification hierarchy and down it—basically, don't let the same gate guard check both directions, because apparently humans can't be trusted to apply rules consistently without dedicated hardware or software doing it for them. This means upward flows (lower to higher classification) and downward flows (higher to lower) each get their own independent security functions, so if one gets compromised or misconfigured, the other isn't automatically toast. In practice, this usually means separate gateways or at minimum logically isolated enforcement within your CDS, though I've seen organisations convince themselves that "independent functions" means two checkboxes in the same software—you'll want to avoid that.

annotations.ai_view: Organisations must regularly review samples of security events from their cross-domain solutions at least quarterly to check whether data transfers are following established security policies and to catch any system failures or policy breaches. This periodic assessment helps detect when gateways aren't operating as intended, allowing teams to fix problems before they lead to unauthorised data movement or security incidents.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Every three months, you need to actually look at what your Cross Domain Solution is doing—specifically pull a sample of events showing data transfers and check whether they're following your security policies, then document whatever failures you inevitably find. Yes, this means you have to have security policies for your CDS in the first place, and yes, this means actually reviewing logs instead of letting them silently accumulate on a forgotten server; the fact that this needs to be spelled out in a control probably tells you something about how often it gets skipped in practice.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must verify that content filtering systems work correctly and cannot be circumvented through thorough security testing before deployment. This ensures that filters actually block the malicious or inappropriate content they're designed to stop, rather than providing false protection that attackers could exploit. Regular testing is critical because filters are a key line of defence against malware, phishing, and other web-based threats targeting your systems.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to actually test your content filtering gateways—not just deploy them, cross your fingers, and hope they work. This means rigorous security testing to verify they catch what they're supposed to catch and that determined users can't just walk around them with a bit of creativity. Yes, everyone thinks their filters are bulletproof until someone finds a bypass in about fifteen minutes, so treat this as the continuous activity it actually is.

annotations.ai_view: System owners must formally register each system with the authorising officer responsible for it, creating an official record of ownership and accountability. This ensures that someone in authority knows what systems exist, understands who is responsible for them, and can make informed decisions about security requirements and resource allocation. Without this registration, systems can operate without proper oversight, making it harder to enforce security standards or respond to incidents effectively.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: System owners need to formally register their systems with whoever holds the authorising officer title, which sounds simple until you realise nobody agrees on what counts as a "system," who the authorising officer actually is, or where said registration is supposed to happen. If you manage to get past those minor definitional hurdles, you'll at least create a paper trail proving that *someone* was nominally aware the system existed, which is apparently the security equivalent of locking your car doors while leaving the windows down.

annotations.ai_view: System owners must continuously monitor each system’s security posture, manage emerging cyber threats, assess risks, and keep controls effective over time.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Continuous monitoring usually means a dashboard nobody watches until an alert screams.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must deploy firewalls that have been independently tested and certified between your internal networks and the internet or other public networks. This prevents unauthorised traffic from reaching your systems and helps detect suspicious outbound activity. Using evaluated (certified) products ensures the firewall has been properly scrutinised and is fit for protecting your critical boundaries.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to stick an evaluated firewall between your network and the internet—which, yes, means an actual firewall that someone competent has tested and verified works as advertised, not the checkbox appliance your budget-conscious manager bought three years ago and forgot about. This is the bare minimum gatekeeping that should've been standard practice since the 90s, yet somehow remains the hill organisations die on when they skip it or deploy it incorrectly.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that classified information at SECRET or TOP SECRET level must only be stored and processed in cloud environments that are either dedicated to your organization (private cloud) or shared exclusively with other Australian government agencies (community cloud)—never in public clouds shared with commercial customers. This matters because public cloud providers cannot guarantee the same level of security oversight, data isolation, and compliance with Australian government requirements needed to protect highly sensitive information from unauthorized access or foreign interference.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You can't use public clouds like AWS, Azure, or GCP for your SECRET and TOP SECRET data—only community clouds (think: government-only shared infrastructure) or private clouds (entirely your own) will do. Yes, this means you'll probably end up running your own expensive datacenter or paying premium rates to a government-approved provider, because apparently the theoretical risk of a hyperscaler's infrastructure being compromised by a foreign power is worse than the guaranteed risk of your org running underfunded legacy systems in a shed somewhere. The upside is this control is blissfully unambiguous: either your cloud is public or it isn't.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that servers, network devices and cryptographic equipment holding classified information must be stored in physical security containers (such as locked cabinets or safes) that match the classification level of the data and the security characteristics of the surrounding environment. It matters because physical theft or unauthorised access to these systems could expose classified information or compromise cryptographic keys, regardless of how well your software security is implemented—making this a critical foundation for protecting sensitive government assets.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to lock your classified gear in a container that actually matches what you're protecting—so don't put SECRET data in a filing cabinet you got off Facebook Marketplace. The "security zone combination" bit means you can't just slap the same container everywhere; a PROTECTED server in a public office needs different containment than one in a secure facility, because apparently proximity to randos matters. Yes, this means you probably need to upgrade from that cardboard box in the corner, and no, the vendor's assurance that "it'll be fine" doesn't count as suitable containment.

annotations.ai_view: Don't rely on VLANs alone to isolate your organisation's internal networks from public internet infrastructure—use additional security controls like firewalls or network segmentation instead. VLANs are easy to misconfigure or bypass, so treating them as a primary boundary between your systems and external networks creates an unacceptable risk. This control ensures you implement robust, defence-in-depth protections rather than assuming network isolation alone will keep unauthorised external traffic out.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Don't use VLANs as your security boundary between your internal networks and the internet—they're a convenient fiction that makes everyone feel separated until someone realizes layer 2 isn't actually a security layer. This control exists because yes, every second organisation treats VLANs like a magic forcefield, and yes, they consistently aren't. Use proper firewalls and network segmentation instead, because VLANs are for traffic management, not for pretending you've solved the hard problem of keeping the internet out.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must create, put in place, and regularly update a written mobile device policy that covers how phones, tablets, and laptops are managed and secured. This policy should address device setup, access controls, data protection, and what happens when devices are lost or staff leave. A clear, enforced policy reduces the risk of unauthorised access to sensitive information and ensures consistent security practices across all mobile devices used to access your systems and data.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to write down how you're going to manage mobile devices, then actually follow that policy instead of letting everyone's personal iPhone become an unofficial government workstation. Yes, you need to maintain it too—which means updating it when you inevitably discover half your workforce is running unsupported iOS versions and storing sensitive files in Notes.

annotations.ai_view: When printers and multifunction devices are no longer needed or at end-of-life, you must physically remove and destroy the printer ribbons (the inked fabric or film that produces printed output). This prevents sensitive information from being recovered from discarded ribbons, which could otherwise be extracted and read by someone with access to the device. Destruction ensures that any text or images that passed through the printer cannot be reconstructed or forensically recovered.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Yes, you actually need to physically remove and destroy printer ribbons from your printers and multifunction devices, because apparently someone decided that ink-saturated fabric containing fragments of every document your organisation has ever printed is worth securing like classified material. In practice this means your facilities team needs to bag and bin these things rather than leaving them in the device or tossing them in recycling, since a determined adversary could theoretically recover ghosted impressions of sensitive text. It's technically sound; it's also why every printer closet smells faintly of paranoia and thermite.

annotations.ai_view: You must create and maintain documented processes to prevent sensitive Australian government data (classified as SECRET, TOP SECRET, and RELEASABLE TO EYES ONLY) from being transferred to foreign systems that don't meet security standards. This protects classified information from unauthorized foreign access and ensures compliance with Australia's protective security requirements. The processes should cover both traditional documents and other data formats, and include clear procedures for staff to follow when handling data transfers.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need written processes and procedures that actually prevent classified Australian data—whether it's sitting in a Word doc, a spreadsheet, or buried in someone's PowerPoint—from wandering off to foreign systems that don't meet our security standards. Yes, this means you'll need to figure out what "unsuitable" means at your organisation, document it, and then somehow enforce it despite every user who thinks their cloud storage provider is definitely trustworthy. Good luck explaining to your CISO why the data ended up in someone's personal Google Drive anyway.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that every database query issued by applications, along with any crash or error messages that result, be recorded in a central logging system. Centralized logging enables detection of anomalous queries, aids forensic investigations, and ensures accountability for database interactions.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Because nothing says “we care about security” like dumping every SQL statement and stack trace into a single log that nobody ever reviews. At least you’ll have a nice paper trail when the inevitable breach happens.

annotations.ai_view: Security-relevant database events must be centrally logged, covering access or modification of important content, user and privilege changes, privilege‑escalation attempts, suspicious queries, alerts, structural changes, admin actions, executable commands, and logons/logoffs. This comprehensive logging enables detection of misuse and supports forensic investigations.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You’re expected to log every time someone sneezes at the database—privilege changes, weird queries, admin logins—so that when something inevitably goes wrong you have a paper trail. Most orgs will still only log the bare minimum and call it a day.

annotations.ai_view: Configure DMARC authentication records across all your organisation's domains and subdomains so that email servers automatically reject any messages that fail authentication checks, preventing attackers from spoofing your domain to deceive recipients. This stops malicious emails pretending to come from your organisation, which is a common attack vector for phishing, fraud and credential theft. Setting DMARC to reject (rather than just monitoring) ensures the protection is enforced at the mail server level rather than relying on user vigilance.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to set up DMARC records across all your domains and subdomains with a policy that actually rejects non-compliant mail—not just reports on it, which is what most organisations do while congratulating themselves on their email security. This is less "cutting edge" and more "email authentication 101," but apparently it still needs saying since most places leave their DMARC policies set to `p=none` in perpetuity, which is about as useful as a screen door on a submarine. The control exists because DMARC rejection actually stops spoofing attacks, whereas mere monitoring lets them through while you sit around analysing failure reports.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires disabling Object Linking and Embedding (OLE) package activation in Microsoft Office applications to prevent malicious code execution through embedded objects in documents. OLE packages are a common attack vector where adversaries embed executable files or scripts in Word, Excel, or other Office documents that automatically execute when opened, potentially compromising your system. Implementing this restriction significantly reduces the risk of document-based malware infections and aligns with Essential Eight recommendations for reducing targeted cyber intrusions.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Disable OLE (Object Linking and Embedding) in Microsoft Office because it's a vector for malware that's been exploited since before most junior security analysts were born—attackers embed executable content in Word docs and spreadsheets, users open them, and boom, you're compromised. Yes, this means some legacy workflows that depend on magical inter-application object embedding will break, and yes, someone will complain about it. Configure it anyway, because the alternative is explaining to your CISO why you left a known attack surface wide open for convenience.

annotations.ai_view: You must create and maintain an up-to-date list of all approved wireless and infrared devices (like mobile phones, wireless headsets, and remote controls) allowed in your classified work areas, then regularly check that only authorised devices are actually present. This prevents unauthorised communications equipment from being smuggled in to eavesdrop on sensitive discussions or transmit classified information out of secure facilities.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to maintain an actual, honest-to-god registry of every RF and IR device that enters SECRET and TOP SECRET spaces—phones, wireless mice, body cameras, the works—and keep it current through regular audits because apparently devices have a tendency to breed in the dark corners of server rooms. Yes, someone will inevitably forget to log their Bluetooth speaker, and yes, you'll discover contraband WiFi dongles during your quarterly verification, but at least you'll have documented proof that you *tried* to know what was in there.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to deploy Microsoft's curated list of applications that are blocked from running on your systems to prevent known dangerous or risky software from executing. This blocklist targets inherently unsafe applications—such as those that can disable security controls or facilitate malware—and helps prevent both accidental misuse and intentional compromise. By implementing this technical barrier, you reduce attack surface and limit the tools available to potential adversaries while maintaining system stability.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Implement Microsoft's application blocklist to prevent execution of known dangerous software—basically letting Redmond tell you which apps are too sketchy to run, which is either reassuring or horrifying depending on your faith in their threat intelligence. This sits at the intersection of "free security control" and "outsourcing your judgment to Microsoft," and yes, you still need to maintain and test it because the blocklist won't magically stay current while you're busy with everything else that's on fire.

annotations.ai_view: Before anyone can use a system or access its data, they must prove who they are through some form of authentication—such as passwords, biometrics, or security tokens. This prevents unauthorized users from gaining access to sensitive information and ensures that all system activities can be traced back to a specific individual. Without this foundational security measure, attackers could easily impersonate legitimate users and compromise your organization's data and systems.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Require users to actually prove who they are before handing them the keys to your systems—a concept so blindingly obvious that its continued necessity as a formal control is a damning indictment of how often it gets skipped in practice.
