Authentication is your first and last line of defence, assuming you've bothered to implement it properly and not just left the default password unchanged since the system was installed. If you're not doing this, congratulations, you've already lost.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must create and maintain documented processes and procedures that define how data backups are performed, including who is responsible, how often they occur, where they are stored, and how they are tested. This matters because reliable backup processes ensure you can recover critical data and systems after incidents like ransomware attacks, accidental deletion, or hardware failures—without working backups, a security incident can become a business disaster. Regular maintenance of these procedures keeps them relevant as systems and threats evolve.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need documented processes and procedures for backing up your data—and yes, you actually have to maintain them, which means updating them when your infrastructure inevitably changes and nobody tells the backup team. This is simultaneously the most basic requirement in information security and the control that gets ignored right up until someone deletes production and suddenly everyone becomes very interested in whether those backups actually work.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires your organisation to create and maintain documented procedures for restoring data from backups, then put those procedures into practice and keep them current. annotations.ai_view: Credentials must be delivered over a protected communication channel; if that’s impossible, they are split so the user receives one part and their supervisor the other. This reduces the risk of interception or unilateral misuse.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: If you can’t send the password over TLS, you’re expected to play secret‑sharing with the user’s boss—half the password here, half there. Most teams just email the whole thing and hope the auditor doesn’t notice.

annotations.ai_view: Any credentials handed to a human user must be changed immediately upon first login. This prevents the initial secret from remaining known to administrators or being reused.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You give a user a temporary password and they’re supposed to change it on first login—because nothing says security like trusting a user to pick a strong password after they’ve just been handed ‘Password123’.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires users to maintain unique credentials for each system they access, rather than reusing the same password or username combination across multiple applications or services. If one system is compromised, reusing credentials would give attackers immediate access to other systems, multiplying the damage from a single breach. Using distinct credentials limits the blast radius of security incidents and makes it harder for attackers to move laterally through your organisation's systems.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: This control requires that users have unique passwords for each system rather than recycling the same credentials everywhere—a straightforward request that apparently still qualifies as aspirational security in most organisations. The logic is sound: if one system gets compromised, at least the attacker doesn't immediately own your entire estate. Treating password reuse as something that needs explicit prohibition rather than basic hygiene probably says everything you need to know about the state of enterprise credential management.

annotations.ai_view: When users enter passwords or other login credentials into systems, those characters must be hidden from view—typically displayed as dots or asterisks—so that shoulder surfers, screen recordings, or people looking over someone's shoulder cannot capture sensitive authentication information. This prevents credentials from being exposed during the most vulnerable moment of entry, reducing the risk of unauthorized access even if someone is physically present or monitoring the screen.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Hide password entry so shoulder surfers and security cameras can't capture what users type—yes, this means asterisks or dots instead of plain text, which somehow still needs saying in 2024. It's one of those controls that feels obvious until you inherit a legacy system where passwords display in full clarity, at which point you'll understand why this made the manual. Implement it everywhere credentials go in: web forms, terminal applications, physical kiosks, the works.

annotations.ai_view: After IT equipment is serviced or repaired, you must inspect it to verify the configuration hasn't changed and no unauthorised modifications were introduced. This prevents maintenance work from becoming a vector for tampering, malware installation, or configuration weakening that could compromise security. Regular post-maintenance checks ensure your approved security baseline remains intact across your equipment fleet.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: After someone cracks open your equipment for maintenance, actually look at it before powering it back on—verify the configuration matches what you approved and that nobody's installed a surprise USB implant or swapped critical components. Yes, this means someone has to physically inspect the gear, document it, and confirm nothing fishy happened; apparently trusting the maintenance contractor's assurance that "it's fine" doesn't meet compliance requirements, shocking as that may be.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to implement handling procedures for IT equipment that match the sensitivity of the information it processes or stores—for example, computers containing classified data need more protective measures than those handling public information. It matters because improper handling (such as careless storage, transport, or disposal) can expose sensitive data, allow unauthorised access, or enable equipment theft. By matching protection levels to actual risk, organisations reduce the chances of breaches while avoiding unnecessary costs on low-risk devices.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must apparently treat classified equipment differently from unclassified equipment—a concept so self-evident that its inclusion here suggests someone, somewhere, was storing PROTECTED data on the same laptop they use to browse Reddit. This control essentially mandates physical security proportionate to sensitivity: classified gear gets locked down, official-sensitive gets basic precautions, and unclassified gets... the benefit of the doubt. Watch it fail spectacularly the moment someone leaves a PROTECTED USB drive on a desk because "it's just for fifteen minutes."

annotations.ai_view: Before using any new storage media (such as USB drives, external hard drives, or backup tapes), you must completely erase or overwrite any existing data to ensure no residual information remains that could be exploited. This prevents accidental exposure of sensitive data that may have been on the media during manufacturing or previous use, and ensures you start with a clean environment free from malware or hidden files. This is especially critical for classified or sensitive information systems where any pre-existing data could compromise security.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You must wipe new media before use—a principle so straightforward that its consistent violation across the Australian public sector is genuinely impressive. Yes, this includes that USB stick your vendor handed you, the one they definitely didn't plug into their unpatched laptop first. Nobody does this, of course, but the control exists so you can at least point to it during the inevitable incident review when someone restores from that "clean" drive and inherits three years of someone else's malware.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations using Microsoft products to enable and configure attack surface reduction rules, which are built-in security features that block common malware attack techniques such as suspicious script execution and credential theft. Implementing these rules reduces the likelihood of successful malware infections by preventing attackers from exploiting well-known weaknesses in applications and operating systems. This is a practical hardening measure that improves security posture with minimal operational overhead since the rules are native to Microsoft systems.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Deploy Microsoft's attack surface reduction (ASR) rules to restrict potentially dangerous application behaviours—essentially asking Windows to stop itself from shooting itself in the foot, a security measure that remains perpetually "under review" in organisations that have somehow convinced themselves that legacy LOB applications definitely need DLL injection capabilities. Yes, this actually works; no, you won't implement it because someone's 2007 VB6 application will break and the business will simply accept ransomware instead.

annotations.ai_view: Organisations must ensure all relevant people—including staff, management, vendors, and other parties—receive copies of security policies and procedures, plus timely updates whenever these documents change. This prevents security gaps caused by people following outdated practices and ensures everyone operates consistently under the same current rules and expectations.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must actually tell people about their security policies and, more importantly, tell them *again* when those policies change—a concept apparently revolutionary given how many enterprises treat their documentation like classified intelligence that stakeholders aren't meant to know exists. Yes, this includes that one team in finance who definitely still thinks the old password policy is in effect, and no, a Teams message from 2019 does not count as "communication to all stakeholders."

annotations.ai_view: Disable any authentication methods that allow an attacker to intercept and reuse captured login credentials without needing to know the actual password—such as unencrypted challenge-response systems or protocols without timestamp validation. This prevents attackers from gaining unauthorized access by replaying old authentication traffic they've captured on the network, which is particularly important for systems handling sensitive data or critical functions.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Systems must prevent authentication mechanisms that allow an attacker to intercept and replay captured credentials—think HTTP Basic Auth, unencrypted NTLM, or that one legacy application nobody wants to touch—because apparently we're still having this conversation in 2024. Yes, this means actually implementing TLS, proper nonce handling, and timestamp validation; no, your organisation won't do it until someone demonstrates the attack in a boardroom, which they probably won't because it's obvious and depressing. Disable the vulnerable methods entirely rather than hoping developers will "be careful," which is the infosec equivalent of believing in Santa.

annotations.ai_view: When you use software to partition a single physical server into isolated environments (such as virtual machines or containers), you must harden that software's configuration by disabling unnecessary features and tightly controlling who can access its management interface. This prevents attackers from exploiting unused functionality or gaining administrative access to break down the isolation between environments, which would allow them to move laterally across your system or access data they shouldn't reach.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your hypervisor, container runtime, or whatever isolation du jour you've chosen will be thoroughly misconfigured by default, so remove the bells and whistles and lock down that management interface before someone with admin credentials and a sense of entitlement accidentally bridges your carefully separated environments. Yes, this includes disabling that convenient web UI that felt intuitive during the POC and now sits exposed on your management network with a password someone wrote on a sticky note. It's a straightforward concept that organisations consistently fail to execute, usually discovering this fact during an incident rather than before one.

annotations.ai_view: When you use software-based isolation (like virtual machines or containers) to run multiple environments on a single physical server, you must harden the underlying operating system that hosts them. This matters because if that base operating system is compromised, an attacker could potentially break out of the isolation and access all the virtual environments running on it, defeating the security separation you intended to create.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Ah yes, the hypervisor host OS that nobody patches because "it's not user-facing" and "we're too busy managing the VMs." This control requires you to actually harden that underlying operating system—disable unnecessary services, apply security patches, implement proper access controls—the fundamentals that somehow remain revolutionary concepts in organisations running production workloads on hypervisors. You'd think the fact that a compromised host OS can see directly into every guest's memory would motivate compliance, but here we are, watching Windows Server 2012 R2 quietly sit in someone's vSphere cluster.

annotations.ai_view: When you run multiple isolated environments on a single physical server, you must promptly apply security patches and updates to both the isolation software itself and the underlying operating system it runs on. This matters because gaps in patching create vulnerabilities that attackers could exploit to break out of one isolated environment and compromise others or the host system, defeating the whole purpose of the separation.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Look, when you've decided that containerisation or virtualisation is your path to enlightenment and you're running multiple workloads on the same physical hardware, you need to actually patch both the isolation layer *and* the host OS—shocking, I know. The isolation mechanism itself is just software with its own CVEs, so treating it like set-and-forget middleware is how you end up with container escape vulnerabilities that would make a penetration tester weep with joy. Apply patches to both promptly, or accept that your "separation" is mostly theatrical.

annotations.ai_view: When multiple isolated environments run on the same physical server (such as virtual machines or containers), you must monitor the integrity of the isolation software itself and log all security events from both the isolation layer and the underlying operating system to a centralised location. This prevents attackers from breaking out of their isolated environment undetected or tampering with the isolation mechanism, and ensures you have the forensic evidence to investigate any potential compromise.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to monitor the integrity of your hypervisor and log everything it does, because virtualisation is a lovely way to pretend you have separate environments while actually having one catastrophic failure domain—and no one wants to discover that via a compliance audit. Yes, everyone deploys VMs without this. Yes, they're shocked when a compromised guest escapes and takes out the whole stack. Yes, they blame the vendor.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must check any pre-built system environments obtained from external vendors for malware and unsafe configurations before deploying them. This prevents attackers from compromising your systems through backdoors or weak settings hidden in third-party software, which could otherwise give them immediate access to your network or sensitive data.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must scan third-party Standard Operating Environments for malware and misconfigurations before deployment, a requirement that sounds reasonable until you realise nobody can actually agree on what "scanned" means or accepts liability when the scan misses something. The control exists because vendors ship hardened images with the same enthusiasm most people bring to reading terms and conditions, and somehow your organisation is now responsible for catching their negligence with tools that have a detection rate you'll never truly know.

annotations.ai_view: Before your incident response team continues monitoring an active intrusion to gather additional evidence, you must first check with the system owner to get their approval. This ensures the owner understands the risks of leaving the compromise active, agrees it's worth the operational impact, and has a say in decisions affecting their systems. Getting this agreement upfront prevents misunderstandings and ensures incident response actions are coordinated with business priorities.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Before you let attackers keep dancing around on a compromised system so you can gather more forensic evidence—the theory being that witnessing additional malice might somehow prove more useful than the intrusion already in progress—you're apparently meant to ask the system owner's permission first, which will either take six weeks or they'll say yes without reading the email. The control is technically sound: deliberate tolerance of active compromise is a conscious risk decision that someone accountable should actually know about, rather than discover during the incident review when they ask why nobody told them their file server was being ransomware-staged for three days straight while you were "collecting data."

annotations.ai_view: Organizations must have a documented procedure for accessing systems during emergencies when normal access methods fail or are unavailable, and they must test this procedure when it's first set up and whenever major infrastructure changes occur. This ensures critical services can continue operating during incidents while maintaining security, and regular testing confirms the emergency access method actually works when needed rather than discovering problems during a real crisis. Without a tested emergency access plan, organizations risk either prolonged outages that damage operations or insecure workarounds that bypass security controls.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Document how you'll break your own glass when everything's on fire, then actually test it once so you can watch it fail spectacularly during the real emergency. The "tested each time infrastructure changes" bit is particularly delicious—yes, that means every VM migration, every network redesign, every time someone decides the authentication system needs tweaking; in practice, nobody tracks this because documenting emergency access procedures is apparently something organisations do the week before their audit.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that emergency administrative accounts (break glass accounts) be reserved exclusively for situations where the normal login process is unavailable or inoperable—such as during system outages or authentication system failures. By restricting their use to genuine emergencies only, you reduce the risk of these powerful accounts being misused for routine tasks, which could expose them to compromise or create unauditable access trails. This approach balances operational resilience with security by ensuring these high-risk accounts remain a genuine last resort rather than a convenient backdoor.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: So you need a way to actually get into your systems when the normal auth goes sideways—fair enough, that's why break glass exists. The control asks you to *only* use them in actual emergencies, which is delightful in its simplicity and devastating in its execution, given that somewhere right now someone's using their break glass account as their daily driver because they forgot their password again. Document when you use them, keep them locked down harder than everything else, and maybe—just maybe—your auditors won't find them scrawled on a Post-it note.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to establish and strictly limit "break glass" emergency accounts—high-privilege credentials used only when normal access methods fail—to pre-approved scenarios such as disaster recovery or critical incident response. These accounts pose a significant security risk because they often bypass standard authentication controls, so their use must be tightly scoped, monitored, and documented to prevent abuse or unauthorised access. By restricting break glass accounts to legitimate emergencies only, you reduce the window of exposure and maintain an auditable record of when privileged access was truly necessary.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Maintain break glass accounts for genuine emergencies only—you know, those theoretical scenarios that somehow never materialise until 3 AM on a Friday, at which point everyone has forgotten the password anyway. Document what these accounts actually do and audit their use relentlessly, because the moment you stop looking, someone will use them to reset their mate's password or debug production at 2 AM without telling anyone. Yes, this is technically the policy every organisation adopts and then watches collect dust while break glass credentials circulate via sticky notes in desk drawers.

annotations.ai_view: Organisations must maintain a central, auditable record of all access and use of break glass accounts — these are emergency accounts designed to bypass normal authentication when legitimate access is blocked. This logging requirement ensures that emergency account usage is traceable and can be reviewed for legitimacy, preventing misuse while still allowing access during genuine outages or security incidents. Without central logging, emergency accounts become a security blind spot where unauthorised access could occur without detection.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: When your carefully architected access controls inevitably fail—and they will—at least document who's frantically logging in as "EMERGENCY_ADMIN_DO_NOT_USE" at 3am on a Sunday. This control requires centralised logging of break glass account usage because your audit team will need *something* to point to when they ask how Linda from Finance obtained database credentials. Yes, people actually use these accounts; no, they don't always tell you about it first.

annotations.ai_view: When emergency "break glass" accounts are used by anyone other than the account custodian, those account credentials must be changed immediately afterward. This prevents unauthorised access using the same credentials after the emergency situation is resolved, ensuring that only the intended custodian can use the account going forward. It's a critical safeguard for high-privilege accounts that bypass normal security controls and should rarely be accessed.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: When your break-glass account—the one that exists specifically for the scenario where normal access controls have catastrophically failed—actually gets used, you're supposed to rotate its credentials afterward. Theoretically sound; practically, you'll watch this happen approximately never, because either the custodian won't know it was used, won't remember to do it, or will file it under "we'll deal with it next quarter." The control is correct; the implementation will be a dumpster fire.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to regularly test their emergency access accounts (break glass accounts) after updating their passwords or credentials to ensure they still work when needed in a genuine emergency. Testing verifies that the accounts haven't been accidentally misconfigured and confirms staff know how to use them, so you're not discovering access failures during an actual incident when time is critical. It's a simple but essential check that prevents emergency procedures from failing when systems are unavailable through normal access methods.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Yes, you need to actually *test* that your emergency access accounts still work after you rotate their passwords—a concept organisations consistently discover only after their primary authentication fails at 3 AM and the break-glass account hasn't been touched since 2019. It's theoretically straightforward: change the credentials, verify access still functions, document it, move on. In practice, this lives in that twilight zone where everyone assumes someone else tested it, so nobody does.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must establish a formal process for people to safely report security vulnerabilities they discover in your software or services, and you need to respond to and remediate these reports promptly. This program helps you identify and fix security weaknesses before attackers can exploit them, reduces the risk of breaches, and demonstrates good security practices to users and partners. A well-managed vulnerability disclosure program turns external researchers and users into additional eyes helping you maintain secure products.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need a formal mechanism for people to report security bugs without getting arrested or sued—a concept that apparently requires explicit instruction because organisations' default setting is "shoot the messenger." This applies to anything you develop or run, and yes, this includes that internal tool nobody's touched since 2019 that's still somehow critical to payroll. The fact that we're in version three of this control suggests nobody actually reads it until after a researcher finds something the hard way.

annotations.ai_view: Your Chief Information Security Officer must regularly examine and refresh your organisation's security program to keep it effective against current threats and aligned with business goals. This ensures your security investments remain relevant rather than becoming outdated, and helps you identify emerging risks and opportunities before they become problems. Regular reviews also demonstrate that security leadership is actively engaged and accountable for the program's performance.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: The CISO must periodically dust off the cyber security strategy and confirm it hasn't been completely invalidated by last quarter's budget cuts, the new CTO's legacy application acquisitions, or whatever threat landscape emerged since the last review—which is genuinely important, though in most organisations this happens exactly once per compliance audit cycle. "Regularly" remains conveniently undefined, which is why you'll find many CISOs interpreting it as "whenever the audit firm asks," and no one seems bothered enough to argue. Yes, this is necessary; yes, most places do it backwards, usually by reviewing whether threats exist rather than whether anyone's actually doing anything about the program itself.

annotations.ai_view: The Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) must actively oversee how your organisation detects, responds to, and recovers from cyber security incidents, ensuring coordinated and effective action across all teams involved. This matters because incidents require decisive leadership and accountability—without clear CISO oversight, response efforts can be fragmented, slower, and less effective at containing damage and preventing recurrence. This control establishes a single point of responsibility for incident management at the highest security level.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: The CISO needs to actually be involved in incident response rather than learning about breaches through the morning news or a strongly-worded email from the board. This means oversight, not just the ceremonial appearance at the post-mortems where everyone agrees nothing like this could ever happen again. Yes, this is apparently novel enough to require stating in writing.

annotations.ai_view: Service accounts used by applications and services must be created as group Managed Service Accounts, which are special accounts that automatically manage their own passwords and reduce the risk of credential compromise. This approach eliminates the need for administrators to manually set and rotate passwords, preventing common security weaknesses like hardcoded credentials or shared passwords that could be exploited if discovered. Group Managed Service Accounts also provide better auditing and access control, making it easier to track what each service is doing and limit its privileges.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Service accounts must be configured as Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs) so the system handles password rotation automatically, which is theoretically brilliant until your infrastructure team discovers their legacy application from 2004 doesn't support it and quietly switches back to hardcoded credentials anyway. Yes, this applies across all classification levels, which means someone's definitely already got a PROTECTED service account running under a password they wrote on a sticky note. At least when the audit comes around, you'll have a crisp control requirement to point at while accepting their remediation plan that promises compliance in Q3.

annotations.ai_view: Add privileged user accounts to Active Directory's Protected Users security group, which enforces stronger authentication protections like requiring Kerberos encryption and preventing credential delegation. This prevents attackers who compromise one system from using stolen credentials to move laterally across your network and access other high-value systems. It's a critical hardening step that makes credential theft significantly harder to exploit.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Ah yes, the Protected Users group—Active Directory's way of saying "we've made it slightly harder for attackers to steal your admin credentials, provided you actually use this feature that nobody remembers exists." It requires your PAM-adjacent privileged accounts to join this security group so they get hardened Kerberos protections and can't be used for pass-the-hash attacks, which is lovely in theory. You'll know it's working when you discover three years later that half your privileged accounts have been exempted "for legacy systems," and the one that matters is still sitting in Domain Admins with a 180-day password that's written on a Post-it note.

annotations.ai_view: Disable or remove Windows PowerShell 2.0 from your systems, as this older version lacks modern security features and cannot enforce execution policies effectively. PowerShell 2.0 is vulnerable to attacks that bypass protections available in newer versions, making it an unnecessary attack surface. This control is essential for preventing attackers from using legacy PowerShell to execute malicious scripts or bypass security controls on your network.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: PowerShell 2.0 must be disabled or removed because it lacks modern security features—TLS 1.2, constrained language mode improvements, logging enhancements—and hasn't received updates since 2009, which is apparently ancient history in software terms but somehow still running on half the servers in your estate. Yes, organisations will absolutely claim they "need it for legacy scripts," those same scripts which could be updated in the time they spend defending why they haven't updated them. This is one of those controls where compliance is trivially easy and widespread non-compliance is purely a choice.

annotations.ai_view: PowerShell must be configured to run in Constrained Language Mode, which restricts the language features and cmdlets available to users and scripts, preventing execution of potentially dangerous operations like direct memory access or unrestricted .NET API calls. This limits the damage an attacker or malicious script can do if they gain access to a PowerShell session, reducing the risk of lateral movement, data theft, or system compromise. This is a key hardening step because PowerShell is a powerful administrative tool that attackers commonly exploit if left unrestricted.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: PowerShell needs to run in Constrained Language Mode, which blocks .NET reflection, COM object instantiation, and other advanced features that attackers leverage to turn your "trusted admin tool" into a weaponised nightmare — though implementing this universally tends to break legacy scripts and get quietly disabled by the third support ticket. Yes, it actually works. No, organisations rarely enforce it properly because someone's ancient monitoring dashboard needs `Add-Type` to function, and rewriting it is apparently classified as "too hard."

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to collect PowerShell activity logs—including module loads, script block executions, and session transcripts—in a central location where they can be monitored and retained. PowerShell is a powerful administration tool that attackers commonly exploit to move laterally or execute malware, so centralised logging lets you detect suspicious activity, investigate incidents, and maintain an audit trail of who ran what commands and when. Meeting this requirement at maturity levels 2 and 3 means establishing reliable log collection that covers your systems consistently.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must send PowerShell module logs, script block logs, and transcription events to a centralised logging system—a requirement that sounds straightforward until you discover that most environments have PowerShell logging disabled, misconfigured, or sending data to a folder nobody monitors. This control exists because PowerShell is essentially a skeleton key to Windows, and at least *documenting* what attackers (or your own staff) did with it provides a fighting chance at post-incident archaeology, even if nobody's actually looking at the logs in real time.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to enable PowerShell's Protected Event Logging feature, which encrypts and protects script block execution records to prevent attackers from tampering with or disabling logging of malicious commands. Script blocks are the actual code snippets PowerShell executes, and protecting these logs ensures you have reliable evidence of what ran on your systems even if an attacker gains administrative access. This matters because attackers commonly use PowerShell to move laterally and exfiltrate data, so tamper-proof logs are critical for detecting breaches and supporting incident investigations.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Enable Protected Event Logging so PowerShell script block logs get encrypted with a certificate that only SYSTEM can decrypt—a technical speedbump against the inevitable moment someone with local admin rights needs to see what they just ran, then claims they didn't. Yes, this actually stops casual log tampering. No, this will not stop determined attackers or your developers from just using `Set-PSReadlineKeyHandler` to disable logging entirely, which they've already done in production twice this month.

annotations.ai_view: Organisations must establish and continuously manage a formal program to identify, assess and mitigate risks posed by people with access to sensitive systems and information—whether employees, contractors or business partners. This matters because insiders can cause significant harm through deliberate sabotage, negligence, or credential compromise, so a structured approach helps detect warning signs, implement appropriate safeguards, and respond quickly to suspicious behaviour. The program should cover screening, access controls, monitoring and investigation procedures tailored to your organisation's threat environment.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must actually have a documented insider threat program rather than simply hoping their staff are trustworthy, which they demonstrably are not. This requires identifying risks, implementing preventative controls (access reviews, monitoring, offboarding procedures), and detecting anomalies—basically all the things you'd think would be automatic by now. The program needs maintenance because, shockingly, threats evolve; also because after six months someone will have decided it's too inconvenient and stopped doing it anyway.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must obtain legal advice before developing and implementing measures to identify and manage insider threats. This ensures your program complies with employment law, privacy legislation, and surveillance regulations while remaining effective. Legal guidance protects both your security posture and your organisation's legal standing when monitoring staff behaviour and responding to suspected threats.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must consult their legal team before building an insider threat program, which is precisely the kind of sensible governance requirement that will be completely ignored in favour of "just monitoring everyone's emails" until someone inevitably gets sued. Yes, you need lawyers involved—turns out security theatre without proper liability frameworks is both ineffective and expensive. The fact this needs stating separately suggests someone finally learned this lesson the hard way, though not hard enough apparently.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to prevent inbound connections from anonymity networks (like Tor or VPNs used to mask user identity) from reaching your systems. This matters because anonymity networks make it difficult to identify attackers, trace malicious activity, or take action against compromised sources—blocking them reduces your attack surface and helps you maintain visibility over who is accessing your organisation's systems.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Block inbound traffic from Tor, VPNs used for anonymity, and similar networks—a control that looks sensible on a compliance checklist and is violated by the first contractor who insists they need to "test from home securely" by tunnelling through whatever they installed last week. Technically sound in principle; practically, you'll spend your career explaining why this matters to people who've already decided it doesn't apply to them. The usual outcome is a firewall rule that catches nothing because everyone's anonymity traffic is already outbound.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to prevent users and systems from accessing anonymity networks (such as Tor or VPNs used for anonymous browsing) through outbound network filtering. Anonymity networks can conceal user activity and bypass security monitoring, making it difficult to detect malicious behaviour, enforce acceptable use policies, or investigate security incidents. Blocking these connections helps maintain visibility over network traffic and reduces the risk of unauthorised data exfiltration or access to malicious content.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Yes, block your users from accessing Tor, VPNs, and similar anonymity networks—a control that sounds straightforward until you realise half your workforce will simply use their personal phones on 4G, and the other half will find a proxy you somehow missed. The theory is sound: prevent data exfiltration and lateral movement through encrypted tunnels you can't inspect. The practice is watching someone tunnel through DNS over HTTPS three weeks after implementation and wondering why you bothered with the firewall rules at all.

annotations.ai_view: When using Diffie-Hellman key agreement to establish encryption session keys, you must select the mathematical modulus and parameters following the standards specified in NIST SP 800-56A Rev. 3. This requirement ensures your key exchange uses proven, secure parameters rather than weak or custom values that could be exploited by attackers. Following established standards protects against both known mathematical weaknesses and reduces the risk of implementation errors that could compromise the confidentiality of encrypted communications.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must select DH parameters from NIST SP 800-56A Rev. 3 when using Diffie-Hellman for session key agreement—a surprisingly specific requirement that somehow becomes negotiable the moment anyone mentions "legacy systems" or "it's only internal traffic." The good news is that most implementations will simply copy parameters from Stack Overflow and move on, secure in the knowledge that at least *someone* chose them correctly once, somewhere, probably.

annotations.ai_view: You must document and maintain a comprehensive list of every supplier providing operating systems, applications, hardware, equipment, or services that connect to or support your systems. This creates visibility over your supply chain so you can assess security risks, monitor vendor performance, and respond quickly if a supplier is compromised or poses a threat. Knowing who your suppliers are is foundational to managing cyber supply chain risks effectively.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to know who's actually supplying your critical kit — OS vendors, app makers, hardware manufacturers, the lot — which sounds blindingly obvious until you realise most organisations couldn't produce an accurate list if their security clearance depended on it. The control exists because somewhere, someone deployed a mystery third-party application in production and nobody could explain where it came from or who maintained it, and this happened at least twice before the organisation bothered to check. Maintain a register and actually use it, otherwise you're just hoping your supply chain hasn't been compromised by someone you couldn't identify at gunpoint.

annotations.ai_view: Before buying operating systems, applications, hardware, or services, verify that suppliers have a demonstrated history of protecting their own systems from security threats. This reduces the risk of introducing compromised or poorly maintained products into your environment, which could become an entry point for attackers. Supplier security track records—shown through certifications, breach history, security assessments, or industry reputation—help you avoid vendors whose products may carry hidden vulnerabilities or security weaknesses.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must actually verify that vendors aren't security disasters before handing them access to critical systems—a concept simultaneously blindingly obvious and universally ignored until the third incident. In practice, this means reviewing supplier security posture through audits, certifications, or breach history, though most procurement teams will interpret "strong track record" as "they answered the phone and their invoice format was acceptable." The control exists because someone, somewhere, decided a vendor with seventeen unpatched critical vulnerabilities was cost-competitive.

annotations.ai_view: System owners must work with their authorising officer to clearly define what their system covers, how critical it is to business operations, and what security protections it needs—all based on realistic thinking about what damage could occur if attackers compromised it. This ensures organisations invest security effort proportionally: critical systems get stronger defences, while lower-risk systems get appropriate but lighter-touch protection. Getting this right upfront prevents both wasted resources on over-protecting minor systems and dangerous gaps in protecting important ones.

Theoretically, this prevents organisations from waking up mid-breach to realise nobody ever agreed on whether that database was actually important.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must create and keep current a detailed register of all cloud services you've outsourced to external providers, regularly checking that it remains accurate and complete. annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to clearly mark building management cables (such as power, cooling, and access systems) with yellow labels showing their purpose in black text, placed every five metres along the cable run. Expect to find 60% compliance on day one, declining to 15% within six months as facilities staff treat labels as suggestions and contractors treat them as target practice.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that cables physically connected to foreign systems (such as equipment or networks operated by other countries or external entities) be clearly labelled wherever they can be inspected within Australian facilities. Inspectors love ticking this box; cable audits are where dreams go to die.

annotations.ai_view: After using a degausser to erase magnetic media, you must physically damage the internal platters (for example, by bending or breaking them) to prevent any possibility of data recovery. This two-step approach ensures that sensitive information cannot be retrieved even if someone defeats the degaussing process or uses advanced data recovery techniques. This control applies to all security classifications and is essential for securely destroying storage devices before disposal or reuse.

Yes, this does mean you're performing two separate destruction methods on the same media, which is redundant in theory but oddly comforting in practice, since I've personally watched someone confidently return a "degaussed" drive to the recycler, only to have it sold on, booted up, and everything still there. Do the platter deformation. Every single time.

annotations.ai_view: Before reusing storage media (such as USB drives, external hard drives, or backup tapes) across different security domains or classification levels, you must completely erase all data on it using approved sanitisation methods. This prevents sensitive information from one environment—such as classified material or personal data—from accidentally leaking into a different security domain where it shouldn't exist. Proper sanitisation ensures media can be safely repurposed without risking data breaches or compliance violations.

Yes, organisations consistently skip this because the drive "only had the quarterly report on it," and yes, that's how you accidentally leak something classified to the unclassified network, which then gets shared with a contractor, which then gets asked about in an audit.

annotations.ai_view: Maintain a detailed record that tracks every version and patch of applications, drivers, operating systems, and firmware across your systems—essentially a complete history of what's installed and what updates have been applied. This enables you to quickly identify vulnerable systems missing critical patches, supports incident investigations by showing what software was running when something went wrong, and ensures your organization knows exactly what needs updating when new security flaws are discovered.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Maintain a complete registry documenting software versions and patch histories across applications, drivers, operating systems, and firmware—a seemingly elementary concept that somehow remains the first thing organisations abandon once they reach production scale. Yes, this means actually knowing what's installed and when it was patched, not discovering six months later during an audit that half your infrastructure is running versions so old they're practically archaeological. Consider it the infosec equivalent of keeping receipts: tedious, undervalued, and absolutely the first thing people ignore until regulators ask uncomfortable questions.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires staff to avoid discussing sensitive or classified information over the phone in public spaces where others might overhear—such as cafes, public transport, or open offices—unless they take steps to prevent eavesdropping. It matters because conversations containing classified details are a common target for foreign intelligence services and criminals, and public settings offer easy opportunities for someone nearby to capture valuable information. Taking practical precautions like moving to a private area, using background noise masking, or scheduling calls for secure locations significantly reduces this espionage and data theft risk.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must prevent sensitive conversations from being casually conducted within earshot of the guy on the next table with a laptop and a recording app. Yes, this apparently requires documented policy in 2025. No, verbally telling staff not to discuss classified matters at the airport café will not suffice, though that is invariably what passes for compliance in practice.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must create and keep up-to-date diagrams showing the physical layout of your buildings, particularly where communications equipment and infrastructure are located. This helps you understand your security perimeter, identify unauthorised access points, manage physical security effectively, and respond appropriately during incidents or emergencies. Regular verification ensures these diagrams remain accurate and useful for security planning and oversight.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your organisation needs to draw pictures of where the network cables actually go, keep those pictures current, and occasionally pretend to check them against reality. Sounds simple until you discover the floor plan from 2019 shows cabling that was ripped out in 2021, your "regular basis" verification happens once every three years if someone remembers, and the only copy lives in someone's email because the shared drive got archived. This control exists because someone eventually needs to know whether that mysterious crimped cable running behind the server rack actually connects to what you think it does, or if it's just a monument to someone's 2015 mistakes.

annotations.ai_view: Floor plan diagrams must show cable paths (including floor ingress/egress), reticulation and conduit routes, floor concentration boxes, wall outlets, and network cabinets. Complete diagrams aid in managing and protecting the physical network infrastructure.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to automatically disable privileged access accounts (such as administrator or system owner permissions) after 12 months of inactivity unless the account owner actively confirms they still need that access. It matters because unused privileged accounts become a significant security risk—they may belong to staff who've changed roles, left the organisation, or simply forgotten about the access—creating opportunities for attackers to exploit dormant high-level permissions that no one is actively monitoring.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Privileged accounts must be automatically disabled after 12 months of inactivity unless someone actually remembers to revalidate them—a control that sounds reasonable in theory and is universally ignored in practice because the account owner left eighteen months ago and no one noticed until the password reset request arrives from their replacement. Yes, this means you need to track which privileged users are still legitimate, which requires the kind of hygiene that organisations typically only discover they lack during an incident response. The 12-month window is neither short enough to catch drift nor long enough to avoid the awkward conversation with that executive's EA about why their shared admin account got disabled.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to automatically disable privileged user accounts that haven't been used for 45 days or longer, preventing unauthorised access through dormant high-permission accounts. It matters because inactive privileged accounts represent a significant security risk—they're often overlooked during access reviews, may be compromised without detection, and could provide attackers with powerful credentials to move through your systems. Enforcing automatic suspension reduces this risk window and ensures only actively managed accounts retain sensitive access rights.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Disable privileged account access after 45 days of inactivity—a control that sounds straightforward until you discover your organisation's "inactive" sysadmin account still has root access because nobody wants to deal with the reactivation process when they inevitably need it in week seven. The 45-day window is a reasonable compromise between security and the universal human tendency to keep emergency backdoors warm, so naturally most shops either don't implement it or implement it in ways that silently re-enable access without anyone noticing. At least when the audit fails—and it will—you'll have a clear, written instruction to point at.

annotations.ai_view: Just-in-time administration means granting privileged access rights only when an administrator actually needs them to perform a specific task, then removing those rights immediately afterward—rather than giving administrators permanent elevated privileges. This limits the window of opportunity for attackers to exploit compromised administrator accounts and reduces the risk of privilege creep, where unused permissions accumulate over time. It's essential for protecting critical systems because even if an administrator's credentials are stolen, an attacker can only abuse those elevated permissions during the narrow timeframe they're active.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Just-in-time (JIT) administration means you grant privileged access only when it's actually needed, then revoke it shortly after—a concept so theoretically sound that organisations have been ignoring it since 2022 while their admins maintain permanent root access "for efficiency." You'll need to implement automated provisioning and de-provisioning of elevated privileges, ideally with audit logging that nobody will actually review until the inevitable incident occurs. Yes, it's more operationally complex than handing someone a standing admin account; yes, that's precisely why it works and precisely why most places won't do it.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to capture and store audit records of all administrative activities—such as account creation, permission changes, and group membership updates—in a single, monitored location rather than scattered across multiple systems. This centralised logging lets security teams detect suspicious privileged activity, investigate security incidents, and demonstrate compliance with audit requirements. Without it, attackers could abuse admin accounts to cause widespread damage while remaining undetected.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your organisation must send privileged account changes and security group modifications to a central logging system where they will sit, unmonitored, until an auditor asks why someone made a domain admin a member of themselves three years ago. At least when the breach happens, you'll have irrefutable evidence of exactly how thoroughly it was enabled.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to disable or uninstall Internet Explorer 11 from their systems. Removing this browser eliminates an unnecessary attack surface and reduces the chance of compromise through web-based threats.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Remove or disable Internet Explorer 11 entirely, which is remarkable advice primarily because anyone still running IE11 in 2024 has already demonstrated they're comfortable with choices that ended badly for everyone. This control exists because IE's security model was designed during an era when the web was mostly animated GIFs and frames, making it less a browser and more a vulnerability delivery mechanism with a toolbar problem. Yes, some ancient line-of-business application probably still requires it—they all do—which is precisely why you'll find this control acknowledged in policy documents and actively ignored in every network you'll ever audit.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to disable or remove .NET Framework 3.5 from your systems unless it is actively needed for a business application. annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to deploy application control software on servers that don't connect to the internet to restrict which programs can run and execute on those systems. Limiting what applications are allowed to run prevents unauthorized software, malware, and insider threats from compromising internal servers that often process sensitive data or support critical business functions. annotations.ai_view_snarky: Implement application whitelisting on servers that don't face the internet, because apparently the threats live exclusively on the public DNS records. The control is sound; the execution is where organisations consistently discover new definitions of "that's not going to happen."

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to restrict what programs, scripts, and code can run on your systems to only those your organisation has explicitly approved—preventing unauthorised or malicious software from executing. By maintaining an allowlist of approved executables, you significantly reduce your systems' exposure to compromise.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: This control requires you to maintain an approved-application whitelist and actually enforce it—a concept that sounds reasonable until you encounter your first user who needs "just this one tool" they found on SourceForge, or your developers who'd rather die than submit their build pipeline to review. annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to restrict which device drivers can run on your systems to only those your organisation has explicitly approved. Spoiler: it's ML3 for a reason—most organisations get stuck at ML1, shrug, and move on.

annotations.ai_view: Implement Microsoft's vulnerable driver blocklist to prevent exploitation of known-risky device drivers that attackers commonly use to bypass security controls and gain system access. annotations.ai_view: Application control systems must record all allow and block decisions in a central location where security teams can review and analyse them. annotations.ai_view: This control prevents Microsoft Office applications from launching other programs or processes, which blocks a common attack vector where malicious documents execute hidden code to install malware or steal data. Set it via Group Policy, AppLocker, or attack surface reduction rules, then watch the helpdesk requests roll in from people who absolutely need that macro-enabled template for "just this one thing."

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to prevent Microsoft Office applications (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, etc.) from executing or generating code, macros, or other executable files that could run on your system. annotations.ai_view: Block PDF readers from spawning new processes, preventing attackers from using vulnerable PDF applications as a backdoor to execute malware or gain system access. annotations.ai_view: This control requires disabling the ability of Microsoft Office macros to interact directly with Windows system functions (Win32 API calls), which attackers commonly exploit to execute malware or gain system access after compromising a document. Technically sound, practically ignored, and yes, the attacker's macro will absolutely still work because someone exempted Excel.exe anyway.

annotations.ai_view: This control prevents malicious macros from running in Microsoft Office documents by restricting execution to three safe scenarios: sandboxed environments that limit what code can do, pre-approved Trusted Locations on your system, or macros with valid digital signatures from publishers you trust. annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to regularly check and verify which publishers are trusted to run macros in Microsoft Office applications, at least once per year. Tick the box, hope no one asks follow-up questions about what "validation" actually looked like.

annotations.ai_view: Require multi‑factor authentication for any human user accessing third‑party online services that handle the organisation’s sensitive data. This reduces the risk of credential theft giving attackers access to confidential information.

This prevents attackers from exploiting the gateway's network connections to intercept or hijack administrative access, which would give them control over critical security chokepoints. annotations.ai_view_snarky: Requires gateway management traffic to traverse a network completely separate from anything the gateway actually protects—a principle universally acknowledged by every organisation that then implements it by SSH-ing from the corporate VLAN anyway. The isolation must be genuine: dedicated hardware, separate authentication, the works. You will find this control violated within six months of implementation, usually defended with arguments about "operational efficiency" and "but our team is really trustworthy."

annotations.ai_view: When staff manually import data into systems, any files or records that fail security checks—such as malware scans or format validation—must be isolated and held for review before anyone can use them. An authorized person then decides whether to release, clean, or delete the flagged data. This prevents malicious or corrupted content from entering your systems while giving you a chance to investigate what went wrong and learn from the incident.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Requires that data failing security checks during manual import gets locked away pending human review—a theoretically sound concept that assumes someone will actually review it before the business stakeholder gets impatient and approves it anyway, or IT just deletes the quarantine folder to free up space. Yes, this control exists because organisations kept importing malware and misconfigured datasets with the confidence of someone microwaving fish in a shared office kitchen.

annotations.ai_view: When staff manually export data from systems, any data that triggers security alerts must be isolated and held pending human review—someone must then decide whether it's safe to release or must be blocked entirely. This matters because manual exports bypass automated controls and create a window where sensitive or malicious content could slip out undetected; quarantining suspicious exports gives you a chance to catch and prevent accidental data leaks or policy violations before they reach their destination.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Requires organisations to actually stop and think before yelling data across the network—specifically by catching exports that fail security checks and locking them in a virtual holding cell until someone with a clipboard decides whether they're safe or not. Theoretically sound; practically implemented by precisely zero organisations that don't have a dedicated compliance officer who sends increasingly frantic emails. The gap between this control and reality is where most of your incidents live.

annotations.ai_view: Organisations must integrate security practices throughout their software development lifecycle using automated tools and continuous monitoring, rather than treating security as a final step before release. This approach—combining development, security, and operations—enables teams to detect and fix vulnerabilities early when they're cheaper and easier to address, and to deploy updates quickly without introducing new risks. Embedding security from design through to production reduces the window of exposure to known flaws and helps prevent common attack vectors from reaching live systems.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must integrate security into their development pipeline from day one—continuous scanning, automated testing, security gates in CI/CD, the whole tedious affair—rather than bolting it on afterwards like a spoiler on a Commodore. This is the control everyone nods seriously about in meetings before returning to deploying to prod without a code review because the sprint deadline was yesterday. It works remarkably well when actually implemented, which happens roughly as often as finding a properly maintained network diagram.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to encrypt all data traveling across your network infrastructure—whether it's internal traffic between systems, data sent to cloud services, or communications with external partners. Encryption prevents attackers from intercepting and reading sensitive information even if they gain access to your network cables or wireless signals, which is critical since unencrypted data can be captured and misused by unauthorized parties. This applies across all classification levels and system types, making it a foundational security practice for protecting information in transit.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Encrypt everything traversing your network—yes, *everything*, including that internal traffic you're convinced nobody cares about—because eventually someone will prove you catastrophically wrong by sniffing it. This means TLS for web, encrypted tunnels for management, and IPSec for anything that matters, which somehow still surprises organisations who thought their private network was security enough. You will find this hasn't been done. You will raise it in a meeting. Nothing will happen for six months.

annotations.ai_view: Your organization must use a protective DNS service that automatically blocks access to known malicious domain names, preventing users from accidentally visiting websites used for phishing, malware distribution, or other attacks. This stops threats at the DNS level before they can reach your systems, protecting both endpoints and the network. This is particularly important because DNS-based threats are common attack vectors and blocking them early is more efficient than trying to detect infections after they occur.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Deploy a DNS filtering solution to block queries to known malicious domains — a genuinely useful control that somehow remains "aspirational" at most organisations until approximately 3 months after their first confirmed compromise. Yes, it requires actual maintenance of threat feeds and the occasional awkward conversation with users who suddenly can't access "definitely legit" sites; yes, it won't stop sophisticated adversaries; but it does stop the baseline malware and phishing attempts that comprise 87% of actual incidents. Implementation is straightforward enough that the only rational explanation for widespread non-compliance is that someone decided it conflicted with "user freedom" or "DNS performance."

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must ensure that the public IP address ranges you own or use are cryptographically signed through Route Origin Authorisation records, which prevent attackers from hijacking your internet traffic by falsely claiming to own your addresses. This protects your network from being intercepted, redirected, or used as a platform for attacks by making it technically difficult for unauthorised parties to announce your IP addresses to the internet. Without this protection, legitimate traffic intended for your systems could be rerouted to attacker-controlled infrastructure.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your organisation needs to create and maintain Route Origin Authorisation (ROA) records for every public IP address it owns, cryptographically signing them so the global routing system can theoretically verify you actually control what you claim to control—a security posture that sits somewhere between "theoretically excellent" and "practically ignored by 70% of the internet." Yes, this prevents BGP hijacking. Yes, your ISP probably hasn't enabled RPKI validation. Yes, you will still fail this control in three years when someone forgets to renew a ROA expiry, discover it during an audit, and have a brief panic attack about whether you've been routing traffic through someone else's data centre the whole time.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must test its incident response plan through practical exercises at least once a year to ensure staff know their roles, communication channels work, and procedures are effective when a real cyber incident occurs. Regular exercises identify gaps, keep the team prepared, and reduce response time and damage during actual incidents. This hands-on practice is critical because cyber incidents demand quick, coordinated action—and plans that sit unused often fail when needed most.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to actually *run* your incident response plan once a year—not just dust it off, nod solemnly at it, and file it away until the next audit. This means tabletop exercises, simulations, or the occasional unplanned crisis that teaches you everything is broken; all three methods work, though only one generates the delightful surprise of discovering your incident response coordinator left the organisation six months ago. Yes, this is annually, which somehow remains a challenging concept for organisations that would happily update their tea procurement policy with greater frequency.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must establish, document, and regularly update a formal policy that defines how you manage relationships with suppliers and service providers. This policy should cover expectations for security, performance, communication, and dispute resolution to ensure suppliers meet your security requirements and understand their obligations. Strong supplier management prevents security gaps at your boundaries, reduces risks from third-party failures, and provides a clear framework for addressing issues if a supplier's performance or security practices fall short.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need a written policy on how you'll manage suppliers—not just winging it via email chains and whoever picked up the phone last. Yes, this means actually documenting what you expect from them, how you'll monitor them, and what happens when they inevitably fail to meet those expectations, which they will. Nobody does this properly, but at least now you have a policy that says you're *supposed* to, which is apparently the Australian government's threshold for governance.

annotations.ai_view: You must create and keep up-to-date a list of approved suppliers that your organisation is authorised to work with. This limits your exposure to security risks by ensuring you only engage vendors who have been vetted and meet your security requirements, rather than allowing ad-hoc procurement from untrusted sources. A maintained list also provides visibility over your supply chain and makes it easier to enforce consistent security standards across all external relationships.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Maintain a documented list of suppliers you've actually vetted and approved, then watch in quiet despair as procurement bypasses it entirely because someone's mate offers a discount. The control itself is straightforward—keep the list current, actually use it, and document why suppliers made the cut—which is precisely why you'll find it gathering dust in a shared drive while business units are already three months into a contract with a provider nobody's heard of.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must purchase operating systems, applications, hardware, and services only from suppliers you've formally approved and assessed as trustworthy. This prevents you from inadvertently introducing compromised, counterfeit, or poorly supported products into your environment, and ensures suppliers meet your security requirements before they enter your supply chain.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need an approved suppliers list and the discipline to actually use it instead of whatever Dave in procurement grabbed from the cheapest email he received at 4:47pm on a Friday. Yes, this includes that sketchy firmware update and those "refurbished" network switches from the liquidation bin, which somehow never made it onto any approval process because nobody could quite figure out who was supposed to do the approving. The control itself is straightforward; the tragedy is watching organisations maintain immaculate supplier lists while systematically ignoring them under deadline pressure.

annotations.ai_view: Organisations must identify and maintain relationships with multiple suppliers for critical systems, applications, equipment and services rather than relying on a single vendor. This reduces the risk of supply chain disruption, vendor lock-in, and the security vulnerabilities that come from over-dependence on one provider. Having alternative suppliers available ensures you can quickly switch if a vendor experiences a breach, becomes compromised, or fails to meet security standards.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need multiple suppliers for critical kit so you're not completely helpless when your sole vendor decides to hold you ransom, disappears, or simply stops supporting that ancient operating system your entire estate apparently depends on. In theory this sounds sensible; in practice you'll watch organisations spend eighteen months negotiating with Vendor A, then discover Vendor B costs three times as much, then stick with Vendor A anyway and call it risk acceptance. The real lesson here is that having identified multiple suppliers means absolutely nothing if procurement, finance, and the business have already made their decision in the car park.

annotations.ai_view: Organisations must identify critical IT and operational technology equipment and maintain adequate spare parts or backup units to quickly restore systems if failures occur. This prevents extended downtime that could be exploited by attackers or leave systems vulnerable during recovery periods, and ensures business continuity when equipment fails unexpectedly.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need spare hardware on hand for the kit that actually matters, because apparently ordering replacements after a failure is something organisations discover they can't do at 2 AM on a Sunday. This reads simpler than it is: you'll need to identify which equipment is actually "critical" (which everyone agrees on until budget season), determine how many spares constitute "sufficient" (even less agreement), and then actually maintain them somewhere that isn't a forgotten cupboard in Perth. Most organisations will source these spares once, feel virtuous, watch them quietly disappear into other projects, and then explain to management why a failed network switch took out operations for three weeks.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that operating systems, applications, equipment and services reach your organisation in a trustworthy state—free from tampering, corruption or malicious modification during storage and transit. You need to verify the integrity of what you receive, such as checking digital signatures or comparing checksums against publisher-provided values, and maintain secure delivery channels to prevent interception or alteration. This matters because compromised software or hardware introduced during procurement could undermine your entire security posture before you even deploy it.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to ensure that whatever arrives at your door—OS, app, widget, or outsourced service—hasn't been tampered with in transit, which sounds reasonable until you realize half your vendors ship binaries via HTTP and the other half can't spell "cryptographic hash." This means cryptographic verification, secure supply chains, and actually checking the box before plugging it in, though in my experience this is the moment everyone discovers they have urgent meeting elsewhere.

annotations.ai_view: When you receive operating systems, applications, hardware, or services from suppliers, you must verify they haven't been tampered with, corrupted, or compromised before accepting them into your organisation. This check prevents malicious code, vulnerabilities, or unauthorised modifications from entering your systems through the supply chain. Performing acceptance testing and integrity verification—such as checking checksums, validating signatures, or running security scans—ensures you're deploying trustworthy products.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to actually verify that the operating systems, applications, and equipment you're about to let into your network haven't been tampered with or compromised before acceptance—a sensible requirement that organisations routinely ignore by plugging in whatever arrived on the delivery truck and calling it a day. Yes, this means checksums, certificates, provenance checks, or at minimum not accepting "we pinky swear it's fine" as an integrity assurance strategy. The fact that this needs to be explicitly mandated suggests someone has learned this lesson the hard way, probably multiple times.

annotations.ai_view: When you receive operating systems, applications, equipment or services from suppliers, you must verify they are genuine and haven't been tampered with or substituted before accepting them into your organisation. This prevents attackers from inserting malware, counterfeit hardware, or compromised software into your systems during the supply chain. Checking authenticity is a critical security gate because once fake or malicious products are deployed, they become difficult and costly to detect and remove.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to actually verify that the stuff you're buying is genuine before you accept it—not just assume the vendor sent what they said they sent, which apparently requires stating explicitly in 2025. Yes, this includes checking that your Windows licence isn't a masterpiece of forensic counterfeiting and that your Cisco gear didn't take a creative detour through a warehouse in Shenzhen. No organisation does this consistently, which is why we keep finding unlicensed software, cloned hardware, and that one time someone's entire "secure" network was running on what can only be described as optimistic firmware.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must ensure that any external service providers managing your data undergo independent security assessments at least every two years, using the current government security standards. This requirement matters because regular third-party audits verify that service providers actually maintain the security controls they've promised, reducing the risk that weaknesses in their systems could compromise your sensitive information. Without these scheduled assessments, you have no objective evidence that outsourced services remain secure as threats and technologies evolve.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your managed service providers must get an independent IRAP assessment every 24 months using whichever ISM version was current when they started—which means yes, they'll probably use an outdated baseline and everyone will pretend that's fine. This is the control that separates organisations that actually verify their outsourced security posture from those that simply assume their MSP's marketing brochure constitutes due diligence, which explains why you're currently running on infrastructure last assessed during the Turnbull administration.

annotations.ai_view: You must include a clause in contracts with service providers requiring them to give you at least one month's notice before making significant changes to their own suppliers or outsourcing arrangements. This matters because unexpected changes in your provider's supply chain—such as moving data processing to a new subcontractor or switching infrastructure providers—could introduce new security risks or compliance issues that you need time to assess and approve.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need your suppliers to tell you—in writing, contractually binding, one whole month ahead—before they outsource their bits to yet another vendor, because apparently organisations can't be trusted to notice when their critical infrastructure suddenly operates from someone's garage.
