This is a lovely control that reads beautifully in compliance reports and is routinely ignored until the supply chain audit finds out someone's been running your data through a reseller in a jurisdiction you've never heard of. At least it's simple: get it in the contract, make it hurt if they don't comply, and try not to develop an eye twitch when they claim they "didn't think that counted."

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that passwords for privileged accounts—including built-in Administrator accounts, emergency break glass accounts, local administrator accounts, and service accounts—must be at least 30 characters long. Longer passwords significantly increase resistance to brute-force attacks and are much harder to crack even if attackers obtain password hashes. This applies across all security classifications and protects the most sensitive access points in your systems, as these accounts are prime targets for attackers seeking to gain control of infrastructure.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Thirty characters minimum for your break glass accounts — the password that nobody writes down, everybody forgets, and somehow ends up in a shared Excel file anyway. Yes, this genuinely matters; yes, organisations skip it because "we'll remember it" or "it's too hard to manage"; yes, you will absolutely find an 8-character service account password at 2 AM during an incident response. Enforce this at provisioning time or watch it be quietly circumvented by the first person who finds it inconvenient.

annotations.ai_view: Developers must digitally sign executable files using certificates that can be verified back to a trusted source, creating a verifiable chain of trust. This prevents attackers from distributing malicious or tampered code by ensuring users and systems can confirm that executable files genuinely came from the expected developer and haven't been modified. Signed code also enables automated security tools to validate software authenticity before execution, reducing the risk of running compromised software.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Every executable needs a valid code-signing certificate with an unbroken chain back to a trusted root, because apparently trusting that your developers didn't accidentally ship malware is an insufficient control strategy. This one actually works—until someone distributes unsigned binaries "temporarily" during a crisis, discovers no one can verify the certificate chain anyway, and then the practice quietly dies until the next audit. The technical requirement is sound; the implementation gap is approximately the size of the national deficit.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that any installers, patches, and updates distributed to users must include either a digital signature or cryptographic checksum that allows recipients to verify the software hasn't been tampered with or corrupted during distribution. This matters because without verification, attackers could intercept and modify software in transit, potentially injecting malware that users would unknowingly install. By checking the signature or checksum before installation, organizations and users can confirm they're running legitimate, unaltered code from the intended developer.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Installers, patches and updates need digital signatures or cryptographic checksums so you can at least *detect* when someone's replaced them with malware—a thrilling reminder that in 2025 we're still fighting the battle against unsigned binaries, as if code signing wasn't solved circa 2005. Yes, this means your developers actually have to set up signing infrastructure and your ops team has to verify it, which apparently requires the same level of organisational commitment as maintaining a balanced diet. Watch as organisations tick this box by documenting they *plan* to sign things, then ship unsigned patches for the next three years while insisting compliance is definitely happening.

annotations.ai_view: Organizations must create and publish clear guidance documents (hardening guides or loosening guides) that explain how to securely configure their software products, making these resources readily available to customers. This matters because secure default configurations alone are insufficient—users need practical instructions to further strengthen security posture based on their specific risk environments, or to understand trade-offs when relaxing settings for operational needs. Without this guidance, organizations leave customers guessing about safe configuration options, increasing the likelihood of misconfigurations that create security gaps.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You must document how to actually secure the thing you've built and hand it to customers, which sounds simple until you realise half the industry ships products in their default-insecure state and calls it "flexibility." Yes, this includes both hardening *and* loosening guides—because apparently some organisations need written permission to weaken security controls, as if they weren't going to do it anyway. The depressing part is watching vendors treat this as optional theatre while their customers run everything with default credentials and wonder why they got breached.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires your organisation to configure email systems to automatically reject any incoming messages that fail DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) authentication checks. DMARC verification confirms that emails claiming to come from a domain are actually authorised by that domain's owner, preventing attackers from spoofing trusted sender addresses to conduct phishing attacks or spread malware. By rejecting non-compliant messages outright, you eliminate a major attack vector and significantly reduce the risk of staff being deceived by fraudulent emails.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your mail server should reject anything that fails DMARC validation, which means actually configuring SPF and DKIM records and then—here's where it gets interesting—enforcing the policy you've theoretically set. Yes, this will initially bounce legitimate emails from that one critical vendor who still uses a 1997 email setup, prompting three weeks of escalations before someone admits they never bothered with the configuration in the first place. Still, it's the right call: DMARC rejection stops the most tedious flavour of phishing attack, assuming your organisation has the discipline to not whitelist the whole internet when it gets awkward.

annotations.ai_view: Before connecting a network device to your network, you must install the official firmware directly from the manufacturer to ensure the device operates with known, trustworthy code. This prevents devices from being compromised by malicious or outdated firmware that could be pre-installed, allowing attackers to intercept traffic or gain network access. This practice is particularly critical because network devices are often trusted points in your security perimeter.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must flash network devices with vendor-trusted firmware before deployment—a foundational control that somehow still surprises people despite being the cybersecurity equivalent of "don't leave the factory defaults on." Yes, this means you need to actually verify firmware integrity and not just unbox the Cisco and plug it in, though we both know half your estate is running two-year-old versions with known CVEs anyway. It's almost comforting how predictable the breach timeline becomes once you skip this one.

annotations.ai_view: Network devices such as routers, switches, and firewalls must be restarted at least once per month to clear temporary memory, apply pending security updates, and eliminate potential persistence mechanisms that attackers might have established. Regular restarts help prevent memory-based exploits from accumulating and ensure devices operate with fresh configurations. This practice reduces the risk of undetected compromise and helps maintain the integrity of your network infrastructure.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Restart your network devices monthly so accumulated memory leaks, state table bloat, and that one zombie BGP session don't metastasise into a silent failure at 3am on a Friday. Yes, vendors ship firmware that doesn't need this; yes, your organisation will skip it for eighteen months and blame "stability"; yes, when something finally breaks catastrophically, no one will remember this existed.

annotations.ai_view: You must only use cryptographic equipment that the Australian Security Establishment has formally approved and operate it strictly according to the current security instructions that come with it. This matters because approved equipment has been tested to reliably protect classified information, and following the latest instructions ensures you maintain that protection as threats and best practices evolve.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must use only ASD-approved High Assurance Cryptographic Equipment and operate it according to the latest ACSI, which is a straightforward requirement that somehow still manages to surprise people who've been buying unauthorised gear for six years. Yes, the equipment needs explicit ASD sign-off; no, that laminated approval certificate from 2019 doesn't count as "latest version." This control exists because someone, somewhere, once thought it was acceptable to encrypt classified traffic through a black-box appliance from a vendor that no longer exists.

annotations.ai_view: A cyber security incident register must record the incident date, discovery date, description, response actions, and reporting recipients for every incident.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: A spreadsheet that gets filled out after the breach, mostly to satisfy auditors.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that your contracts with service providers include documented clauses allowing you to exit the agreement if they fail to meet agreed security standards. This matters because it gives you a concrete enforcement mechanism to protect your data and systems—if a provider doesn't maintain adequate security, you can terminate the relationship rather than remaining locked into a problematic arrangement.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Yes, you need to write down the circumstances under which you can actually fire a service provider for being catastrophically bad at security—which sounds obvious until you realise most organisations discovered their break clauses don't exist, or worse, are written so narrowly they'd only trigger if the vendor literally burned down the datacentre themselves. The theoretical idea is sound: contractual teeth to enforce consequences when providers achieve new creative forms of negligence. In practice, you'll spend six months negotiating this, your procurement team will accidentally delete it in a redline, and then you'll discover it after the breach anyway.

annotations.ai_view: A denial‑of‑service response plan for video conferencing and IP telephony must cover detection of an attack, identification of its source, maintenance of capabilities during the attack, and response actions. Having a plan ensures rapid, coordinated mitigation.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Write a playbook for when the phones go silent: spot the flood, find the culprit, keep talking, and actually do something — because hope isn’t a strategy.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to eliminate or change any default user accounts and passwords that come pre-configured in applications before putting them into use. Default credentials are a well-known security weakness because they're publicly documented, easily guessable, and often overlooked—leaving your systems vulnerable to unauthorised access if attackers gain network access to the application.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Disable or change every default credential before the application goes live—admin/admin, sa/sa, the works. Yes, this includes that vendor account that "definitely shouldn't be touched" and the documentation says you need for support; contact the vendor anyway and get them to generate a unique one. You will discover during your third incident that someone left this unchanged in production because "the dev team said it would break something," and they were wrong.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must use automated tools to discover and inventory assets on your network at least every two weeks, so you can identify which systems need vulnerability scanning and patching. This prevents attackers from exploiting unpatched devices you don't know exist or have forgotten about. Regular automated discovery catches new hardware, virtual machines, or cloud resources before they become security risks.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to run automated asset discovery at least every fourteen days so you know what's actually sitting on your network before you try to scan it for patches—a prerequisite so fundamental it's genuinely depressing that it required its own control statement. Most organisations will interpret "at least fortnightly" as "we'll schedule it for Tuesdays and then turn it off when it starts finding things in production nobody remembers buying." The control is technically sound, which makes watching it fail repeatedly all the more character-building.

annotations.ai_view: Organizations must use automated scanning tools with current vulnerability databases to regularly check systems for missing patches and security flaws. This ensures vulnerabilities are detected promptly before attackers can exploit them, which is essential because unpatched systems are a common entry point for breaches. Keeping the scanner's vulnerability database up-to-date means new threats are recognized as soon as they're discovered.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need a vulnerability scanner that actually knows what vulnerabilities exist, which requires feeding it a database updated more recently than the last time your organisation claimed to care about patching. Yes, "up-to-date" means yesterday's zero-day, not last quarter's advisory—organisations universally fail this by running scanners with databases from 2019. The real fun starts when you realise your scanner works perfectly and your patch management process still doesn't, but at least you'll have comprehensive documentation of what you're ignoring.

annotations.ai_view: When unsupported applications, operating systems, network devices, or networked IT equipment cannot be immediately removed or replaced, compensating security controls must be put in place until they can be retired. This mitigates the risk of running vulnerable, unpatchable components.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You can’t kill the legacy box today, so you wrap it in a security blanket of compensating controls and hope the auditor buys it. Spoiler: the blanket usually has holes.

annotations.ai_view: Backups must be coordinated so that when you restore systems after an incident or failure, all your data, applications and settings reflect the same moment in time rather than different points. This prevents inconsistencies that could corrupt data, break dependencies between systems, or leave you with partial recoveries that don't work together. Synchronized backups are essential for effective disaster recovery and ensure you can actually rely on your backups to restore your environment to a known, consistent state.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must ensure their backups are all pointing to the same moment in time so they can restore to a consistent state rather than assembling a Frankenstein system from Tuesday's database, Wednesday's application binaries, and last month's configuration files. This is theoretically straightforward—synchronise your backup jobs to run within a defined window—and yet somehow remains the first thing to degrade when the backup window extends from four hours to twelve and eventually to "it'll happen when it happens." The control exists because a "recovered" system that's internally inconsistent is arguably worse than the ransomware that prompted the recovery in the first place.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to keep copies of your data, applications, and system configurations stored securely and in a way that protects them from loss or damage. It matters because backups are your safety net—if systems fail, get attacked, or data gets corrupted, you can only recover if backups are properly protected and readily available when needed. Without secure, resilient backups, a single incident can become a permanent loss of critical information.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must maintain backups that are both secure (encrypted, access-controlled, the usual suspects) and resilient (geographically dispersed, tested regularly, ideally not stored in the same building as the systems they're backing up, though we both know someone will). The "retained in a secure and resilient manner" language is deliberately vague enough that most places will interpret it as "we have a backup tape in a locked cabinet," which will be discovered during an incident to have been corrupted since 2019. Test your restores quarterly or admit you don't actually have backups—just expensive insurance against hope.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that regular user accounts be prevented from accessing backups of other users' data—ensuring that one person cannot browse or restore another person's files through backup systems. It matters because backups often contain sensitive information, and without proper access restrictions, a compromised or malicious user account could expose confidential data, circumvent file-level permissions, or sabotage others' work by tampering with their backup copies.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Segregate backup data by user account so that one person's accidentally-shared credentials can't decrypt someone else's backups—a concept so fundamentally obvious that it somehow remains the smoking gun in 60% of breach post-mortems. Implement access controls at the filesystem, database, or encryption layer, depending on your backup architecture; yes, this means actually thinking about your backup design instead of bolting on permissions as an afterthought. Watch it get quietly ignored in favour of "everyone needs full backup access for recovery purposes," then nod knowingly when the contractor's compromised account exfiltrates the entire personnel database.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that regular users cannot restore or retrieve their own backup files, even if those backups contain data they normally have access to. This prevents users from circumventing security controls or audit trails by restoring deleted files, malware-infected versions, or data they've been denied access to, and protects backups from being altered or exfiltrated by compromised user accounts.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Prevent users from directly accessing or restoring their own backups, because apparently we've learned nothing from the seventeen times someone with a grudge restored themselves a copy of the CEO's email to sell to a competitor. It's a neat theoretical control that assumes backup systems exist separately from your production infrastructure and that someone actually monitors who's poking at the backup storage—both assumptions that have yet to survive contact with reality in any organisation I've encountered. Implement segregated backup access controls with audit logging, understand that this will require actually maintaining those controls, and accept that it will be the first thing ignored during the 3 a.m. "critical restore incident."

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that regular users cannot alter or remove backup files—only authorized administrators should have these privileges. It matters because backups are your last defence against data loss from ransomware, accidental deletion, or system compromise; if attackers or disgruntled staff can delete backups, you lose the ability to recover. By restricting these permissions, you ensure backups remain reliable and available when you need them most.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Restrict unprivileged accounts from modifying or deleting backups—a control so blindingly obvious that its existence as a numbered requirement speaks volumes about what organisations actually do in practice. Yes, your developer with sudo access will promise they "only need it for emergencies," and yes, three months later you'll be explaining to executives why last week's backup mysteriously went missing. Implement proper RBAC, immutable storage where feasible, and prepare yourself for the conversation where someone insists they absolutely must be able to touch the backups because their process is "special."

annotations.ai_view: Event logs must be stored in a way that prevents unauthorised users—including system administrators—from altering or erasing records, typically through read-only access controls or write-once storage. This protection is critical because logs are your evidence of what happened on a system; if attackers or insiders can modify them, they can cover their tracks and you lose the ability to detect breaches or investigate security incidents.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your logs need write-once storage or equivalent immutability controls—because apparently the five-point briefing about "don't let operators delete their own audit trail" didn't stick the first four times you deployed this. Yes, this includes keeping logs away from the very people who generate them, which creates the thrilling operational friction you'll spend the next eighteen months "resolving" with exceptions. At minimum, ensure privileged users can't touch logs after creation, though you'll eventually find some creative soul has logged in as a service account with unlogged local admin access, rendering the whole thing ornamental.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to protect the authoritative (master) copy of your software source code from unauthorised changes—for example, by restricting write access to only approved developers and logging all modifications. It matters because if someone modifies the source code without authorisation, they could inject malicious code, backdoors, or vulnerabilities that would then be built into every release, compromising the security and integrity of your entire software supply chain.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Prevent unauthorised changes to your source code repository — which sounds straightforward until you realise half your developers still have admin access to prod, Git credentials are living in Slack, and that contractor from last year probably still has push rights. Lock down your version control with proper access controls, code review enforcement, and audit logging, then watch in quiet despair as someone inevitably commits database passwords and calls it "security testing."

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to verify the identity and permissions of any client application that calls your web APIs and accesses sensitive data not meant for public use. Without proper authentication and authorisation checks, unauthorised users could exploit internet-accessible APIs to steal confidential information. Implementing these checks—such as API keys, OAuth tokens, or mutual authentication—ensures only legitimate clients with appropriate permissions can retrieve restricted data.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Requires that internet-accessible APIs actually authenticate who's calling them and check whether those callers should be allowed to see the data being served—a concept so foundational that its need for explicit documentation is itself a damning indictment of the industry. Will be ignored in favour of "we'll just use an API key in the request body" or, more commonly, "authentication is the frontend's problem." Implement token-based auth, validate on every call, and prepare to explain this to developers who've read a Medium article about REST and believe that constitutes security architecture.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that any web-based application interface allowing data changes over the internet must verify who is accessing it (authentication) and confirm they have permission to make those changes (authorisation). This matters because uncontrolled internet-facing APIs are a common attack vector—without these checks, attackers could modify or destroy your organisation's data without restriction. Implementing strong authentication and authorisation ensures only legitimate, approved users can make changes through these interfaces.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must actually verify who's calling their internet-facing APIs before letting them change anything, which sounds obvious until you discover the third-party integration running with hardcoded credentials from 2019. Authentication (proving you are who you claim) and authorisation (confirming you're allowed to do this thing) both matter here—one without the other is just security theatre with extra steps. The control helpfully applies to everything from NOT CLASSIFIED to TOP SECRET, which is the ISM's polite way of saying "this should not require a policy exception, yet somehow it will."

annotations.ai_view: When your organisation detects a cyber security incident, you must immediately activate your documented incident response plan to coordinate your response actions. This control ensures you have a structured, pre-planned approach ready to execute rather than scrambling to decide what to do during an active incident, which helps you contain damage, preserve evidence, and communicate effectively with the right people at the right time.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: When you detect a cyber incident—and you will, because your perimeter is held together with hope and legacy systems—you're supposed to actually *activate* your incident response plan rather than discover it doesn't exist or is still in a shared drive labeled "Final_FINAL_v3_ACTUAL.docx." This control requires that plan to transition from theoretical comfort object to actual operational reality within whatever timeframe your organisation's definition of "immediately" happens to mean that week. The fact this needs to be a mandatory control tells you everything you need to know about how many organisations treat incident response planning as a checkbox exercise and then panic-hire consultants when the inevitable happens.

annotations.ai_view: Use a consistent colour scheme for cables connecting to individual systems so that authorised personnel can quickly identify which cables belong to which system. This makes it easier to detect unauthorised cable modifications or connections, reduces the risk of accidental disconnections during maintenance, and helps prevent someone from surreptitiously intercepting or tampering with data in transit. Clear cable identification is a simple physical security measure that supports your ability to monitor and control access to critical infrastructure.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Establish and maintain a consistent colour scheme for network and power cables across your organisation—a deceptively simple requirement that somehow manages to be violated by approximately 100% of facilities within six months of implementation. Yes, this does technically improve traceability and reduce the catastrophic "which cable do I pull" incidents; no, your contractors will not care and will continue using whatever was in the van. The real value emerges only when someone actually enforces it, which almost never happens, making this one of infosec's most honoured and most ignored recommendations.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that cables carrying the highest classification of information (TOP SECRET) must never share the same cable bundle or conduit with any other cables—they need their own separate, dedicated pathways. This separation prevents potential physical security breaches where an attacker could access multiple classified and unclassified systems by compromising a single shared conduit, and it reduces the risk of accidental cross-connection or electromagnetic interference that could expose sensitive communications.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Cables carrying TOP SECRET must have their own dedicated conduit or bundle—they cannot share physical infrastructure with cables of lower classification, because apparently electromagnetic leakage respects bureaucratic hierarchies and not just physical proximity. Yes, this means that organisation you're auditing cannot route that TOP SECRET fibre alongside their unclassified network because the control said so, which they will argue about for six months before grudgingly complying. It's tedious, it's expensive, and it's also genuinely sensible if you've actually thought about signal emanation for more than thirty seconds.

annotations.ai_view: Use a consistent colour scheme for wall outlet boxes connected to individual systems so staff can quickly identify which outlets serve which equipment. This visual consistency reduces the risk of accidentally unplugging critical systems, connecting devices to the wrong network, or inadvertently damaging infrastructure during maintenance or emergency situations. Clear, standardized outlet identification supports safer physical infrastructure management across your organisation.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must paint their outlet boxes in a consistent colour—a control that somehow made it into an information security manual despite being neither security nor manual in any meaningful sense. Yes, this theoretically helps identify which systems outlets belong to, and yes, someone will ignore it and daisy-chain peripherals across three different coloured boxes anyway. The real security value arrives only when combined with actual asset tracking, which most sites skip directly to the part where they buy the paint.

annotations.ai_view: Security settings in office productivity suites are immutable to users, preventing them from disabling macros, protected view, or other hardening measures. User‑driven changes are a frequent vector for malware delivery.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: We all know the first thing a user does is “enable all macros” for that one spreadsheet, so the config is now immutable. Good luck explaining why the “Enable Content” button is greyed out.

annotations.ai_view: PDF viewer security options such as JavaScript execution, external connections, and privilege escalation are locked to prevent users from weakening them. Malicious PDFs exploit these features for code execution and data exfiltration.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Users love enabling “Enable JavaScript” to view that fancy form, so we lock the settings down. Now the only thing they can change is the zoom level.

annotations.ai_view: Configuration of security products (AV, EDR, firewalls) is locked to prevent users from disabling protections or altering policies. Tampering with security controls directly undermines the defense posture.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Because the first thing a compromised admin does is turn off the AV, we make the config read‑only. Hope the vendor’s “tamper‑proof” claim holds up in court.

annotations.ai_view: When selecting server applications, choose vendors who actively build security into their development process from the start (Secure by Design) and ship secure default configurations (Secure by Default), with a strong preference for those using memory-safe programming languages like Python, Java, or Go rather than C or C++. This reduces the likelihood of common vulnerabilities like buffer overflows and memory corruption bugs that attackers frequently exploit. Prioritising vendors with demonstrated secure coding practices means fewer security flaws make it into production systems, reducing your exposure to exploits and the need for constant patching.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must now apparently evaluate vendors on their commitment to security principles before deployment—a delightful exercise in theory that will collide with procurement's three-year-old contract and the business unit's insistence on that one legacy Java application nobody understands. Memory safety matters, yes, and the ISM's gentle preference for actual memory-safe languages over "practices" is the closest thing to a wink you'll get from government guidance acknowledging that C++ won't magically become safe just because someone promised to be careful.

annotations.ai_view: Domain controller administration must use separate user accounts that are only used for that purpose, not shared with other system administration tasks. This limits damage if a domain administrator account is compromised—an attacker can't use it to pivot to other systems. Since domain controllers are critical infrastructure that can grant attackers organisation-wide access, isolating their administration reduces the blast radius of potential breaches.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Requires that domain admin accounts used to manage Active Directory are segregated from accounts used to administer literally everything else your organisation runs—a simple principle that somehow remains aspirational at organisations with hundreds of servers. Yes, this means your sysadmin cannot use the same account to patch Windows, manage printers, and unlock user accounts; yes, we all know they will anyway because credentials are sticky and privilege separation is inconvenient. The technical bar here is not high; the compliance bar is apparently floor-level.

annotations.ai_view: Disable the Print Spooler service on Active Directory domain controllers to remove an unnecessary attack surface that could be exploited to compromise these critical systems. Domain controllers should run only essential services; the Print Spooler is not required for their core function and has been a vector for privilege escalation and remote code execution attacks. Removing this service reduces risk without affecting domain controller operations.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Disable the Print Spooler service on your domain controllers—yes, apparently this needed to be explicitly mandated because someone, somewhere, thought it was reasonable to run a decades-old, historically vulnerable print queue processor on the machines that literally guard your entire Active Directory infrastructure. This is the infosec equivalent of reminding someone not to store passwords on a sticky note: technically obvious, yet empirically necessary. The service serves no legitimate purpose on a DC and presents yet another attack surface that your threat actors would be absolutely delighted to find you've left running.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to avoid storing passwords in Active Directory Group Policy Preferences, as these passwords are stored with weak encryption that can be easily decrypted by attackers with domain access. Group Policy Preferences were historically used to deploy credentials across systems, but this practice creates a significant security vulnerability since the encryption keys are publicly known. Instead, use secure credential management alternatives like managed service accounts, password vaults, or other approved credential storage methods to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive passwords.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Microsoft Group Policy Preferences will happily store passwords in XML files on domain controllers, encrypt them with a publicly documented key, and then act shocked when pentesters extract them in under five minutes—so don't do that. This control exists because it turns out that "security through obscurity using a static 32-bit key disclosed in 2012" is not, in fact, security. Yes, every organisation swears they don't use GPP for passwords, and yes, you will find them doing exactly that in the third week of your engagement.

annotations.ai_view: All security‑relevant events from the AD core servers must be forwarded to a central logging solution. Centralised logs enable timely detection of anomalous activity such as privilege escalation or replication abuse.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Central logging is the infosec equivalent of a gym membership—everyone signs up, few actually go. Expect the SIEM to be flooded with noise and the alerts to be ignored until the next audit.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that you only assign Service Principal Names to service accounts and computer accounts in Active Directory—not to regular user accounts. Service Principal Names are used for Kerberos authentication, and restricting them prevents attackers from using compromised user accounts to impersonate services or escalate privileges across your network.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Restrict SPN registration to service and computer accounts only—a control that exists primarily because someone, somewhere, registered SPNs on user accounts and accidentally created a Kerberoasting buffet. Technically sound in principle; infinitely ignored in practice because apparently asking the application team to use managed service accounts feels like requesting they learn Ancient Sumerian. Audit this quarterly if you enjoy disappointment.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that when you create user accounts in Active Directory, you only grant them the specific permissions and group memberships needed to do their job—nothing more. This reduces the damage that could occur if an account is compromised, since attackers would only gain access to the resources and functions that account legitimately needs rather than having broad permissions across your systems.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Give users only the permissions they actually need to do their job, not the full administrative access they'll inevitably request or the blanket domain admin role some overworked sysadmin hands out to make the tickets stop coming. Yes, this is obvious. Yes, every organisation swears they do this. No, they don't — you'll find nested security groups from 2009 granting permissions to people who left in 2012, and the one person with a legitimate need for elevated rights now has seven different privilege paths because nobody documented the original setup or bothered to clean it up.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to ensure that Service Principal Names (SPNs) are unique across your Active Directory domain, with no duplicates assigned to different accounts. Duplicate SPNs create confusion in authentication and can allow attackers to impersonate services or perform credential-based attacks by targeting the wrong account. Regularly auditing and removing duplicate SPNs prevents these security gaps and maintains the integrity of your service authentication infrastructure.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Requires regular audits to ensure no Service Principal Names are duplicated across the domain, because apparently allowing multiple SPNs for the same object is a credible escalation vector that organisations consistently discover during forensics. Most environments will find duplicates within five minutes of actually looking, having accumulated them like technical debt through years of half-completed migrations and decommissioning processes that stopped halfway through. The fact this needed formalising into a control speaks volumes about what passes for account hygiene in practice.

annotations.ai_view: Mark privileged user accounts in Active Directory with the "sensitive and cannot be delegated" attribute to prevent attackers from using these accounts for lateral movement across your network. This setting stops an attacker who compromises a privileged account from impersonating it to access other systems, containing the damage from a breach. It's a critical hardening step that limits how far an attacker can spread once inside your environment.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Mark your privileged accounts as "sensitive" in Active Directory and disable delegation—a setting so straightforward that it somehow gets missed at organisations that claim to care about security, then surprises absolutely no one when an attacker pivots through an unpatched service account running under a domain admin. This prevents those accounts from being used for Kerberos constrained delegation attacks, which is theoretically useful if your environment isn't already a delegated-trust house of cards someone built in 2009 and forgot about. The control exists, it works, and it will sit unconfigured in your organisation's AD until the third-party audit arrives.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that user accounts in Active Directory must have Kerberos pre-authentication enabled, which means users must prove their identity before the authentication server issues them a ticket to access network resources. Without pre-authentication, attackers can request authentication tickets for any account without knowing the password, then attempt to crack those tickets offline—a technique called AS-REP roasting. Enabling this protection makes it significantly harder for attackers to compromise accounts through this attack vector.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Requires enabling Kerberos pre-authentication on AD user accounts, which prevents attackers from offline-cracking AS-REQ messages—a control so fundamental that its existence as a separate line item is itself a minor indictment of the state of things. Yes, this is enabled by default in modern AD, yet here we are documenting it anyway, presumably because somewhere an organisation disabled it for "compatibility reasons" and forgot to re-enable it circa 2009. Auditors love this one because it's easy to check and impossibly hard to actually enforce across a sprawling estate.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that user accounts in Active Directory have password expiration enabled and passwords set as mandatory—preventing accounts from using default or indefinite credentials that attackers could exploit. Enforcing password changes and requiring passwords reduces the window of exposure if credentials are compromised and closes a common misconfiguration gap that leaves accounts permanently accessible with static or missing passwords. This is a foundational hardening step that supports credential management and limits lateral movement opportunities for attackers.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Disable "Password Never Expires" and "Password Not Required" flags on AD user accounts—a control that somehow remains necessary in 2024, suggesting organisations still haven't grasped that immortal passwords are both a compliance box and a security theatre prop. Yes, this includes service accounts, which will predictably trigger outages the moment you enforce it, but that's what you get for letting infrastructure teams ignore this for seven years. Standard password expiry policy (though debatable in efficacy) still beats the alternative of credentials valid since the last server migration.

annotations.ai_view: Ensure that Active Directory user accounts do not rely on the UserPassword attribute for authentication, instead using modern credential mechanisms like passwords stored through standard authentication protocols. This prevents the storage of credentials in a legacy format that may be less secure or more prone to exposure if the directory is compromised. This requirement strengthens authentication security by eliminating weaker, outdated password storage methods from your identity management system.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Active Directory still stores plaintext passwords in the UserPassword attribute if you're not careful, which is delightful because it's 2024 and organisations regularly discover this after a breach. This control requires you to ensure the attribute remains unpopulated and unused—which you'd think would be automatic, but apparently explaining that "don't store passwords in a readable field" needs to be in writing. The fact this got updated in 2024 suggests someone finally noticed people were still doing this.

annotations.ai_view: Don't allow standard user accounts to view or access fields in Active Directory that might contain passwords or password-like information, as unprivileged users could exploit these details for unauthorized access. This prevents sensitive credentials from being exposed through user-accessible account properties like description fields, comments, or other writable attributes. By restricting what information is visible to non-admin users, you reduce the attack surface and limit how far an attacker with basic user access could escalate their privileges.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: This control requires that organisations not store passwords in AD user object fields that unprivileged users can read—think Description, Notes, or any of the other convenient fields where someone inevitably decides to document credentials "just temporarily." The fact that this needed to be written down suggests that somewhere, right now, a password is sitting in a user's "Office" attribute, and the person who put it there genuinely believed nobody would notice. Technically sound advice; practically, you'll find this violation in roughly 40% of organisations that claim to take security seriously.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that Active Directory user account passwords are stored using non-reversible encryption (such as salted hashing), rather than methods that allow passwords to be decrypted back to their original form. Reversible encryption creates a critical security risk because if an attacker gains access to the directory database, they can easily recover plaintext passwords to compromise user accounts and move laterally through your network. By enforcing non-reversible encryption, you significantly reduce the impact of potential directory breaches and limit attackers' ability to exploit stolen password data.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Disable reversible encryption for AD passwords because storing credentials in a format that can be decrypted is, shockingly, a security problem—yet this remains one of the most commonly missed hardening steps, particularly when someone enables it "just temporarily" for a legacy application in 2003 and forgets about it for twenty years. The control exists because once an attacker has your directory, reversible passwords are functionally equivalent to plaintext. This is not controversial or debatable, despite what your vendor's documentation from the Bush administration might suggest.

annotations.ai_view: This control prevents regular users from joining computers to your Active Directory domain, restricting that capability to authorized administrators only. Allowing unprivileged users to add machines creates security risks by enabling attackers or compromised accounts to connect rogue devices that could steal data or spread malware across your network. By limiting domain-join permissions, you maintain control over which devices are trusted members of your environment and reduce the attack surface available to unauthorized actors.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Restrict the "Add workstations to domain" right so only privileged accounts (Domain Admins, delegated admins) can join machines to AD—a control that sounds reasonable until you watch a contractor with basic user permissions somehow join seventeen rogue laptops to your domain because someone delegated it to a group that had "maybe IT people in it." This prevents casual domain pollution and reduces the attack surface for lateral movement, though it does require actually auditing who has the permission, which organisations tend to skip in favour of hoping nobody notices.

annotations.ai_view: Use separate, dedicated service accounts with limited permissions specifically for joining computers to your Active Directory domain, rather than reusing general administrator accounts. This prevents attackers who compromise a machine-joining process from gaining broad administrative access across your entire network. Limiting these accounts to only domain-join permissions reduces the blast radius if credentials are exposed or misused.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Rather than allowing every admin with a Domain Admin credential to casually join workstations to the domain like they're adding friends on Facebook, you're meant to create a separate service account with precisely the permissions needed for that task and nothing else — a concept so straightforward that roughly 80% of organisations will ignore it in favour of just handing out DA credentials to anyone who asks nicely. Yes, it's marginally more work to set up and maintain, but it does prevent that one contractor's compromised laptop from becoming your entire domain's problems at 2 AM on a Sunday.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to regularly audit Active Directory accounts that have unconstrained delegation enabled—a capability that allows these accounts to impersonate any user across the domain—and remove those that lack a Service Principal Name (SPN) or legitimate business justification. Unconstrained delegation is a high-risk configuration because compromised accounts can be weaponised to gain widespread access to other systems and data. Annual reviews ensure that only genuinely necessary delegation permissions remain active, significantly reducing the attack surface available to threat actors.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to actually look at your AD accounts once a year and yank out any with unconstrained delegation that either don't have a Service Principal Name or whose "business requirement" is someone's vague assertion that it probably does something important. In practice, this means finding accounts that were delegated broad authentication forwarding privileges in 2009 and nobody's touched since, then having a awkward conversation with whoever created them to confirm they're not secretly critical to your payroll system.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to prevent regular computers (excluding domain controllers) from being configured to automatically delegate user credentials to other services. If a compromised computer is trusted for delegation, attackers can impersonate legitimate users to gain unauthorised access to other systems and services across your network. Disabling this capability limits the damage an attacker can do if they gain control of a standard computer.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Disable unconstrained delegation on non-DC computer accounts—essentially preventing them from obtaining service tickets on behalf of other users, which would let an attacker weaponise a compromised workstation to impersonate anyone in AD. This is both technically sound and universally ignored, usually discovered during a penetration test when the pen tester sighs and demonstrates it for the sixteenth time. The fact that this still needs to be explicitly documented in 2024 speaks volumes about how organisations configure their infrastructure the moment the setup wizard finishes.

annotations.ai_view: When you disable a user account, you must immediately remove that user from all security groups they belonged to. This prevents disabled accounts from retaining access rights to systems and data, closing a common gap where former or inactive users could potentially be re-enabled with their original permissions intact. It's a simple but critical cleanup step that reduces your attack surface by ensuring disabled accounts cannot be exploited to gain unauthorised access.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: When you disable a user in AD, their group memberships should evaporate like your faith in proper offboarding processes—except they almost never do, because someone always forgets to run the cleanup script or thinks "disabled = already secured." The control exists because orphaned group memberships are a reliable path to privilege creep and the kind of access audit findings that make managers ask uncomfortable questions three years later. Yes, it's technically straightforward; no, this will not stop your organisation from discovering stale memberships during a forensic investigation.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to ensure that user accounts are not members of the Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access security group in Active Directory, as this group grants broad permissions that increase risk if compromised. Removing user accounts from this legacy group reduces the attack surface and prevents unnecessary privilege escalation, since the group is primarily intended for legacy system compatibility rather than regular user access.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Remove user accounts from the Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access group because that security boundary exists for a reason, even if that reason is now older than most of your junior staff. Yes, legacy compatibility is important; no, it doesn't require handing out pre-2000-era permissions like they're still valid. You will find user accounts in this group. You will find many of them. Someone will explain this is necessary for "that one critical system," and they will be wrong, but you will spend three weeks proving it anyway.

annotations.ai_view: The control requires rotating the KRBTGT service account password twice, with a replication interval between changes, whenever the domain is compromised, suspected of compromise, or the password hasn't been changed in six months. This limits an attacker's ability to forge Kerberos tickets and maintain persistent access.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You’ll change the KRBTGT password twice, wait for replication, and pretend that fixes the golden‑ticket problem—because nothing says “secure” like a scheduled password reset after the breach.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to replace virtualization software or operating systems that are no longer receiving vendor support when you're running multiple isolated environments on a single physical server. Unsupported software no longer receives security patches, leaving vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit to break out of virtual machines or compromise the isolation between environments. By replacing outdated software promptly, you maintain the security boundary that protects each isolated workload from interference or attacks by others sharing the same hardware.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: When your hypervisor or container runtime hits end-of-life, you replace it rather than limping along on patches that stopped arriving three years ago—a straightforward requirement that somehow always surprises people at the 2 a.m. incident call when a zero-day drops and there's nothing left to patch with. Yes, this includes the host OS underneath your virtualisation layer, not just the management console you've been meaning to upgrade since the last government reshuffle. You'd think organisations running multiple security domains on shared hardware would treat their isolation layer like critical infrastructure, but here we are.

annotations.ai_view: Organisations must apply OWASP's Top 10 Proactive Controls when building web applications to prevent common security flaws before they reach production. These controls provide developers with concrete techniques—such as input validation, secure authentication, and protection against injection attacks—that address the most significant threats to web applications. Implementing these controls early in development is more cost-effective than fixing vulnerabilities later and reduces the risk of data breaches or system compromise.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must integrate OWASP's Top 10 Proactive Controls—a curated list of secure coding practices that have somehow remained controversial despite existing since 2016—into their software development lifecycle. Yes, this means actually using them during development rather than discovering them in a penetration test three years later. Remarkably, this applies across all classification levels, though the difference between how OFFICIAL and SECRET systems ignore this particular requirement is purely theatrical.

annotations.ai_view: Web application developers must identify and address the ten most critical security vulnerabilities listed in the OWASP Top 10, which include issues like broken authentication, injection attacks, and cross-site scripting. This control matters because these vulnerabilities are the most commonly exploited weaknesses in web applications and fixing them significantly reduces the risk of data breaches and unauthorized access. By building security controls into the development process rather than trying to patch problems later, organisations protect both their systems and user data from the most predictable attack methods.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must actively identify and remediate the ten most common web application vulnerabilities, which OWASP helpfully publishes annually so that attackers know exactly what to look for. This is the control equivalent of "please implement basic hygiene"—technically essential, universally ignored until after a breach, and somehow still treated as optional by developers who believe their bespoke authentication logic is the exception to twenty years of accumulated wisdom. The fact that this made it into the ISM suggests someone finally got tired of explaining why SQLi in 2024 is unacceptable.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must address the ten most common security risks in web APIs identified by the OWASP project—such as broken authentication, excessive data exposure, and injection attacks—during development and testing. This matters because APIs are frequent attack targets that, if compromised, can expose sensitive data or allow unauthorised access to your systems and user information. Implementing these protections reduces the likelihood of attackers exploiting known API vulnerabilities to breach your organisation.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your developers must actually address the OWASP API Security Top 10—you know, those ten categories of vulnerabilities that have remained essentially unchanged since 2019 and yet somehow surprise organisations quarterly. This means authentication, rate limiting, injection prevention, and all the other fundamentals that get deprioritised until a contractor finds your API keys in GitHub, at which point everyone suddenly pretends it was always a priority. Practically speaking, this requires threat modelling, secure coding practices, and testing, though the fact we need a specific control to remind people not to ship obvious API vulnerabilities speaks volumes about how the industry is doing.

annotations.ai_view: Standard (unprivileged) user access must be restricted to the minimum necessary for the user’s role. Least‑privilege reduces the attack surface and limits potential damage from compromised accounts.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Give users just enough rope to do their jobs—no more, no less, because they’ll inevitably hang themselves otherwise.

annotations.ai_view: Users must authenticate to multifunction devices before they can print, scan, or copy documents, ensuring only authorised personnel can access printed or scanned information.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Of course, because nothing says security like making people swipe a badge before the printer eats their confidential memo.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must maintain central logs that record all printing, scanning, and copying activities on multifunction devices, including temporary files that devices may create during document processing. This ensures you can track who accessed what documents and when, helping detect unauthorised use, data theft, or compliance violations. Without this visibility, sensitive documents could be copied or scanned without your knowledge, and you'd have no audit trail to investigate security incidents or prove data protection requirements were met.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must enable centralised logging on multifunction devices—those networked printers that everyone treats as secure waste bins because "it's just a copier." This includes capturing temporary files and cached documents that the device helpfully creates without telling anyone, which is particularly relevant since most organisations discover their MFD logs six months after a breach, if they discover them at all. Yes, this applies to PROTECTED and above; no, most facilities managers have never heard of it.

annotations.ai_view: Configure your IT equipment to match hardening standards from the Australian Signals Directorate and your equipment vendor, applying the stricter standard when the two conflict. This removes unnecessary features and default settings that attackers could exploit, significantly reducing your attack surface. Consistent hardening across all equipment makes your systems harder to compromise and helps prevent attackers from moving laterally through your network.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Take your baseline hardening from ASD's guidance, layer in whatever your vendor bothers to publish, and when they contradict each other—which they will, because vendors think security is a suggestion—pick the one that makes your systems actually defensible rather than merely compliant-looking. Most organisations will skip this entirely, apply only what fits their architecture, and then express genuine surprise when their "hardened" Windows server arrives from the vendor with fifteen unnecessary services already screaming on the network.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires you to configure office applications like Word, Excel and PowerPoint according to the strictest applicable hardening guidelines—prioritising Australian Signals Directorate advice over vendor recommendations when they conflict. Hardening these widely-used applications reduces attack surface by disabling risky features, blocking macros, and enforcing safer defaults, which is critical since office documents are a common infection vector for malware and credential theft.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must apply hardening baselines to Office applications—preferably the ASD's guidance, or vendor recommendations if those exist, or whichever is stricter when they inevitably contradict. The precedence rule exists because someone once had to explain why Finance was running Excel with macros enabled at maximum permissiveness, which apparently requires legislation. You will implement this, your users will complain it breaks their workflow, someone in management will ask why we're being "so restrictive," and then a macro will exfiltrate something embarrassing.

annotations.ai_view: Configure PDF applications to block potentially dangerous features like JavaScript, embedded files, and automatic content loading by following the Australian Signals Directorate's hardening guidance alongside your PDF software vendor's security recommendations—applying the stricter setting whenever the two conflict. This matters because PDFs are frequently weaponised in targeted attacks to deliver malware or exploit vulnerabilities, so reducing their attack surface significantly lowers your organisation's risk from this common attack vector.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Configure your PDF readers to reject anything more complex than a grocery list, following ASD's hardening guide whilst also genuinely reading whatever your PDF vendor published, then apply whichever one forbids more features because apparently the one thing organisations consistently get wrong is letting PDFs do things. Yes, this includes disabling JavaScript execution, which reminds you that PDFs somehow became a programming language, which should concern everyone equally.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires enabling Local Security Authority (LSA) protection on Windows systems to prevent attackers from extracting cached credentials and authentication tokens from memory. When enabled, LSA runs in a protected process that's harder to compromise, making it significantly more difficult for malware or attackers with local access to steal credentials that could be used for lateral movement or further attacks. This is a foundational hardening measure that directly supports credential protection and reduces the risk of unauthorized access to systems and data.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Enable LSA protection on Windows systems—basically, convince your organisation to flip a switch that prevents attackers from harvesting credentials straight out of memory, which they'll definitely do if you don't. Yes, this has been technically feasible since Windows 8.1, and yes, you'll still find seventeen legacy applications in 2025 that mysteriously "need" it disabled because some vendor wrote their integration in 2009 and never bothered updating. Watch your change management process grind to a halt, then enable it anyway when the audit comes around.

annotations.ai_view: Keep the real addresses of your web servers hidden from the internet by routing all traffic through your firewall, and ensure only the firewall and your authorised management systems can communicate directly with those servers. This prevents attackers from bypassing your firewall defences by targeting servers directly, and limits the paths an attacker could use to access your systems. It's a key part of hardening your network so that your firewall remains the single point of control for all web traffic.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Hide your origin servers behind the WAF like they're witnesses in protective custody, because the moment someone discovers your real IP, every script kiddie and their cousin will start hammering it directly while your expensive WAF watches from the sidelines. Restrict access to those origin IPs to the WAF itself and your management networks—a remarkably straightforward concept that organisations somehow manage to bungle by leaving SSH open to the world, hardcoding IPs in client-side code, or simply not bothering to implement network segmentation. Yes, we all know you'll discover this control violation during an incident in six months while someone asks why the attacker bypassed your security gateway entirely.

annotations.ai_view: Management interfaces (like SSH, RDP, or web consoles) used to configure IT equipment must not be directly accessible from the internet. This prevents attackers from discovering and exploiting these interfaces, which are high-value targets because successful compromise gives them administrative control. You should only allow management access through secure internal networks, VPNs, or bastion hosts that add authentication and monitoring layers.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your management interfaces—SSH, SNMP, web consoles, whatever—need to live behind a firewall or bastion host, not sitting on the public internet like a misconfigured S3 bucket waiting to be adopted. This is apparently still worth saying in 2024, which tells you everything you need to know about the state of network hygiene across the Australian public service. You will ignore this control anyway, deploy your Cisco UCS management interface on a /32 public IP, panic when the ransomware arrives, then blame the vendor.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires your organisation to create, put in place, and regularly update a written policy that clearly defines how staff and contractors should use your systems—covering acceptable activities, prohibited behaviours, and consequences for misuse. A system usage policy matters because it sets clear expectations upfront, helps prevent accidents and intentional misuse, reduces legal risks, and provides a reference point for investigation and enforcement when security incidents occur.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need a documented policy that explicitly tells users what they can and cannot do with systems, then actually tell them about it—a concept apparently revolutionary enough to warrant formal control status. Every organisation will draft a policy that says "don't do bad things," file it somewhere, and then act shocked when users do exactly what they want anyway. The policy itself isn't security; it's just the legally defensible record that you tried.

annotations.ai_view: Before staff members get access to a system, they must acknowledge and agree they understand the rules for how they can use it. This creates a clear record that users know what's expected of them and the consequences of misuse, which helps prevent accidental or deliberate security breaches. It's a foundational step that makes accountability possible when security incidents occur.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Personnel must acknowledge system usage policies in writing before access is granted—a straightforward requirement that somehow becomes controversial every time someone claims they "didn't know" they couldn't store their daughter's wedding photos on the classified network. Yes, they should read it; no, they won't; yes, you still need them to sign it anyway, because when the breach inquiry happens, you'll need something to point at while explaining why Jake from Accounting had admin rights to the finance system. It's not a substitute for actually enforcing those policies, which is where things get interesting.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires organisations to prevent employees from saving classified information onto their personal phones, laptops, or computers when accessing sensitive work systems. It matters because personal devices are typically less protected than company-managed equipment and are more vulnerable to loss, theft, or compromise, which could expose classified government data. Implementing this usually involves technical restrictions like disabling download or copy functions for classified content on personal devices.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Organisations must prevent personnel from storing classified data on their personal devices—a requirement that assumes you've somehow solved the organisational problem of actually *knowing* what's happening on devices you don't control, which you haven't. The control is technically sound in its intent; the implementation will involve either aggressive mobile device management that employees will immediately circumvent, or trusting people to self-regulate, which is comedy. In practice, this means you'll spend considerable effort on endpoint controls while watching someone email themselves a spreadsheet marked PROTECTED anyway, because the control can't actually stop determined users from being careless.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that any mobile device accessing sensitive or classified government data must use an operating system that has been independently tested and certified to meet international security standards, and must be configured according to the Australian government's official hardening guidelines. This matters because mobile devices are frequent targets for compromise, so using certified platforms with security-focused configurations significantly reduces the risk of unauthorised access to sensitive government information.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your agency's mobile devices must run platforms that have cleared Common Criteria evaluation against the Mobile Device Fundamentals PP v3.3 or later, then be locked down further via the ASD hardening guides—which is a pleasant fiction that will be honoured in the breach by everyone using personal iPhones for "just checking email." The control is technically sound, which makes it all the more depressing when you discover that the organisation has deployed Windows Mobile running on a five-year-old Samsung that never received the security config update.

annotations.ai_view: This control requires that mobile devices handling classified information (SECRET and TOP SECRET) cannot use removable storage like SD cards or USB drives unless the Australian Signals Directorate has explicitly approved it beforehand. Removable media creates significant security risks because it can be easily lost, stolen, or infected with malware, potentially exposing sensitive government information outside the organisation's protective environment. Requiring advance approval ensures that only necessary and properly secured removable storage is used, and that risks have been assessed before deployment.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Don't put USB drives, SD cards, or any other removable storage on your SECRET or TOP SECRET phones and tablets—unless ASD has pre-approved it, which they almost certainly haven't and won't. In practice, this means your organisation's executives will carry classified data on personal USB sticks anyway, discover them in the carpark three months later, and someone will tick the "approved" box retroactively. The control is sound; the compliance is theater.

annotations.ai_view: Organisations must create and regularly update a complete inventory of all IT equipment that isn't connected to a network, such as standalone computers, printers, or storage devices, and periodically verify this register remains accurate. This matters because non-networked equipment can still hold sensitive data, be vulnerable to theft or misuse, and pose security risks if not properly tracked and accounted for. Regular verification ensures you know what equipment exists, where it is, and can take appropriate protective measures.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: You need to actually know what non-networked equipment you own—yes, that means the printer in the corner that nobody remembers buying and the laptop someone "borrowed" in 2019—and keep records that reflect reality rather than the fantasy in your asset management system. Maintain it regularly (which organisations universally interpret as "once when an auditor asks") and verify it still matches what's actually sitting in your building, which it won't, because people are fundamentally incapable of telling you when they move things. The control is theoretically straightforward; the implementation suggests we're asking humans to do something they find actively repugnant.

annotations.ai_view: Restrict what applications and scripts can run in user profiles and temporary folders—places where operating systems, web browsers, and email clients store files and cache data. This prevents attackers from easily executing malware hidden in these common locations, since temporary folders are frequent targets for malicious code injection. Blocking unauthorized execution here significantly reduces the risk that compromised downloads or malicious attachments can spread across your system.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Right, so you need to lock down the folders where browsers cache your users' entire browsing history, where temp files containing credentials languistically decompose, and where email clients dump attachments like a digital hoarder—because apparently trusting operating system defaults is a luxury we can't afford. Yes, even ML1 organisations somehow manage to skip this one while frantically patching ransomware. Apply whitelisting/blacklisting to these paths; if you're relying on "users won't execute malware from AppData," you've already lost.

annotations.ai_view: Application control means using whitelisting technology to restrict which programs can run on a computer. This control requires you to enable it across your system except in the standard user, browser cache, and email temporary folders where these applications legitimately need flexibility to function. This matters because it prevents unauthorized or malicious software from executing, significantly reducing the risk of malware infection and insider threats.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Restrict executable code execution to hardened directories, which sounds simple until you realise this means actually *enforcing* it on systems where half your user base has local admin rights and the other half keeps shortcuts to "definitely-safe" applications on their Desktop. Yes, the carve-out for OS temp folders and browser caches is technically necessary for functionality; no, this will not stop the determined from putting their dodgy installer in AppData and calling it a day. The fact this made it to ML2 suggests someone optimistic believes organisations will actually configure AppLocker or equivalent without immediately exempting C:\\ after the first complaint.

annotations.ai_view: Multi‑factor authentication used for human users of online services must be phishing‑resistant. This means using factors that cannot be easily intercepted or replayed.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Phishing‑resistant MFA is now mandatory for online services — so you can finally stop accepting SMS codes and start buying hardware tokens. The budget request writes itself.

annotations.ai_view: Your online customer services must offer a multi-factor authentication option that cannot be defeated by phishing attacks—such as hardware security keys or biometric authentication—rather than methods that users can be tricked into providing (like one-time codes sent via SMS). This prevents attackers from accessing customer accounts even if they successfully deceive users into revealing passwords or intercepting standard authentication codes. Implementing phishing-resistant methods significantly reduces the risk of credential compromise and protects both your customers and your organisation from account takeover.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Your online customer service must offer phishing-resistant MFA—think passwordless or hardware keys—because users will absolutely click that link in the email that looks almost like your domain. Yes, SMS OTP technically isn't phishing-resistant, and yes, every organisation tells you they'll implement this and then quietly deploys Duo SMS anyway. The fact that this landed at ML2 suggests someone finally noticed that "something you have" stops working when the thing is a SIM card in a attacker's pocket.

annotations.ai_view: Your organisation must ensure that when customers log into your online services, the multi-factor authentication method used is resistant to phishing attacks. This means avoiding methods like SMS codes or email links that attackers can intercept or trick users into revealing, and instead using technologies like hardware security keys or biometric verification that directly authenticate the user to your legitimate service. This protects customer accounts from being compromised through social engineering or credential theft, which is essential for maintaining trust in your online services and protecting sensitive customer data.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: So you need phishing-resistant MFA for your customer portal—meaning passwordless auth or cryptographic binding to the device, not SMS codes that your users will dutifully paste into whatever convincing fake login page they've been sent. Revolutionary concept, I know. The fact this required its own control statement in 2023 suggests we've collectively spent the last decade watching organisations deploy Okta and call it done, while their customers remain one convincing email away from becoming someone else's problem.

annotations.ai_view: Systems must be scanned at least monthly to detect any credentials stored in clear text. Regular scanning reduces the chance that passwords or keys are inadvertently left exposed in files or configuration.
annotations.ai_view_snarky: Run a monthly grep for “password=” and act surprised when you find the admin’s sticky note in a config file.

annotations.ai_view: Organisations must install security patches for online services within 48 hours when vendors classify them as critical or when active exploits are known to exist.
